title: LIPPS Learn — University-readiness QA
text:
Version audited: v1.7
Scope: Epidemiology Weeks 1–12; Health Communication Weeks 1–12; public Quarto lessons; Moodle GIFT banks; course and assessment pages.


The LIPPS Learn architecture is strong enough for a university pilot, but the two courses are not yet ready to be sold as validated, stand-alone high-stakes courseware.
The strongest elements are the course sequence, applied public-health framing, clear weekly learning cycle, causal/interpretive restraint in Epidemiology, and the unusually strong treatment of risk communication, community engagement, infodemics, ethics and equity in Health Communication.
The main weakness is assessment validity. The existing Moodle banks are large, but item count should not be mistaken for assessment quality. Many Health Communication items are three paraphrased recognition questions built around the same definition; many Epidemiology items are repeated numerical variants of the same calculation template. These are useful practice generators, but a university-facing mastery bank must contain a much larger proportion of genuinely new scenarios, interpretation problems and decision questions.
A second weakness is constructive alignment. Weekly objective quizzes alone cannot adequately assess skills such as audience analysis, counselling, message design, community engagement, campaign planning, outbreak reasoning or critical appraisal. Both courses need authentic assessed products alongside quizzes.

The sequence from epidemiological thinking → frequency → association → description → study design → bias/causal reasoning → diagnostic testing → surveillance/outbreak → critical appraisal is coherent.
Weeks 1–3 are particularly rich and explanatory.
The course distinguishes what the attached CDC source supports from later LIPPS extensions.
Week 9 correctly separates confounding, mediation, collider bias and effect modification.
Week 10 avoids the common error of treating sensitivity, specificity and predictive value as interchangeable.
Week 12 gives the course an appropriate interpretive endpoint rather than ending with formula recall.





Assessment repetition: large blocks of parameterised items test the same operation repeatedly. Keep some as practice, but mastery banks should sample different reasoning steps.
Infectious-disease foundations: natural history, agent–host–environment reasoning and chain-of-infection concepts are underrepresented for a broad introductory epidemiology course. Add them as a concise supplement or embed them in Week 11.
Standardisation: age adjustment is introduced but not practised deeply. A short applied exercise would improve population-comparison competence.
Sampling: Week 5 introduces sampling logic, but probability sampling, cluster effects and weighting should link more explicitly to the Methods library.
Authentic outputs: add a short study-design critique, outbreak-analysis exercise and final critical-appraisal memo.
Assessment timing: current timings must remain pilot values until actual response-time data are available.





The course does not reduce communication to posters and media products; it treats communication as a decision and implementation process.
Behavioural theory is linked to diagnosis rather than added decoratively after campaign design.
Health literacy, culture, interpersonal communication and community engagement appear before channels and media strategy.
Risk/crisis communication and infodemic management are given their own substantial weeks.
Ethics, equity, privacy, AI and manipulation are integrated rather than treated as footnotes.
The LIPPS SIGNAL framework creates a useful capstone planning structure.





Depth: most weeks are around 1,000–1,300 words. For stand-alone digital courseware, add deeper explanations, comparative tables, worked communication products and assigned readings.
Question bank redesign: the largest current weakness. Many items repeat the same definition in three forms (definition → context label → term recognition). These should be reclassified as practice flash questions, not mastery assessment.
Performance assessment: health communication competence cannot be established using MCQs alone. Students should design, pre-test, revise and evaluate actual communication products.
Theory week overload: Week 2 covers HBM, TPB, Social Cognitive Theory, social-ecological thinking, COM-B and diffusion. Retain the overview, but add a comparison matrix and make students justify theory selection in a case.
Clinical communication: Week 4 needs an assessed teach-back or counselling transcript/role-play task.
Community engagement: Week 5 should assess stakeholder mapping, listening and feedback-loop design.
Media strategy: Week 7 should include a channel-mix budget or reach/frequency trade-off exercise.
Digital communication: Week 8 should distinguish platform engagement metrics from meaningful communication and health outcomes using a worked dashboard example.
Referencing: add a stable core-reading page and week-specific readings.




The Health Communication sequence is broadly consistent with current public-health communication practice. WHO’s communication framework emphasizes communications that are accessible, actionable, credible, relevant, timely and understandable. WHO’s 2024 RCCE competency framework emphasizes professional behavioural competencies for community-centred emergency programmes. CDC’s Clear Communication Index provides a research-based tool for assessing public communication materials, while the current CDC CERC manual remains a practical emergency-communication reference. These should be treated as core benchmarks, not as the only evidence base.
The attached CDC Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition remains a strong foundational source for the Epidemiology course, but it is an older introductory text. LIPPS should retain it as a foundation while clearly identifying modern extensions and updating applied examples and methodological guidance.






15% — weekly mastery quizzes: objective, randomised, mostly interpretation/application.
20% — applied measurement exercises: frequency, association, diagnostic testing and descriptive epidemiology.
20% — study-design critique: critique one published or simulated epidemiological study.
20% — field/outbreak analysis: line list, descriptive output, hypothesis and investigation plan.
25% — final critical-appraisal memo: interpret design, effect estimates, bias, precision, applicability and claim strength.





15% — weekly mastery quizzes: objective checks, but no longer dominated by term recognition.
20% — audience and behaviour diagnosis brief: define audience, determinant and theory-informed response.
20% — message design + pre-test assignment: draft, pre-test evidence, revision rationale.
15% — risk-communication simulation: first announcement, uncertainty statement, action message and update.
30% — campaign capstone: strategy, channel mix, community feedback, implementation indicators, outcome evaluation and ethics/equity review using LIPPS SIGNAL.

These weights are a proposed pilot blueprint and should be adapted to institutional regulations.




Do not delete the current banks. Reclassify them:

Foundation/practice pool: definition checks and repeated calculations.
Mastery pool: genuine scenarios, interpretation, comparison and decision-making.
Institutional assessment pool: separately reviewed, exposure-controlled items with documented blueprint coverage.

A sensible target for the next revision is 25–35 high-quality mastery items per week, not 50 superficially different items. Smaller, better banks are preferable to large templated banks.



LIPPS should not describe either course as high-stakes-ready until all of the following are complete:

second subject-matter-expert review;
explicit course assessment blueprint;
authentic assignments and rubrics;
mastery-bank rewrite;
accessibility review;
native Quarto render and browser/mobile testing;
Moodle import test on the actual hosted instance;
student pilot;
item analysis after pilot;
revision based on completion, difficulty, discrimination and response-time data; and
local curriculum/credit-hour mapping by the adopting institution.




Proceed to pilot. Do not market the current version as a finished high-stakes assessment product.
The curriculum is strong enough to justify a real university pilot. The next build priority is not more content categories; it is assessment quality, authentic student work, references/readings and pilot evidence.



Health Communication Week 1 has now been rebuilt against the recommended assessment standard: 30 distinct scenario-based items in Practice, Mastery and protected Institutional pools, plus an authentic Communication Diagnosis Brief and analytic rubric. Weeks 2–12 remain queued for the same overhaul.

title: About
text:
LIPPS takes inspiration from the Signor–Lipps effect in palaeontology: an incomplete observed record can misrepresent the timing or pattern of what actually occurred.
Research faces the same underlying challenge. Samples are partial. Measurements contain error. Records are missing. Models rely on assumptions. Associations can be misread. Context matters.
Evidence is never the whole story.
LIPPS exists to teach people to reason carefully from evidence rather than merely produce outputs.



Teach concepts before software.
Teach methods through real problems.
Make learners interpret rather than merely calculate.
Treat every result as evidence that requires scrutiny.




Add the founder biography, selected professional work, publications, teaching, CV, ORCID and GitHub links here before public launch.

title: Study Design
text:
Choosing a study design means matching a research question, estimand, source population, feasible data-collection process and threat-to-validity profile.



Cross-sectional studies
Case-control studies
Cohort studies
Randomised controlled trials
Quasi-experimental designs
Before-and-after studies
Interrupted time-series studies
Ecological studies
Diagnostic-accuracy studies
Implementation research designs
Operational research
Programme evaluation designs


What could fool us?
A sophisticated analysis cannot rescue a design that cannot answer the stated question. LIPPS therefore treats causal language—effect, impact, outcome, attributable to—as a design decision, not a writing preference.

title: Survey Analysis Strategies
text:
Survey analysis should begin by reconstructing how the observations entered the dataset. The sampling design determines the weights, dependence structure, variance estimation and often the appropriate modelling strategy.


Define the target population and estimand; reconstruct inclusion probabilities; estimate prevalence or means with uncertainty; then analyse associations using methods appropriate to the outcome and design.



Account for within-cluster correlation and the sampling design. Naïve analyses that treat all observations as independent usually understate uncertainty.



Retain the stratification information in estimation and variance calculation. Disproportionate allocation often requires weights.



Track selection probabilities at every stage: primary sampling units, secondary units, households and individuals. Distinguish household-level from person-level estimands.



Clarify whether facilities were sampled or assessed as a census, distinguish facility-level from service- or patient-level denominators, document tracer-indicator construction, and avoid treating composite readiness scores as inherently comparable without validating the scoring model.



Define constructs before scoring them. Avoid arbitrary categorisation of knowledge or attitude scores unless a defensible threshold exists. Assess item behaviour and measurement properties where appropriate.



Document inaccessible areas, population-frame uncertainty, cluster selection, non-response and operational compromises. Avoid reporting precise sub-area rankings when the design was only powered for pooled estimation.

What could fool us?
Ignoring weights, clustering or stratification can produce estimates that look precise while representing the target population poorly—or confidence intervals that are far too narrow.

Interpretation and Reporting
Move from model output to defensible scientific statements. Separate statistical evidence from causal claims, programme implications and policy recommendations. Connect analyses to relevant reporting standards where appropriate.

The course progresses from foundations → theory → audience → interpersonal/community → message/channel → digital/emergency information environments → campaign evaluation → ethics/capstone.
Every week opens with a realistic problem, teaches concepts, applies them to an integrated scenario, and ends with practice plus a timed mastery specification.
The banks are deliberately larger than the quiz delivered to any student, but the current bank is not yet predominantly scenario-oriented. A substantial proportion consists of repeated concept-recognition templates. These are suitable for practice and retrieval but should not dominate mastery or formal assessment.
Timing is a pilot parameter, not an accessibility restriction. Approved accommodations must remain available.
Copy/paste is not treated as the primary integrity control. Random banks, scenario-based reasoning, shuffled options and short calibrated windows are the main design choices.
Health Communication is not reduced to mass messaging: service barriers, trust, power, community engagement, ethics, accessibility and evaluation are embedded throughout.
Risk communication, RCCE and infodemic management are aligned with current WHO framing.
The final week integrates the course through LIPPS SIGNAL: Situation; Intended audience and insight; Goal; Narrative and needed action; Access; Listen and learn.




The Moodle banks are candidate teaching and pilot-assessment items, not yet psychometrically validated high-stakes exam banks. After student use, analyse item difficulty, discrimination, distractor performance, response times and differential performance before institutional high-stakes deployment.



A deeper audit found that raw item count overstated assessment maturity. Many concepts were represented by three close paraphrases of the same recognition task. Before institutional assessment use, split the bank into foundation/practice, mastery and protected assessment pools and rewrite the latter two toward novel application scenarios. See QA-UNIVERSITY-READINESS.md.



Week 1 is now the benchmark for future bank revision. The previous 48-item recognition-heavy bank was replaced with 30 distinct scenario-based questions mapped to learning outcomes and cognitive demand. It is explicitly separated into Practice, Mastery and protected Institutional pools.
The redesign also adds an 800–1,000 word Communication Diagnosis Brief with a 20-mark analytic rubric. This ensures that Week 1 assesses more than rapid option recognition.
Remaining Weeks 2–12 retain their v1.8 candidate banks and should be rewritten progressively against the Week 1 standard before high-stakes institutional deployment.

text:
LIPPS uses objective quizzes for efficient weekly retrieval and application checks, but a university course should assess more than recognition under time pressure. These pilot blueprints combine quizzes with authentic public-health work.

title: Epidemiology
text:
The 12-week course


01


Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking


Population thinking, distributions, determinants, comparison groups and the difference between a clinical question and an epidemiological question.

Applied task: Turn a vague district health concern into an answerable epidemiological question.Start Week 1 →



02


Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health


Counts, proportions, prevalence, incidence, mortality and the importance of the denominator.

Applied task: Decide which measure correctly describes three different service and disease scenarios.Start Week 2 →



03


Measures of Association and Effect


Risk ratios, odds ratios, prevalence ratios, risk differences and interpretation of relative versus absolute effects.

Applied task: Choose the most informative effect measure for contrasting public-health questions.Start Week 3 →



04


Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time


Case definition, epidemic curves, spot maps, stratification, pattern recognition and hypothesis generation.

Applied task: Describe an outbreak dataset and identify the next question the pattern raises.Start Week 4 →



05


Cross-sectional Studies


Prevalence, simultaneous measurement, temporality, sampling and appropriate causal restraint.

Applied task: Critique a cross-sectional study that uses causal language.Start Week 5 →



06


Case-Control Studies


Cases, controls, source populations, exposure ascertainment, odds ratios and selection challenges.

Applied task: Select an appropriate control group for an outbreak investigation.Start Week 6 →



07


Cohort Studies


Follow-up, risk, rates, losses to follow-up, person-time and prospective versus retrospective cohorts.

Applied task: Interpret incidence and relative risk from a cohort table.Start Week 7 →



08


Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs


Randomisation, allocation, comparison groups, before-after designs and when causal claims become stronger.

Applied task: Choose between a trial and feasible quasi-experimental alternatives for a service intervention.Start Week 8 →



09


Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification


Selection bias, information bias, confounding, interaction and why adjustment can sometimes make an analysis worse.

Applied task: Separate a confounder, mediator and effect modifier in a simple causal scenario.Start Week 9 →



10


Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation


Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, thresholds, serial testing and the role of prevalence.

Applied task: Explain why the same test can have a different positive predictive value in two populations.Start Week 10 →



11


Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology


Surveillance attributes, signals, verification, line lists, descriptive analysis and outbreak investigation logic.

Applied task: Move from an unusual surveillance signal to a defensible initial investigation plan.Start Week 11 →



12


Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal


Association, causality, effect, impact, precision, validity, applicability and disciplined interpretation of evidence.

Applied task: Rewrite an overstated conclusion so it matches the design and results.Start Week 12 →

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 05





Foundation Cross-sectional Prevalence Survey reasoning

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text: Foundation Cross-sectional Prevalence Survey reasoning

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
This week in one sentence
Use cross-sectional designs to estimate prevalence and describe populations while recognising the limits created by simultaneous measurement of exposure and outcome.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
Cross-sectional Studies
section: ORIENT · The survey found an association. What happened first?
text:
ORIENT · The survey found an association. What happened first?
A university surveys 2,000 students during one semester. Current depressive symptoms and current heavy social-media use are measured in the same questionnaire. Heavy users have more depressive symptoms.
What can the study establish?
It can estimate the prevalence of each measured state and quantify their association at the time of measurement. But unless the timing of exposure and outcome is reconstructed with credible additional information, the design does not tell us whether heavy social-media use preceded depressive symptoms, whether symptoms changed social-media use, or whether another factor influenced both.
That is the central discipline of cross-sectional interpretation: a strong snapshot is still a snapshot.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 1 · What makes a study cross-sectional?
text:
LEARN 1 · What makes a study cross-sectional?
The defining feature is not simply “a questionnaire.” It is the measurement structure: a sample is observed at a point or short period, and exposure and outcome status are measured at essentially the same time.
Cross-sectional studies can use interviews, records, examinations, laboratory tests or several sources together. A health-facility readiness assessment can also be cross-sectional even though the unit is a facility rather than a person.
The attached CDC source characterises cross-sectional studies as simultaneous measurement of exposures and health outcomes and notes their value for documenting prevalence.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 2 · The natural frequency measure is prevalence
text:
LEARN 2 · The natural frequency measure is prevalence
If a survey asks who currently has hypertension, the numerator includes people whose hypertension began yesterday and people who have lived with it for years.
That is prevalence:
\[
P = \frac{\text{existing cases at the specified time}}{\text{population observed at that time}}
\]
A cross-sectional study generally cannot estimate the probability of developing hypertension during a prior period unless incidence information was separately and reliably reconstructed.
This distinction matters because prevalence reflects both incidence and duration. A condition can have high prevalence because many new cases occur, because people live with it for a long time, or both.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 3 · Population language must be precise
text:
LEARN 3 · Population language must be precise
A survey can be technically competent and still answer the wrong population question.
Target population — the population about which you ultimately want to make an inference.
Study population — the population from which study participants can actually be drawn under the protocol.
Sampling frame — the operational list or mechanism used to select units.
Sampling unit — the unit selected at a given sampling stage.
Observation unit — the unit on which measurements are ultimately recorded.
Example: a household survey may target adults in a district, select villages first, households second, and one adult within each household. The village and household are sampling units at different stages; the adult is the observation unit.
If the sampling frame excludes remote settlements, the “district estimate” may not represent the whole district even when the sample size is large.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 4 · A sample becomes an estimate only through its design
text:
LEARN 4 · A sample becomes an estimate only through its design
Simple random sampling is conceptually straightforward because each sampled unit has a known selection probability. Many public-health surveys, however, use stratified, cluster or multistage designs.
Those design features can affect:

weights, because some units have different selection probabilities;
standard errors, because people sampled within the same cluster may be correlated;
precision, because stratification and clustering change the information structure; and
population estimates, when weighted and unweighted distributions differ.


LIPPS extension
The attached CDC chapter defines cross-sectional surveys but does not provide a full complex-survey analysis framework. Survey weights, clustering and stratification are included here because they are essential for analysing modern population surveys correctly.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 5 · Non-response is not just a smaller sample
text:
LEARN 5 · Non-response is not just a smaller sample
Suppose 80% of sampled adults participate. The main question is not merely whether 20% were lost; it is whether non-participants differ systematically from participants on variables related to the outcome.
If people with severe illness are less able to participate, prevalence may be underestimated. If people particularly interested in the topic are more likely to respond, prevalence may be overestimated.
A large final sample does not automatically remove non-response bias. Bias is about systematic difference, not simply sample size.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
LEARN 6 · Comparing prevalence
Two groups can be compared using absolute or relative measures.
If hypertension prevalence is 30% in Group A and 20% in Group B:
Prevalence difference
\[
PD = 0.30 - 0.20 = 0.10
\]
There are 10 additional prevalent cases per 100 people in Group A.
Prevalence ratio
\[
PR = 0.30 / 0.20 = 1.50
\]
Prevalence in Group A is 1.5 times that in Group B.

LIPPS extension
Prevalence ratio and prevalence difference are included as modern cross-sectional effect measures. They are not explicitly developed in the attached CDC cross-sectional section.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 7 · Why the odds ratio can be awkward for common outcomes
text:
LEARN 7 · Why the odds ratio can be awkward for common outcomes
An odds ratio can be calculated from cross-sectional binary data, and logistic regression often produces one naturally. But odds are not risks or prevalences.
When an outcome is common, an odds ratio can be numerically much farther from 1 than the corresponding prevalence ratio. That does not make logistic regression invalid; it means the estimand and wording must be correct.
If the scientific question is about relative prevalence, a prevalence ratio may be easier to communicate. If the model estimates odds, report odds honestly.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 8 · Temporality: the fundamental causal limitation
text:
LEARN 8 · Temporality: the fundamental causal limitation
For many causal questions, the exposure must precede the outcome.
Cross-sectional simultaneous measurement often leaves that order uncertain. This produces several possibilities:

exposure → outcome;
outcome → exposure (reverse causation);
a third factor → both; or
measurement artifacts producing the association.

A survey showing that people with chronic back pain exercise less cannot by itself establish whether low exercise increased pain risk or pain reduced exercise.
Additional temporal questions can help, but retrospective recall introduces its own error. The design should still be described honestly.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
LEARN 9 · Prevalence can select survivors
Because prevalence includes existing cases, it tends to over-represent conditions or cases of longer duration.
Imagine two diseases with the same incidence. Disease A resolves in days; Disease B persists for years. A cross-sectional survey is much more likely to capture Disease B.
This is sometimes called length or prevalence-incidence bias in broader epidemiological literature.

LIPPS extension
The attached text explains that prevalence depends on incidence and duration. The explicit survival-selection interpretation is developed here as an instructional extension.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 10 · Cross-sectional does not mean weak
text:
LEARN 10 · Cross-sectional does not mean weak
“Cannot establish temporal sequence well” is not the same as “useless.”
Cross-sectional designs are excellent for questions such as:

What proportion of health facilities currently have oxygen?
What is the prevalence of hypertension among adults?
What proportion of adolescents report a behaviour?
How does current coverage vary by district?
Which groups currently have the greatest burden?

The strength of a design is judged against the question it was designed to answer. A cross-sectional survey can be the ideal design for prevalence and service-readiness questions.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional district household survey samples 1,800 adults using 30 villages as first-stage clusters. Current hypertension is measured using a standard protocol. Current physical activity, medication use, age, sex and residence are also recorded.
Hypertension prevalence is 28%. Prevalence is 36% among adults reporting low physical activity and 22% among those reporting higher activity.
Before making a causal claim:

Identify the target population, likely sampling units and observation unit.
State the primary frequency measure.
Calculate the crude prevalence ratio and prevalence difference.
Explain why the crude association does not establish that low physical activity caused hypertension.
List at least three plausible confounding or reverse-causation explanations.
Explain why cluster sampling may affect the confidence interval.
State what weighting information you would need to estimate district-level prevalence appropriately.
Rewrite this statement: “Low physical activity increased hypertension by 64% in the district.”

A defensible version might say that low activity was associated with higher hypertension prevalence, while causal direction requires stronger temporal and confounding evidence.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why is prevalence the natural frequency measure in a typical cross-sectional survey?
Can a cross-sectional study ever collect historical exposure information? If it does, does that automatically make the design longitudinal?
What is the difference between the target population and the study population?
Why can 5,000 poorly selected respondents produce a worse population estimate than 1,000 probability-sampled respondents?
If prevalence is 40% versus 20%, what are the prevalence ratio and prevalence difference?
Why might a chronic disease be easier to capture in a cross-sectional survey than a rapidly fatal disease?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
DEMONSTRATE · Week 5 mastery quiz
Pilot Mastery Quiz: 15 objective questions sampled from a Week 5 bank of 50 items.
Initial time limit: 11 minutes.
Question style: design recognition, prevalence calculations, population/sampling logic, PR/PD interpretation, temporality and causal-language correction.
Practice mode: untimed with feedback.
Formal mode: randomised bank, delayed detailed feedback and approved accommodation overrides.

Assessment principle
The quiz is designed so that a prepared learner can read, reason and answer efficiently. Timing is a learning-and-assessment parameter to be calibrated from real response-time data, not a substitute for good question design.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
Source foundation and LIPPS extensions
Primary source foundation: the attached CDC text’s definition and use of cross-sectional studies, simultaneous measurement, prevalence and the limitation of temporal/causal interpretation.
LIPPS extensions: target/study-population distinctions, complex-survey weighting and clustering, prevalence ratio/difference, non-response reasoning and prevalence-incidence selection are added to make the course suitable for applied modern survey analysis.
Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. October 2006; updated May 2012.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 02





Epidemiology becomes useful when counts are placed in the population and time from which they arose. This week develops the language used to describe disease occurrence: ratios, proportions, rates, incidence, prevalence, mortality and selected population-health measures.
Foundation Disease frequency Denominators Applied calculations

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
Epidemiology becomes useful when counts are placed in the population and time from which they arose. This week develops the language used to describe disease occurrence: ratios, proportions, rates, incidence, prevalence, mortality and selected population-health measures.
Foundation Disease frequency Denominators Applied calculations

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
This week in one sentence
Choose the numerator, choose the correct population and time denominator, calculate the measure, and interpret exactly what that measure describes.

The LIPPS lens
Most errors in introductory epidemiology are not arithmetic errors. They are denominator errors, population errors, time errors or interpretation errors. A perfectly calculated fraction can still answer the wrong question.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: ORIENT · Which district has more malaria?
text:
ORIENT · Which district has more malaria?
Consider this fictional teaching scenario.



District
New malaria cases in June
Population




A
900
450,000


B
600
120,000



District A has the larger count.
But if the question is, “Where was new malaria occurrence higher relative to population size?”, the count alone cannot answer it.
For a simplified population comparison:

District A: 900 / 450,000 = 2.0 per 1,000
District B: 600 / 120,000 = 5.0 per 1,000

So District A has more reported new cases, while District B has the higher occurrence relative to its population.

Two answers can both be correct
Where is the larger workload? Possibly District A.
Where is disease occurrence higher relative to population size? District B.
The measure must match the decision.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 1 · Count, ratio, proportion and rate are not interchangeable
text:
LEARN 1 · Count, ratio, proportion and rate are not interchangeable

Count
A count is simply the number of events observed: 120 measles cases, 18 maternal deaths, 450 positive tests.
Counts matter for planning beds, medicines, vaccines, staff and laboratory supplies. But counts alone usually do not permit fair comparisons between populations of different sizes.


Ratio
A ratio compares one quantity with another. The numerator does not have to be part of the denominator.
For example, if a facility has 30 nurses and 10 clinical officers, the nurse-to-clinical-officer ratio is 3:1.


Proportion
A proportion is a ratio in which the numerator is included within the denominator.
If 240 of 800 surveyed adults have hypertension:
240 / 800 = 0.30 = 30%.
All 240 people in the numerator are part of the 800 people in the denominator.


Rate
The attached CDC text defines a rate as a measure of how frequently an event occurs in a defined population over a specified period. The term rate is also used loosely in epidemiology for some measures that are mathematically proportions, such as attack rate and case-fatality rate.

Do not argue from the label alone. Inspect the fraction.
Ask whether the numerator is contained within the denominator, whether time is incorporated, and what population the denominator represents.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 2 · The denominator is part of the scientific question
text:
LEARN 2 · The denominator is part of the scientific question
A denominator should represent the population capable of contributing to the numerator.
If the numerator is new ovarian cancer cases, a denominator including people who cannot develop ovarian cancer would not represent the true population at risk. The CDC lesson uses this kind of example to show that denominators are conceptual decisions, not merely numbers taken from a census.
Before calculating any epidemiological measure, ask:

Who could have become a case?
Who was actually under observation?
At what time were they at risk?
Does the denominator correspond to the numerator?
Is this denominator complete and comparable across groups?


Denominator mismatch
Suppose a hospital reports 300 positive malaria tests among 1,000 people tested. That gives test positivity of 30% among those tested.
It does not automatically give malaria prevalence in the district, because the denominator is people tested, not the district population or a representative sample of it.
The arithmetic may be flawless while the epidemiological interpretation is wrong.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 3 · Incidence proportion: the probability of becoming a case
text:
LEARN 3 · Incidence proportion: the probability of becoming a case
Incidence concerns new events.
The attached CDC lesson distinguishes two common incidence measures: incidence proportion and incidence rate.

Incidence proportion
Incidence proportion is the proportion of an initially disease-free population that develops the health event during a specified period.
[ = ]
It may also be called risk, cumulative incidence, or—particularly during an outbreak—attack rate.


Fictional example
A cohort begins with 2,000 adults without hypertension. During one year, 140 develop hypertension.
[ 140 / 2,000 = 0.07 = 7% ]
Interpretation:

Seven percent of the initially hypertension-free cohort developed hypertension during the one-year period.

Notice what the measure requires:

new cases;
an initially disease-free population;
a defined period;
a denominator representing people who could become new cases.



What incidence proportion is NOT
It is not the proportion who have hypertension at the end of the year. Some participants may already have had hypertension before follow-up, and those belong in a prevalence calculation rather than the new-case numerator.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 4 · Attack rates and secondary attack rates
text:
LEARN 4 · Attack rates and secondary attack rates
During outbreaks, attack rate is commonly used as another name for incidence proportion.

Overall attack rate
[ ]


Exposure-specific attack rate
Suppose 80 wedding guests ate chicken and 32 became ill.
[ 32/80 = 40% ]
The food-specific attack rate among chicken eaters is 40%.
But this still does not tell us whether chicken was associated with illness. We also need the attack rate among people who did not eat chicken. The comparison itself belongs in Week 3.


Secondary attack rate
The CDC lesson describes secondary attack rate as useful for examining transmission among contacts of primary cases in households or other closed populations.
A common form is:
[ = ]
Primary cases are generally excluded from the contact denominator because they are not at risk of becoming secondary cases from themselves.


Fictional example
Twelve primary cases occur in 12 households containing 58 people in total. During the relevant secondary transmission period, 9 additional household members develop the disease.
Contacts at risk = 58 − 12 = 46.
[ 9/46 = 19.6% ]
The secondary attack rate is approximately 19.6%.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 5 · Incidence rate: when follow-up time differs
text:
LEARN 5 · Incidence rate: when follow-up time differs
Incidence proportion treats the starting population as the denominator. That works best when the cohort is reasonably closed and the observation period is clearly defined.
But people often contribute different amounts of follow-up. They enrol late, migrate, die, are lost to follow-up, or develop the outcome at different times.

Person-time solves a different denominator problem
The attached CDC text defines incidence rate (person-time rate) using:
[ = ]
One person followed disease-free for two years contributes 2 person-years. Ten people each followed for six months contribute 5 person-years in total.


Fictional example
A cohort contributes 1,850 person-years of disease-free observation and 37 participants develop tuberculosis.
[ 37 / 1,850 = 0.020 ]
or 20 new TB cases per 1,000 person-years.
This means disease occurred at a rate of 20 new cases for every 1,000 person-years of observed time at risk.


Risk and rate are not the same quantity
Incidence proportion answers approximately: What proportion of this initially at-risk population became cases during this period?
Incidence rate answers approximately: How quickly are new cases occurring in the accumulated time at risk?
Do not attach a percent sign to a person-time rate.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 6 · Prevalence: who has the condition?
text:
LEARN 6 · Prevalence: who has the condition?
Prevalence includes existing cases, not only new ones.

Point prevalence
[ = ]
If 360 of 1,200 adults surveyed today meet the definition of hypertension:
[ 360/1,200 = 30% ]
The point prevalence is 30%.


Period prevalence
Period prevalence includes people who had the condition at any time during a specified interval, whether it was already present when the interval began or developed during it.


Incidence versus prevalence
The source makes the distinction through the numerator:
Incidence numerator → new cases only
Prevalence numerator → all cases present in the relevant period
This is one of the most important distinctions in introductory epidemiology.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 7 · Why high prevalence does not necessarily mean high incidence
text:
LEARN 7 · Why high prevalence does not necessarily mean high incidence
Prevalence is influenced by both new occurrence and duration.
A condition may have high prevalence because:

many new cases are developing;
people remain affected for a long time;
survival has improved without cure; or
several of these processes occur together.

A condition may have low prevalence because:

few new cases occur;
recovery is rapid; or
mortality is rapid.


Two diseases, same incidence, different prevalence
Imagine two conditions generate the same number of new cases each year.
Condition A usually resolves in 5 days.
Condition B commonly persists for 20 years.
A cross-sectional survey is much more likely to find a larger pool of existing Condition B cases.

LIPPS warning
Do not infer the speed of disease occurrence from prevalence alone. Prevalence is a snapshot of the pool of existing disease; that pool is filled by incidence and emptied by recovery, death or other exits.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 8 · Mortality measures: death needs a denominator too
text:
LEARN 8 · Mortality measures: death needs a denominator too
A population mortality rate relates deaths occurring during a period to the population in which those deaths occurred.

Crude mortality rate
All deaths in the population, from all causes, divided by the relevant population.


Cause-specific mortality rate
Deaths from one specified cause divided by the population in which those deaths occurred.


Age-, sex- or other stratum-specific mortality rate
Both numerator and denominator are restricted to the same subgroup.
For example:
[ ]
is an age- and cause-specific mortality measure.


Why specificity matters
If the numerator contains deaths among women aged 15–49, but the denominator is the entire district population, the numerator and denominator do not describe the same population.
Always ask:

Who is represented in the numerator, and is the denominator the population from which those deaths could arise?

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 9 · Crude rates can be distorted by population structure
text:
LEARN 9 · Crude rates can be distorted by population structure
The CDC text uses the contrast between Alaska and Florida to demonstrate an important idea: one population can have a higher crude mortality rate simply because it contains more older people.
When mortality strongly varies with age, comparing crude mortality between populations with different age structures can be misleading.

Two approaches
Stratification: compare age-specific rates within comparable age groups.
Standardisation/adjustment: calculate a summary rate that removes the effect of different age distributions.
Detailed age standardisation is beyond the core calculations for this week, but the reasoning matters now:

A crude difference may partly represent population composition rather than a difference in underlying age-specific mortality.

This same principle will return later when we discuss confounding.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 10 · Case fatality is not population mortality
text:
LEARN 10 · Case fatality is not population mortality

Case-fatality measure
The CDC lesson defines case fatality as the proportion of people with a particular condition who die from that condition.
[ = ]
It is mainly a measure of severity among identified cases, not the frequency of death in the entire population.
If 8 of 200 confirmed cases die:
[ 8/200 = 4% ]
Case fatality = 4%.


Proportionate mortality
Proportionate mortality asks what share of all deaths is due to a particular cause.
[ ]
If 50 of 500 recorded deaths were from road traffic injuries, proportionate mortality due to road traffic injuries is 10%.
This does not mean 10% of the population died from road traffic injuries. The denominator contains deaths, not people in the population.


Three different questions
Population mortality: How often are people in the population dying?
Case fatality: Among people with the disease, what proportion die from it?
Proportionate mortality: Among all deaths, what share is due to this cause?

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 11 · Maternal, neonatal and infant mortality measures
text:
LEARN 11 · Maternal, neonatal and infant mortality measures
The attached CDC lesson presents several mortality measures that use live births rather than a mid-period population as the denominator.

Neonatal mortality
Deaths among infants younger than 28 days during a period divided by live births during that period, commonly expressed per 1,000 live births.


Postneonatal mortality
Deaths from 28 days to under one year divided by live births, commonly expressed per 1,000 live births.


Infant mortality
Deaths before one year of age divided by live births in the same period, commonly expressed per 1,000 live births.
The source explicitly notes an important terminology point: the traditional infant mortality rate is not a pure population rate in the strict mathematical sense because its denominator is live births rather than the mid-year population of infants.


Maternal mortality terminology in the source
The CDC text labels the measure maternal mortality rate, but also explicitly says it is really a ratio, because pregnancy-related maternal deaths are divided by live births rather than by the population of women at risk.
That observation is a useful reminder:

The conventional name of an indicator does not remove the need to understand its numerator and denominator.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
LEARN 12 · Natality measures
The CDC lesson also introduces population-based measures of birth.

Crude birth rate
[ ,000 ]


Crude fertility rate
[ ,000 ]


Low-birth-weight ratio
[ ]
The important lesson is not to memorise a table of indicators. It is to inspect how the denominator changes the question.
A crude birth rate describes births relative to the whole population. A fertility rate narrows the denominator to a population more directly related to childbearing. The low-birth-weight measure asks what proportion of births meet a defined birth-weight criterion.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: GO DEEPER · Years of potential life lost
text:
GO DEEPER · Years of potential life lost
The CDC lesson includes years of potential life lost (YPLL) as a way to describe premature mortality. Rather than treating every death as contributing equally, YPLL gives more weight to deaths occurring earlier than a selected endpoint.
Conceptually:
[ = - ]
for deaths occurring before the endpoint.
This can highlight causes that produce death at younger ages even when they are not the leading causes by total death count.
YPLL is presented here as an extension concept rather than a core Week 2 mastery calculation. The source itself notes that the choice of endpoint embeds a value judgement because earlier deaths contribute more potential years lost.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: APPLY · Choose the measure before calculating
text:
APPLY · Choose the measure before calculating
For each scenario, identify the most appropriate measure and explain the denominator.

Scenario A · New hypertension diagnoses
A closed cohort of 1,500 adults without hypertension is followed for 12 months. Ninety develop hypertension.
Best measure: Incidence proportion.
Denominator: The 1,500 adults at risk at the start.


Scenario B · Different follow-up time
A TB cohort experiences 22 new recurrences during 940 person-years of post-treatment observation.
Best measure: Incidence rate.
Denominator: 940 person-years at risk.


Scenario C · Burden today
A representative district survey finds 420 people with diabetes among 3,000 adults examined during the survey.
Best measure: Point prevalence, if status refers to the survey point/period as defined.
Denominator: The examined target population represented by the survey, subject to the survey design and weighting.


Scenario D · Severity among cases
An outbreak produces 160 confirmed cases and 12 of those people die from the disease.
Best measure: Case fatality.
Denominator: The 160 cases.


Scenario E · Cause among deaths
A district records 1,100 deaths, of which 220 are attributed to malaria.
Best measure: Proportionate mortality due to malaria.
Denominator: All 1,100 deaths.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: WORKED EXAMPLE · One dataset, four different measures
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · One dataset, four different measures
Consider a fictional boarding-school outbreak.
At the beginning of the week there are 500 students, none currently ill. During the week 75 students become ill. The 75 cases occur across several dormitories. In the dormitories of the first 20 cases, there are 80 additional susceptible roommates, and 24 of those roommates develop illness during the relevant secondary period. At the end of Friday, 30 students are still ill.

1. Weekly incidence proportion / attack rate
[ 75/500 = 15% ]
Interpretation: 15% of students at risk at the beginning became cases during the week.


2. Secondary attack rate among susceptible roommates
[ 24/80 = 30% ]
Interpretation: 30% of the defined susceptible contacts developed illness during the secondary-risk period.


3. Point prevalence on Friday
[ 30/500 = 6% ]
Interpretation: 6% of the school population was ill at the specified Friday assessment point, assuming the denominator remains appropriate.


4. Why attack rate and Friday prevalence differ
The attack rate counts new cases accumulated during the week. Friday point prevalence counts people still ill at one point in time. Students who became ill and recovered before Friday contribute to incidence but not Friday point prevalence.

Same population. Same outbreak. Different questions. Different numerators. Different measures.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

1. Which statement BEST distinguishes a proportion from a general ratio?
A. A proportion must include time in the denominator.
B. In a proportion, the numerator is included in the denominator.
C. A proportion must be expressed per 100,000.
D. A proportion can never describe disease.
Answer: B. A proportion describes a part relative to the whole containing that part.


2. A district reports 500 TB cases. What additional information is MOST important for comparing TB occurrence with another district?
A. The font used in the report.
B. The corresponding population denominator, case definition and time period.
C. The number of pages in the report.
D. Whether the analyst used R or Stata.
Answer: B. A count requires population and measurement context before fair comparison.


3. Which numerator belongs in an incidence proportion?
A. All existing cases.
B. New cases occurring during the specified period.
C. All positive tests ever recorded.
D. Deaths from all causes.
Answer: B. Incidence concerns new occurrence.


4. Twenty new cases occur during 2,000 person-years. Which measure is being calculated?
A. Point prevalence.
B. Period prevalence.
C. Incidence rate.
D. Proportionate mortality.
Answer: C. Person-time in the denominator identifies an incidence rate.


5. Which statement about prevalence is correct?
A. It contains new cases only.
B. It is unaffected by disease duration.
C. It includes existing cases in the defined population and time.
D. It always estimates causal risk.
Answer: C. Prevalence describes the pool of existing disease or attributes.


6. A chronic condition has low incidence but very long duration. What could happen to prevalence?
A. It must be zero.
B. It may still be high.
C. It becomes an incidence rate.
D. Duration cannot affect prevalence.
Answer: B. Long duration can maintain a large pool of existing cases.


7. Eight deaths occur among 200 identified cases. What measure is 8/200 × 100?
A. Cause-specific mortality rate.
B. Case fatality.
C. Incidence rate.
D. Crude birth rate.
Answer: B. The denominator is cases, so the measure describes severity among cases.


8. Fifty road-traffic deaths occur among 500 deaths from all causes. What does 50/500 × 100 describe?
A. Risk of dying in the population.
B. Proportionate mortality.
C. Incidence proportion.
D. Case fatality.
Answer: B. It describes the share of deaths attributable to that cause.


9. Why might crude mortality be higher in one district even if its age-specific mortality is not consistently higher?
A. The district may have an older population.
B. A crude rate automatically adjusts for age.
C. Mortality is unrelated to age.
D. The denominator is always deaths.
Answer: A. Population age structure can distort crude comparisons.


10. Which statement BEST reflects the main Week 2 lesson?
A. Memorise every multiplier.
B. Always express health measures as percentages.
C. Match the numerator, denominator, population and time to the question before calculating.
D. Counts should never be reported.
Answer: C. Correct calculation begins with correct measurement logic.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
SUMMARY · The Week 2 decision tree
When you need to describe frequency, ask:
Do I only need the number of events? → Count.
Am I comparing two quantities? → Ratio.
Is the numerator part of the denominator? → Proportion.
Am I measuring new occurrence among an initially at-risk population? → Incidence proportion / risk.
Does follow-up time differ across people? → Incidence rate / person-time.
Am I measuring all existing cases at a point or during a period? → Prevalence.
Am I measuring deaths in a population? → Mortality rate.
Am I measuring deaths among cases? → Case fatality.
Am I asking what share of all deaths came from one cause? → Proportionate mortality.
Then ask one final LIPPS question:

Does this denominator actually represent the population and time about which I intend to make the claim?

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
What moves to Week 3
The attached CDC Lesson Three continues from frequency measures into risk ratios, rate ratios, odds ratios and measures of public-health impact. LIPPS deliberately separates these topics.
Week 2 asks:

How often is the outcome occurring?

Week 3 asks:

How different is occurrence between groups, and how should that difference be expressed?

This separation keeps measurement of frequency conceptually distinct from measurement of association and effect.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: Primary source used to build this lesson
text:
Primary source used to build this lesson
This LIPPS lesson is an original teaching adaptation of Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Lesson Three: Measures of Risk (updated May 2012).
The source material used here includes its treatment of ratios, proportions and rates; morbidity frequency measures; incidence proportion; attack rates; person-time incidence rates; point and period prevalence; mortality measures; age adjustment; case fatality; proportionate mortality; YPLL; and natality measures. Fictional Ugandan and school examples were created for LIPPS and are not claims about actual districts, facilities or outbreaks.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 07





Intermediate Cohort Incidence Follow-up

title: Cohort Studies
text: Intermediate Cohort Incidence Follow-up

title: Cohort Studies
text:
This week in one sentence
Use cohort designs to estimate incidence and compare outcome occurrence between exposure groups while accounting for follow-up, person-time and loss to observation.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Cohort Studies
Cohort Studies
text:
ORIENT · Exposure comes first
A cohort study starts with a group defined by exposure or another baseline characteristic and asks what happens afterwards.
Imagine 2,000 health workers without active tuberculosis at baseline. Half work in high-exposure clinical areas and half in lower-exposure settings. They are followed for two years and new tuberculosis diagnoses are recorded.
Because outcome-free people are observed over time, the design can estimate incidence, not merely prevalence.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 1 · The core structure
The attached CDC text describes cohort studies as observational designs in which participants are grouped by exposure and then followed to document disease occurrence.
Conceptually:
Exposed → outcome / no outcome
Unexposed → outcome / no outcome
The comparison group estimates what disease occurrence might have looked like without the exposure pattern of primary interest.
Unlike an experiment, the investigator does not assign exposure; the exposure occurs under natural or existing conditions.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 2 · Prospective and retrospective cohorts
In a prospective cohort, participants are enrolled before the outcome occurs and are followed forward.
In a retrospective cohort, both exposure and outcome may already have occurred when the study begins, but the logical sequence remains exposure → outcome. Existing records reconstruct the cohort and follow-up.
The attached CDC material emphasises this important point: retrospective does not mean case-control. A retrospective cohort still groups people by exposure and compares subsequent disease occurrence.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 3 · Cohorts estimate incidence directly
If all participants are outcome-free at baseline and follow-up is defined, you can calculate risk:
\[
Risk_E = \frac{\text{new cases among exposed}}{\text{exposed population at risk at baseline}}
\]
and similarly for the unexposed group.
You can then calculate:
\[
RR = Risk_E / Risk_U
\]
and:
\[
RD = Risk_E - Risk_U
\]
These have direct interpretations because the denominators arise from actual populations at risk rather than investigator-selected numbers of cases and controls.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 4 · A worked risk comparison
Suppose 80 of 800 exposed workers develop a condition, compared with 20 of 1,000 unexposed workers.
\[
Risk_E = 80/800 = 10\%
\]
\[
Risk_U = 20/1000 = 2\%
\]
\[
RR = 10\%/2\% = 5.0
\]
\[
RD = 10\%-2\% = 8\text{ percentage points}
\]
A careful interpretation is:

During the specified follow-up, exposed workers had five times the risk and eight additional cases per 100 workers compared with the unexposed group.

Whether that difference is causal depends on confounding, bias, measurement and the wider design.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 5 · Person-time when follow-up differs
Participants do not always contribute equal follow-up. Some enter late, migrate, die, withdraw or develop the outcome early.
Person-time accumulates the time each person remains under observation and at risk.
\[
Incidence\ rate = \frac{new\ cases}{total\ person-time\ at\ risk}
\]
The attached CDC text explains that person-time is useful precisely because it can accommodate different observation periods.
A rate ratio then compares person-time incidence rates between groups.

title: Cohort Studies
section: LEARN 6 · Censoring is not the same as failure
text:
LEARN 6 · Censoring is not the same as failure
A participant who leaves follow-up without developing the outcome does not necessarily become a case or a non-case for the whole intended period. Their observed disease-free time can still contribute information.
This is the idea behind censoring.

LIPPS extension
Formal survival-analysis methods are beyond this introductory week, but learners should understand that incomplete follow-up is handled through time-to-event methods rather than by pretending everyone was observed equally.

title: Cohort Studies
section: LEARN 7 · Loss to follow-up can create bias
text:
LEARN 7 · Loss to follow-up can create bias
Loss to follow-up first reduces information, but it becomes a threat to validity when loss is related to both exposure and outcome risk.
Example: if highly exposed workers who develop early symptoms are more likely to leave employment and disappear from records, the observed exposed cohort may look healthier than the true cohort.
Ask:

How much follow-up is missing?
Why did participants leave?
Does loss differ by exposure group?
Is outcome risk plausibly related to the reason for loss?

The percentage lost is important, but the mechanism of loss matters more.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 8 · Comparison cohort quality
An unexposed cohort should represent a credible baseline for the exposed group.
If exposed workers differ from unexposed workers in age, socioeconomic status, access to care or baseline disease risk, crude outcome differences may reflect those factors rather than exposure.
Restriction, matching, stratification and regression can sometimes address measured differences, but design-stage comparability remains fundamental.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 9 · Time-varying exposure

LIPPS extension Many real exposures change during follow-up. A participant may start medication, change occupation, stop smoking or move between exposure categories.

Treating a changing exposure as if it remained fixed can misclassify person-time and obscure temporal relationships.
At introductory level, the key question is simple:

Does the exposure value at baseline still represent the participant’s exposure throughout the period being analysed?

If not, a more advanced longitudinal analysis may be needed.

title: Cohort Studies
Cohort Studies
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional cohort enrols 3,000 adults free of diabetes. At baseline, 1,000 have a high-risk occupational exposure and 2,000 do not. Over five years, 100 exposed and 80 unexposed participants develop diabetes. Follow-up time totals 4,200 person-years in the exposed group and 8,800 person-years in the unexposed group.

Calculate cumulative risk in each group.
Calculate the risk ratio and risk difference.
Calculate incidence rates per 1,000 person-years.
Calculate the rate ratio.
Explain why risk ratio and rate ratio answer related but not identical questions.
Suppose 20% of exposed participants with early symptoms leave employment and cannot be traced. Explain the potential direction of bias.
Identify at least three baseline variables that could confound the association.
Explain whether this observational cohort can establish causation merely because exposure was measured before disease.
If exposure status changed for many participants, state what additional information should have been collected.
Write a defensible conclusion.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

What feature distinguishes a retrospective cohort from a case-control study?
Why can a cohort estimate incidence directly?
When would person-time be preferable to a single baseline denominator?
How can loss to follow-up introduce bias rather than simply imprecision?
If risk is 10% versus 2%, calculate RR and RD.
Why does prospective follow-up improve temporality without eliminating confounding?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

text:

Initial time limit: 12 minutes because several items use risk and person-time calculations.
Question style: cohort recognition, prospective/retrospective distinctions, incidence, RR/RD/rate ratios, follow-up and loss-to-follow-up scenarios.

Assessment principle

LIPPS extensions: censoring, time-varying exposure and a more explicit loss-to-follow-up causal framework are included as introductory bridges to survival and longitudinal analysis.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 11





Advanced foundation Surveillance Outbreaks Field epidemiology

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text: Advanced foundation Surveillance Outbreaks Field epidemiology

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
This week in one sentence
Use surveillance data to detect and describe public-health signals, evaluate system performance and move systematically from an unusual signal to outbreak investigation, hypothesis testing and control.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: ORIENT · A surveillance signal is not yet an outbreak

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
LEARN 1 · What surveillance is
The attached CDC course describes public-health surveillance as ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination of health data for public-health decision-making and action.
Surveillance is therefore not just data collection.
A useful surveillance cycle is:
Define → Collect → Consolidate → Analyse → Interpret → Disseminate → Act → Evaluate
The surveillance system supplies information for action; the control intervention itself is conceptually distinct from surveillance.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 2 · Start with the objective, not the database
text:
LEARN 2 · Start with the objective, not the database
Surveillance design should follow the intended use.
If the objective is to identify individual cases quickly for treatment or contact follow-up, timeliness and case-level identification may be critical.
If the objective is to monitor a long-term population trend, weekly individual reports may be unnecessary.
Before building or evaluating a system ask:

What health event is under surveillance?
What is the case definition?
Who is the population under surveillance?
What action will the information support?
How quickly is information needed?
Which sources can supply the required data?
Who needs the findings and in what form?

A system that collects abundant data with no defined decision use is not automatically a strong surveillance system.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 3 · Passive, active, sentinel and syndromic approaches
text:
LEARN 3 · Passive, active, sentinel and syndromic approaches
Passive surveillance relies on routine reporting from clinicians, laboratories or facilities without the health authority actively soliciting every report.
Active surveillance involves deliberate case finding, for example calling facilities or reviewing records during an outbreak.
Sentinel surveillance uses selected reporting sites or providers to monitor a condition or trend rather than attempting full population capture.
Syndromic surveillance monitors symptom complexes or proxy signals before definitive diagnosis and can provide earlier warning, but often at the cost of lower specificity and more false alarms.
The attached text explicitly presents syndromic surveillance as a supplement rather than a universal replacement for traditional surveillance.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 4 · Analyse surveillance data by time, place and person
text:
LEARN 4 · Analyse surveillance data by time, place and person
Routine surveillance analysis should repeatedly ask:
Time: Is occurrence rising, falling, seasonal or unusual compared with prior periods?
Place: Where are counts and rates concentrated?
Person: Which age, sex, occupation, exposure or population groups are most affected?
Counts can guide resources; rates can help compare populations.
A single sudden increase deserves data-quality checks before it is interpreted as biological change. The attached source lists possibilities such as population influx, batch reporting, duplicates, laboratory/computer error and changes in reporting practice.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 6 · Cluster, outbreak and expected background
text:
LEARN 6 · Cluster, outbreak and expected background
A cluster is an aggregation of cases in time or place that appears unusual, sometimes before the expected number is known.
An outbreak or epidemic requires occurrence above what is expected for the population, place and period, although terminology and operational use can vary.
The expected level may come from previous years, previous weeks, a comparable season, registry data or another credible baseline.
Do not interpret “more reports” as “more disease” until you have examined how the observation system changed.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 7 · Outbreak investigation is systematic but not rigid

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 8 · Case definitions must serve case finding
text:
LEARN 8 · Case definitions must serve case finding
A field case definition commonly combines clinical criteria with appropriate person, place and time restrictions.
Early in an investigation, a relatively sensitive definition may help identify the full extent of illness. Later analytic work may use a more specific subset, depending on the objective.
The hypothesised exposure should generally remain outside the case definition when that same exposure will be tested analytically.
If the outbreak expands geographically or the clinical picture changes, the case definition may need revision. Document version changes because they can alter apparent counts and rates.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 9 · Case finding and the line list

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 10 · Description comes before analytic testing
text:
LEARN 10 · Description comes before analytic testing
The attached outbreak lesson emphasises descriptive epidemiology as a critical step because it identifies the population at risk, suggests source and transmission hypotheses, exposes data problems and may support immediate prevention.
Epidemic curves, maps and person-specific rates are not decorative outputs. They help determine what analytic question is worth asking.
A case-control study built on a weak or biologically implausible hypothesis can waste scarce outbreak time.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 11 · Choose the analytic design from the population structure
text:
LEARN 11 · Choose the analytic design from the population structure
For a small, well-defined outbreak population—for example, all attendees at a wedding—a retrospective cohort can often enumerate the population, calculate food-specific attack rates and compare risk directly.
When the source population is large or cannot be completely enumerated, a case-control study may be more efficient. Controls must represent the population that produced the cases, and the odds ratio becomes the natural measure.
The design follows the data-generating setting, not investigator preference.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 12 · When the first hypothesis fails

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
LEARN 13 · Action under uncertainty
Field epidemiology is not always afforded the luxury of waiting for perfect evidence.
If a severe and plausible hazard can be controlled with a proportionate, low-harm measure, action may begin while additional evidence is collected.
The standard is not “certainty before action.” It is:

Is the evidence sufficient, given the consequences of delay and the harms of acting, to justify the intervention?

That judgement should be explicit and revisable.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional district normally reports 0–2 suspected viral haemorrhagic fever alerts per month. Over four days, six alerts are received from three health facilities. Two alerts appear to refer to the same patient; one facility recently introduced a new triage checklist; two patients attended the same funeral; laboratory confirmation is pending.
Develop an initial investigation plan:

Decide what must be verified before calling this an outbreak.
Draft a working case definition without embedding funeral attendance as a requirement.
List the first variables for a line list.
State how you would expand case finding.
Describe the data by time, place and person.
Identify the most important data-quality checks.
Propose at least two early hypotheses.
Explain when a retrospective cohort could be used around the funeral and when a case-control design might be preferable.
Name at least five surveillance-system attributes you would later evaluate.
State what control measures could be justified before final laboratory certainty and what harms those measures could create.
Specify who should receive preliminary findings and in what form.
Describe what evidence would make you revise your leading hypothesis.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why is a surveillance signal not automatically an outbreak?
What is the difference between passive and active surveillance?
Why can increasing surveillance sensitivity reduce predictive value positive?
Why should outbreak-investigation steps be treated as conceptual rather than rigid?
When is a retrospective cohort especially useful in an outbreak?
Why should descriptive epidemiology be revisited when an analytic study is unrevealing?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

Assessment principle
The quiz is designed so that a prepared learner can read, reason and answer efficiently. Timing is a learning-and-assessment parameter to be calibrated from real response-time data, not a substitute for good question design.

title: Epidemiology — Core Readings
text:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. Originally published in 2006 and subsequently updated. The LIPPS course uses this source for foundational epidemiological reasoning, frequency measures, association, descriptive epidemiology, basic study designs, surveillance and outbreak investigation.
CDC archive: https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/index.html
CDC Stacks record: https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/13178



The CDC text remains valuable for introductory applied epidemiology, but LIPPS does not treat it as the final word on modern methodology. Course pages explicitly identify later additions such as prevalence ratios, modern causal diagrams, collider bias, cluster-randomised trials, intention-to-treat, quasi-experimental designs, likelihood ratios, ROC analysis and modern critical-appraisal language as LIPPS extensions.
In institutional use, lecturers should pair the course with current discipline-specific reporting standards, ministry/WHO surveillance guidance and contemporary methodological readings appropriate to the programme level.




Weeks 1–4: CDC Lessons 1–3 plus the LIPPS lessons.
Weeks 5–8: CDC study-design sections plus current programme readings on observational and experimental design.
Week 9: current causal-inference and epidemiological-bias reading selected by the lecturer.
Week 10: current diagnostic-accuracy reading and reporting guidance selected by the lecturer.
Week 11: CDC surveillance and outbreak-investigation lessons plus current national/WHO outbreak guidance.

Important

title: Epidemiology — Core Readings

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. Originally published in 2006 and subsequently updated. title: Epidemiology — Core Readings
