title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 04





Foundation Person · Place · Time Epi curves Hypothesis generation

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text: Foundation Person · Place · Time Epi curves Hypothesis generation

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
This week in one sentence
Describe health events systematically by person, place and time, use appropriate denominators and displays, and turn observed patterns into testable hypotheses.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
ORIENT · “Cases doubled” — is that enough?
A district reports 80 malaria cases this week compared with 40 during the same week last year. That sounds like a doubling, but an epidemiologist should immediately ask what else changed.

Did the district population change?
Did testing volume change?
Did the case definition change?
Did a new reporting facility open?
Are the cases concentrated in one place, age group or time period?
Is the comparison week an appropriate expected baseline?

Descriptive epidemiology is not “just making tables.” It is the disciplined first attempt to understand what happened, to whom, where and when, and to decide what deserves explanation.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 1 · Start by defining what you are counting
text:
LEARN 1 · Start by defining what you are counting
A descriptive analysis is only as coherent as its event definition. Before counting, specify the disease, condition, injury, behaviour or other health event.
For outbreak work, a practical case definition commonly combines clinical criteria with restrictions on time, place and person. The suspected exposure should generally not be built into the case definition when that exposure will later be evaluated, because doing so can manufacture an association.
A useful first question is therefore:

If two analysts used this definition independently, would they classify the same people in the same way?

Definitions may legitimately evolve as knowledge improves, but changes must be documented because a broader or narrower definition can change the apparent pattern.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 2 · Build the line list before the story
text:
LEARN 2 · Build the line list before the story
A line list is a compact dataset in which each row represents one case or observation and each column represents a variable needed for description or investigation.
A practical outbreak line list might include:







Domain
Example variables




Identifier
unique case ID


Person
age, sex, occupation, population group


Place
village, parish, facility, residence or exposure location


Time
date of onset, date reported, date admitted


Clinical
symptoms, laboratory status, outcome


Investigation
selected exposures, contact status, vaccination status



Before analysis, check duplicates, impossible dates, missing age or location, inconsistent categories and the relationship between onset date and report date.

A graph can make bad data look authoritative.
Inspect the line list before you admire the curve.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 3 · Time: choose the clock that matches the process
text:
LEARN 3 · Time: choose the clock that matches the process
Time can be described at very different scales.
Secular trend examines long-term change over years or decades.
Seasonality examines recurring patterns within the year.
Day-of-week or time-of-day patterns can reveal scheduled occupational, behavioural or environmental exposures.
Epidemic time focuses on the short interval relevant to an outbreak.
The x-axis should therefore match the biology and operational question. Annual bins can hide a short outbreak; hourly bins can add noise to a chronic-disease trend.
Events such as a new intervention, a reporting change or a suspected exposure can be annotated on a time plot, but temporal coincidence by itself does not prove effect.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 4 · Epidemic curves are compressed epidemiological arguments
text:
LEARN 4 · Epidemic curves are compressed epidemiological arguments
An epidemic curve plots the number of cases by time of onset, diagnosis or another clearly stated event. Its shape can suggest—but does not by itself prove—the pattern of spread.
Common patterns include:

a concentrated peak compatible with a point-source exposure;
a prolonged or irregular pattern compatible with continuous or intermittent common-source exposure;
successive waves compatible with propagated person-to-person transmission.

The curve can also reveal the magnitude and stage of an outbreak, possible outliers and a plausible exposure window when the incubation period is known.
Do not classify an outbreak from shape alone. Reporting delays, mixed exposures, secondary transmission and missing onset dates can distort the curve.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 5 · Outliers can be clues rather than rubbish

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 6 · Place is whatever geography matters to transmission or risk
text:
LEARN 6 · Place is whatever geography matters to transmission or risk
“Place” is broader than residence. Depending on the question, the relevant location may be a workplace, school, hospital ward, water point, market, travel destination or place of exposure.
Two main mapping approaches have different purposes:
Spot maps show where individual events occurred and are useful for small clusters or outbreaks.
Area maps compare numbers or rates across geographic units. When populations differ substantially, rates are usually more meaningful than raw counts.
A map shows spatial pattern; it does not automatically identify the mechanism producing that pattern. Population density, access to care, diagnostic capacity and reporting completeness can all create geographic differences.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 7 · Person: categories can reveal or conceal risk
text:
LEARN 7 · Person: categories can reveal or conceal risk
Person variables can include age, sex, occupation, socioeconomic measures, behaviours, immune status and other characteristics relevant to the problem.
Age deserves particular care. A broad 0–4 year category may hide that nearly all excess disease is concentrated among infants. Category boundaries should therefore be chosen for epidemiological meaning, not merely because they are convenient.
Similarly, an apparent difference between social groups should not be interpreted as an inherent biological difference without examining exposure, access, measurement and structural context.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 8 · Counts answer burden; rates answer comparative frequency
text:
LEARN 8 · Counts answer burden; rates answer comparative frequency
A district with 500 cases may have a lower disease frequency than a district with 100 cases if their populations differ greatly.
Counts are useful for operational planning: beds, medicines, staff and laboratory workload.
Rates or proportions put events in relation to a population at risk and are more useful for comparing groups of different sizes.
Example:



District
Cases
Population
Cases per 1,000




A
500
500,000
1.0


B
100
20,000
5.0



The smaller district has fewer cases but five times the rate.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 9 · Description generates hypotheses; it rarely settles them
text:
LEARN 9 · Description generates hypotheses; it rarely settles them
Suppose cases cluster among children under five, peak after heavy rainfall and are concentrated around two water sources. Those observations can generate hypotheses about exposure and transmission.
A hypothesis should connect the pattern to a mechanism that can be evaluated. For example:

Households relying on selected surface-water sources experienced higher risk of acute watery diarrhoea than households using protected sources.

That hypothesis now suggests what comparison data must be collected.
Descriptive epidemiology therefore bridges observation → hypothesis, while analytic epidemiology adds a comparison capable of testing that hypothesis more rigorously.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional district receives 46 reports of acute watery diarrhoea over 10 days. Thirty-four reports come from two neighbouring villages. Onset dates show a sharp rise over three days, followed by a slower decline. Most patients are children, but one case occurred a week earlier in an adult trader who regularly visits both villages. A new private clinic also began reporting during the same month.
Work through the problem before looking for an exposure:

Draft a usable working case definition.
Identify the minimum variables for the line list.
Decide whether onset date or report date should drive the epidemic curve and explain why.
Calculate village-specific rates if population denominators are available.
Identify which observations might be useful outliers.
List at least three hypotheses suggested by the person-place-time pattern.
Identify at least three non-disease explanations for the apparent increase that must be checked.
State what comparison you would need next to test your leading hypothesis.

The point is not to guess the cause. The point is to produce a description strong enough to justify the next question.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why can an epidemic curve based on report date tell a different story from one based on symptom-onset date?
A village has twice as many cases as another village but ten times the population. Which comparison is more informative: counts or rates, and why?
What is wrong with including “drank from Water Point X” in the case definition when Water Point X is the exposure you plan to test?
Give two plausible explanations for a late outlier on an epidemic curve other than data-entry error.
Why might five-year age bands hide an important disease pattern among infants?
Does a spatial cluster around a health facility prove that the facility is the source of infection? Explain.

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
DEMONSTRATE · Week 4 mastery quiz
Pilot Mastery Quiz: 15 objective questions randomly drawn from a Week 4 bank of 50 items.
Initial time limit: 11 minutes.
Question style: interpretation of person-place-time displays, denominator choice, case-definition logic, epidemic-curve reasoning and hypothesis generation.
Presentation: one question per page; options shuffled where appropriate; one graded mastery attempt.
Practice mode: untimed with explanatory feedback.

Assessment principle
The quiz is designed so that a prepared learner can read, reason and answer efficiently. Timing is a learning-and-assessment parameter to be calibrated from real response-time data, not a substitute for good question design.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
Source foundation and LIPPS extensions
Primary source foundation: CDC Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition, especially its treatment of descriptive epidemiology, time, place, person, epidemic curves, spot maps, case definitions and observed-versus-expected reasoning.
LIPPS additions: the fictional district cases, the explicit data-quality workflow, modern wording around reporting-system changes, and the integrated “disease versus observation system” reasoning are instructional extensions rather than material reproduced from the source.
Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. October 2006; updated May 2012.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text: Intermediate Bias Confounding Effect modification

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
This week in one sentence
Recognise systematic error, distinguish confounding from effect modification, and choose adjustment strategies that answer the intended epidemiological question.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: ORIENT · “We adjusted for everything” is not reassuring
text:
ORIENT · “We adjusted for everything” is not reassuring
A paper reports an association between an exposure and hypertension. The authors say the model is reliable because they adjusted for age, sex, BMI, medication use, clinic attendance, kidney disease, physical activity, income, diet and several laboratory markers.
More adjustment is not automatically better.
Some variables may be confounders. Some may be consequences of the exposure. Some may be consequences of the outcome. Some may be colliders. Some may be measured poorly.
The first question is not “How many variables are in the model?” It is “What causal question is the model trying to answer?”

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LEARN 1 · Bias is systematic error
The attached CDC glossary defines bias as a systematic deviation of results or inferences from the truth. It explicitly notes that epidemiological bias does not imply intentional misconduct.
Random error makes estimates vary unpredictably around a target. Bias moves the expected estimate systematically away from the target.
Increasing sample size reduces random error but does not automatically remove bias. A very large biased study can estimate the wrong quantity with extraordinary precision.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 4 · Confounding is a mixing of effects
text:
LEARN 4 · Confounding is a mixing of effects
The attached CDC glossary defines confounding as distortion of the exposure-outcome association by a third variable related to both.
Suppose coffee drinking appears associated with lung cancer, but smokers drink more coffee and smoking strongly causes lung cancer. Smoking can mix into the coffee-cancer comparison.
A plausible confounder generally:

is associated with the exposure in the source population;
is a cause, marker or proxy of a cause of the outcome; and
is not simply a consequence of the exposure along the causal pathway being estimated.

These are conceptual conditions, not a mechanical checklist based only on statistical significance.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 5 · Crude and adjusted estimates answer different comparisons
text:
LEARN 5 · Crude and adjusted estimates answer different comparisons
Imagine a crude risk ratio of 2.4 between an exposure and outcome. After appropriate age adjustment, the estimate becomes 1.2.
That change may indicate important confounding by age—but the magnitude of change alone does not prove the adjustment set is correct.
Adjustment aims to compare exposure groups as if they were similar with respect to selected confounding variables.
Methods include:

restriction;
matching;
stratification;
standardisation; and
multivariable modelling.

The method matters less than whether the selected variables are appropriate for the causal question.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 6 · A mediator is not a confounder
text:
LEARN 6 · A mediator is not a confounder

LIPPS extension Mediators and collider bias are not developed in the attached CDC text. They are included because modern epidemiological analysis requires students to understand why adjustment can be harmful.

A mediator lies on a causal pathway from exposure to outcome.
Example:
High salt intake → higher blood pressure → stroke
If the question is the total effect of salt intake on stroke, adjusting for blood pressure removes part of the pathway we intend to estimate.
If the question is a direct effect not operating through blood pressure, the estimand is different and stronger assumptions are needed.
Adjustment therefore changes the question.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 7 · Collider bias: adjustment can create association
text:
LEARN 7 · Collider bias: adjustment can create association
A collider is a variable caused by two other variables.
Suppose both severe disease and high socioeconomic status increase the probability of receiving specialist care. If analysis is restricted to specialist-clinic patients, conditioning on clinic attendance can create an artificial association between disease and socioeconomic status even if none existed in the source population.
This is why “adjust for every variable associated with the outcome” is not a safe epidemiological rule.

Adjustment is not a cleansing ritual. Every variable you control for changes the comparison your model is making.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 8 · Effect modification is not bias
text:
LEARN 8 · Effect modification is not bias
Effect modification occurs when the size—or sometimes direction—of an exposure-outcome association genuinely differs across levels of another variable.
Example:
A prevention programme may reduce disease strongly in younger adults but have little effect in older adults.
If the stratum-specific estimates truly differ, averaging them into one number may hide important heterogeneity.
Unlike confounding, effect modification is generally something to describe and understand, not “adjust away.”

LIPPS extension The attached source does not develop effect modification. This treatment is an added modern epidemiology component.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LEARN 9 · Stratified reasoning
Suppose a crude RR is 1.8. After stratifying by sex:

women: RR = 1.1
men: RR = 1.0

The similar stratum-specific estimates, both much closer to 1 than the crude estimate, are compatible with confounding.
Now suppose:

women: RR = 3.0
men: RR = 0.9

Those estimates are not naturally summarised by a single common effect. They suggest effect heterogeneity that deserves interpretation.
This logic should be understood before relying on regression interaction terms.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LEARN 10 · Interaction depends on scale

LIPPS extension Interaction can look different on additive and multiplicative scales.

An exposure may show no multiplicative interaction on the risk-ratio scale while showing an important difference in absolute risk.
Public-health decisions often care deeply about the additive scale because it reflects additional cases that might be prevented.
Do not ask only:

Is the interaction-term p-value below 0.05?

Ask:

On which scale is effect heterogeneity scientifically meaningful for this question?

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LEARN 11 · A practical adjustment workflow
Before fitting a multivariable model:

State the exposure, outcome and causal estimand.
Draw or verbally specify the presumed causal structure.
Identify causes of the outcome that also influence exposure.
Exclude clear descendants of the exposure when estimating total effects.
Avoid conditioning on plausible colliders.
Check measurement quality.
Examine whether meaningful effect modification is expected.
Report crude and appropriately adjusted estimates.
Perform sensitivity analyses when assumptions are uncertain.

This workflow is more defensible than automatic variable selection based on bivariable p-values.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional cross-sectional survey finds that current pesticide exposure is associated with chronic respiratory symptoms: crude prevalence ratio 2.0.
Age is associated with both pesticide work and respiratory symptoms. Smoking is more common among pesticide workers and causes respiratory symptoms. Current clinic attendance is influenced by respiratory symptoms and by employer-provided insurance, which is more common among pesticide workers. Reduced physical activity may be a consequence of respiratory symptoms.

Identify plausible confounders.
Explain why current clinic attendance could behave as a collider.
Explain why reduced physical activity could be a consequence of outcome rather than a confounder.
Propose a defensible minimal adjustment set for the total exposure-outcome association.
Suppose the adjusted PR is 1.35. Interpret the change from 2.0 without claiming that all bias has disappeared.
Suppose adjusted PRs are 2.2 among workers without respirators and 1.0 among workers consistently using respirators. Is respirator use behaving more like confounding or effect modification in this result?
State what further design and measurement information you would need before causal interpretation.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why does a larger sample not remove systematic bias?
What distinguishes selection bias from information bias?
What three conceptual conditions make a variable a plausible confounder?
Why can controlling for a mediator be inappropriate when estimating a total effect?
What is the danger of conditioning on a collider?
Why should genuine effect modification usually be reported rather than averaged away?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
DEMONSTRATE · Week 9 mastery quiz
Pilot Mastery Quiz: 18 objective questions drawn from a Week 9 bank of 60 items.
Initial time limit: 13 minutes.
Question style: bias classification, causal-structure micro-scenarios, confounder/mediator/collider distinctions, crude-versus-adjusted interpretation and effect-modification reasoning.
**No DAG drawing is required in the timed quiz; the assessment tests recognition and interpretation.

Assessment principle
The quiz is designed so that a prepared learner can read, reason and answer efficiently. Timing is a learning-and-assessment parameter to be calibrated from real response-time data, not a substitute for good question design.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
Source foundation and LIPPS extensions
Primary source foundation: the attached CDC text and glossary definitions of bias, selection bias, information bias and confounding, together with its repeated emphasis on valid comparison groups.
LIPPS extensions: differential/non-differential misclassification, mediators, colliders, effect modification, interaction scale and causal adjustment logic are explicitly added because they are not developed in the attached text.
Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. October 2006; updated May 2012.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
text:
LIPPS LEARN · HEALTH COMMUNICATION · WEEK 03





Audience insight Health literacy Culture Accessibility

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
text: Audience insight Health literacy Culture Accessibility

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
text:
This week in one sentence
Use formative audience insight, health-literacy principles and cultural context to design communication that people can access, understand and use.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
text:
ORIENT · One message, three audiences
A cervical-cancer screening programme sends one English-language SMS to all women aged 25–49: “Attend VIA screening at your HCIV. Early detection improves prognosis.” Some recipients do not read English, some share phones with partners, some do not know what VIA means, and some fear that screening is a test for cancer rather than a preventive service.
The technical facts may be correct. The communication design is not audience-centred.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 1 · Audience analysis begins with decisions, not demographics
text:
LEARN 1 · Audience analysis begins with decisions, not demographics
Age and sex can be useful, but an audience is not adequately described by demographics alone. Useful analysis asks what decision is required, what people already know, believe and do, who influences them, what barriers they face, which channels they use and trust, and what services or opportunities are available.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 2 · Primary, secondary and influential audiences
text:
LEARN 2 · Primary, secondary and influential audiences
The primary audience is expected to make the target decision or perform the behaviour. Secondary audiences may support or hinder it. Influential audiences may include partners, parents, peers, religious leaders, health workers, employers or local officials. Communication plans often fail when they address only the person expected to act.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 3 · Segmentation can improve relevance—but can also stereotype
text:
LEARN 3 · Segmentation can improve relevance—but can also stereotype
Segmentation divides a broad audience into groups that differ in determinants, needs or communication behaviour. Good segmentation is based on actionable differences. Bad segmentation assumes that everyone in a demographic category thinks alike or turns culture into a fixed explanation for behaviour.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 4 · Health literacy is interaction, not a deficit label
text:
LEARN 4 · Health literacy is interaction, not a deficit label
Health literacy concerns people’s ability to access, understand, appraise and use health information and services. It is shaped by both individual skills and the complexity of the health system. A confusing form is not proof that a patient is “illiterate”; it may be evidence that the system communicates badly.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 5 · Plain language is precise language
text:
LEARN 5 · Plain language is precise language
Plain language uses familiar words, short sentences, clear organisation and explicit actions. It removes unnecessary jargon without removing essential meaning. Replace “utilise the nearest designated facility” with “Go to the nearest health centre.” Explain unavoidable technical terms the first time they appear.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 6 · Numbers need design, not just accuracy
text:
LEARN 6 · Numbers need design, not just accuracy
People can struggle with probabilities, percentages and changing denominators. Use consistent denominators, natural frequencies where useful, absolute as well as relative risks, and visual displays that do not exaggerate differences. “Risk fell from 2 in 100 to 1 in 100” may be clearer than “50% risk reduction” alone.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 7 · Culture is dynamic and internally diverse
text:
LEARN 7 · Culture is dynamic and internally diverse
Cultural context influences meaning, norms, trust and acceptable messengers, but it should be investigated rather than guessed. Avoid statements such as “this community does not believe in hospitals.” Ask what experiences, histories, costs, norms and power relationships make particular responses reasonable from the audience’s perspective.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 8 · Translation is not the same as adaptation
text:
LEARN 8 · Translation is not the same as adaptation
A literal translation may preserve words while losing meaning. Adaptation considers idiom, examples, tone, reading level, symbolism and local service reality. Back-translation can identify some errors, but comprehension testing with intended users is more informative.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 9 · Accessibility is part of effectiveness
text:
LEARN 9 · Accessibility is part of effectiveness
Communication should account for visual, hearing, cognitive and mobility-related access needs as well as literacy, language, device access, data cost and network reliability. Captions, transcripts, alt text, readable contrast, large text, simple navigation and low-bandwidth options are communication interventions, not cosmetic extras.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: LEARN 10 · Formative research is how you replace assumptions with evidence
text:
LEARN 10 · Formative research is how you replace assumptions with evidence
Useful methods include interviews, focus groups, observation, rapid intercepts, social listening, existing data review and prototype testing. The purpose is not to produce a long report; it is to discover what must change in the communication strategy.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: DEEPEN · Audience insight is more than demographics
text:
DEEPEN · Audience insight is more than demographics
Age, sex and residence describe an audience; they rarely explain a decision. Useful audience analysis asks about goals, constraints, language, trust, routines, social influence, information access, perceived risk and the decision context. Two women of the same age in the same district may require very different communication if one has private smartphone access and supportive family members while the other shares a phone, depends on a partner for transport money and is concerned about confidentiality.

Segmentation without stereotyping
Segmentation groups people because a meaningful communication strategy differs between groups. A segment should therefore be actionable. “Young people” is often too broad. “First-year university students who know where HIV testing is offered but fear being recognized at the clinic” identifies a specific communication and service problem. Personas can help teams imagine decisions, but they must be grounded in evidence and should never become fictional stereotypes presented as research findings.


Health literacy as an interaction
Health literacy is not simply a person’s reading ability. Communication becomes easier or harder depending on how organisations design forms, signs, counselling, instructions and digital interfaces. A universal-precautions approach assumes that anyone can misunderstand complex health information, especially when anxious, ill or under time pressure. Plain language, clear structure, visual support and teach-back are therefore good design rather than remedial treatment for a “low-literacy” group.


Culture is explanatory only when you investigate it
“Culture” should not become a residual explanation for behaviour we have not studied. Ask what specific norm, value, social role, history or practice influences the decision. Then ask whether it is shared, contested or changing. Community members are not culturally identical.


Accessibility and exclusion
Audience analysis should explicitly test whether communication excludes people because of disability, language, literacy, cost, connectivity, gendered phone ownership, geography or social status. The WHO communication framework emphasises accessibility, relevance and understandability, while the CDC Clear Communication Index provides practical criteria for assessing public communication materials.


Formative research toolkit
A rapid audience analysis may combine short interviews, focus groups, observation, service data, call-centre questions, social listening and review of previous campaign data. The purpose is not to collect every possible fact. It is to reduce uncertainty about the decision you are trying to influence.


What could fool us?
The loudest voices in a focus group may not represent the wider audience. Online comments systematically exclude people who are offline. Translating a message accurately does not guarantee that the meaning survives translation. And a subgroup that appears “hard to reach” may actually be easy to reach through channels the programme has not bothered to use.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
section: FIELD LAB · Build a rapid audience-insight protocol
text:
FIELD LAB · Build a rapid audience-insight protocol
Suppose a district wants to improve adolescent use of confidential HIV testing. Before designing messages, collect enough evidence to answer six questions:

Decision: What decision must the adolescent make, and at what moment?
Barrier: What makes that decision difficult—fear, stigma, cost, location, privacy, norms, service experience?
Influencers: Which peers, partners, parents, providers or online voices matter?
Access: Which channels are available privately and affordably?
Language and literacy: What words, formats and visual cues are actually understood?
Trust: What would make the service or messenger believable?

A practical rapid design might include 8–12 individual interviews with adolescents, a few interviews with providers, observation of the service journey, review of routine service data, and a short prototype test. That is often more useful than a large generic knowledge survey.

Evidence-to-segment example
If interviews reveal that school-going adolescents know testing locations but fear being recognised, while out-of-school adolescents lack information about opening hours, these are different communication problems. The first needs privacy and trust solutions; the second needs access information. A single youth message would hide the distinction.


Minimum equity check
For every segment ask: who is absent because of disability, language, geography, phone access, social status or safety concerns? Then decide whether the research method itself needs adaptation.

title: Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A maternal-health programme wants to encourage birth preparedness in an urban informal settlement and a rural district. In the urban area, most women have smartphones but frequently change numbers; many work long hours. In the rural district, radio is common, network coverage is patchy and household financial decisions often involve partners or older relatives. Both settings include women with low literacy and several local languages.

Define the primary and influential audiences in each setting.
Identify which characteristics are actionable for segmentation.
List at least five formative-research questions.
Rewrite “prepare for obstetric emergencies and identify a referral facility” in plain language.
Choose a channel mix for each setting and justify it.
Identify accessibility adaptations.
Explain how you would test whether translations are understood as intended.
Identify one stereotype you must avoid in each setting.

text:

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
text: Theory Behaviour COM-B Social context

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
text:
This week in one sentence
Use behavioural and communication theory to diagnose why a health behaviour occurs and to select plausible communication and non-communication responses.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: ORIENT · “People know—but they still do not do it”
text:
ORIENT · “People know—but they still do not do it”
A community survey finds that almost everyone knows mosquito nets reduce malaria, yet consistent net use remains low. A campaign team proposes another awareness campaign. Before approving it, ask: Is knowledge actually the limiting determinant? Are nets available? Are they uncomfortable in hot weather? Do households reserve them for children? Are there beliefs about chemicals? Do sleeping arrangements make hanging difficult?
Theory helps organise these explanations and prevents communication from treating every behaviour problem as an information deficit.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 1 · Theory is a map, not a magic formula
text:
LEARN 1 · Theory is a map, not a magic formula
Behavioural theories organise plausible determinants and relationships. They help planners decide what to measure, what mechanism to target and what change would count as progress. A theory should be judged by its usefulness for the specific problem, not by how famous it is.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 2 · Health Belief Model: perceived threat and action
text:
LEARN 2 · Health Belief Model: perceived threat and action
The Health Belief Model focuses on perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action and self-efficacy. It can be useful when a person must decide whether a preventive or care-seeking action is worthwhile. Its weakness is that it can understate social, structural and environmental constraints if used alone.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 3 · Theory of Planned Behaviour: intention is socially situated
text:
LEARN 3 · Theory of Planned Behaviour: intention is socially situated
The Theory of Planned Behaviour links attitudes toward the behaviour, perceived social norms and perceived behavioural control to behavioural intention. It reminds communicators that a person may personally favour an action but still avoid it because important others disapprove or because they believe they cannot perform it.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 4 · Social Cognitive Theory: people learn in social environments
text:
LEARN 4 · Social Cognitive Theory: people learn in social environments
Social Cognitive Theory emphasises reciprocal interaction among people, behaviour and environment. Important concepts include self-efficacy, observational learning, outcome expectations, goals and reinforcement. Demonstration and credible modelling can therefore matter as much as factual instruction.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 5 · Social-ecological thinking: behaviour has levels
text:
LEARN 5 · Social-ecological thinking: behaviour has levels
A social-ecological lens examines influences at individual, interpersonal, organisational, community and policy/system levels. Low vaccination uptake, for example, may reflect individual concerns, household decision-making, provider behaviour, clinic waiting time and policy or supply constraints simultaneously.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 6 · COM-B: capability, opportunity and motivation
text:
LEARN 6 · COM-B: capability, opportunity and motivation
COM-B provides a practical diagnostic: behaviour occurs when people have sufficient capability, opportunity and motivation. Capability may be physical or psychological; opportunity may be social or physical; motivation may be reflective or automatic. Communication can influence some of these determinants, but it cannot create vaccine stock or shorten a 30-kilometre journey.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 7 · Diffusion of innovations: adoption is not uniform
text:
LEARN 7 · Diffusion of innovations: adoption is not uniform
New practices spread differently across social systems. Adoption is affected by perceived relative advantage, compatibility with existing values and routines, complexity, trialability and observability. Opinion leaders and peer networks can influence diffusion, but “early adopter” labels should not become stereotypes.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 8 · Choose the mechanism before the message
text:
LEARN 8 · Choose the mechanism before the message
If the problem is low self-efficacy, demonstrate the behaviour and build confidence. If social norms are the barrier, private information alone may do little. If physical opportunity is absent, communication should support service redesign rather than disguise an access problem as a knowledge problem.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: LEARN 9 · From theory to measurable objective
text:
LEARN 9 · From theory to measurable objective
A theoretical construct becomes useful when it can be translated into something observable. “Improve attitudes” is vague. “Increase the proportion of eligible adults who believe hypertension screening is worthwhile despite feeling healthy” is more specific and measurable.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: DEEPEN · From theory to an intervention mechanism
text:
DEEPEN · From theory to an intervention mechanism
A theory becomes useful only when it changes what you measure, design or decide. LIPPS therefore uses a four-step chain:
determinant → mechanism → intervention component → indicator.
If women miss antenatal contacts because they believe later visits add little value, the determinant is not simply “poor knowledge”. A plausible mechanism is low perceived benefit. Communication might therefore use a credible explanation of what later contacts detect that the first visit cannot. An intermediate indicator could be the proportion of women who correctly identify the purpose of later contacts. By contrast, if women intend to attend but cannot afford transport, the dominant problem is physical opportunity. A stronger poster does not create transport.








Diagnostic question
Useful theoretical lens
Example response




Does the person believe the threat applies to them?
Health Belief Model
clarify susceptibility without exaggerating fear


Do important others approve of the behaviour?
Theory of Planned Behaviour
address norms and influential referents


Does the person feel able to perform the behaviour?
Self-efficacy / perceived control
demonstration, rehearsal, skills and problem-solving


Is behaviour constrained by resources or the environment?
COM-B / social-ecological thinking
change opportunity, services or policy as well as communication


Will people see the innovation as useful and compatible?
Diffusion of innovations
demonstrate relative advantage and fit with routines




Theory fit, not theory shopping
A common academic error is to mention several theories because a proposal appears more sophisticated when it has many boxes and arrows. That is theory decoration. A defensible choice begins with evidence about the behaviour, identifies the most plausible determinants, and then selects the smallest theoretical toolkit that helps explain or change them.


Worked example · Hypertension screening
Suppose adults in an urban community agree that hypertension is serious, but many say, “I feel fine, so I do not need screening.” The important barrier is not severity. It is the belief that absence of symptoms implies absence of risk. A useful communication objective might be: increase the proportion of adults aged 30–60 who understand that hypertension may be asymptomatic and who can identify a convenient screening point. If screening sites are open only during working hours, however, the programme must also address opportunity.


What could fool us?
A determinant measured in a cross-sectional survey may be associated with behaviour without being its cause. People who already attend services may subsequently report higher self-efficacy or more favourable attitudes. Social-desirability bias can make stated intentions look stronger than real-world behaviour. Theory should organize inquiry, not manufacture causality from weak data.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
section: FIELD LAB · Diagnose before you communicate
text:
FIELD LAB · Diagnose before you communicate
Use this rapid worksheet before approving a behaviour-change campaign.








Step
Question
ANC example




Behaviour
What exactly should change?
complete the recommended antenatal contacts


Observed gap
What is happening now?
many women attend once but do not return


Candidate determinant
What evidence suggests why?
later visits seen as unnecessary; transport and queues also matter


Theory construct
Which construct helps organise that determinant?
perceived benefit, subjective norm, opportunity


Communication mechanism
What could communication plausibly change?
understanding of the purpose of later visits; partner support


Non-communication action
What must the service/system change?
appointment flow, waiting time, transport barriers


Intermediate indicator
What should change before behaviour?
correct understanding, confidence, partner support


Behaviour indicator
What final action is observed?
attendance at subsequent contacts



The purpose of the table is not to force every programme into one theory. It is to make the causal story visible enough to challenge. If the proposed message has no plausible path to the measured outcome, the strategy needs revision.

Mini worked example
A district survey finds that 88% of women know antenatal care is recommended, 73% intend to return, but only 41% complete later contacts. Interviews show long queues and partner-controlled transport money. A knowledge campaign is therefore a weak first response. The evidence points toward opportunity and household decision-making. Communication may still help by preparing partners and clarifying appointment value, but service redesign is central.


Reflection
Before naming a theory, write one sentence beginning: “The behaviour is not occurring because…” If that sentence is vague, theory selection is premature.

title: Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A district has low completion of four or more antenatal contacts. Interviews suggest that many women intend to attend but face transport costs, partners sometimes control household money, clinic queues are long, and some women believe later visits are unnecessary if the first visit found no problem.

Use COM-B to classify the main determinants.
Apply at least three Health Belief Model constructs.
Identify one relevant subjective norm and one perceived-control issue.
Use a social-ecological lens to identify influences at three levels.
State which problems communication could plausibly address and which require service or policy action.
Write two theory-linked communication objectives.
Propose one message strategy and one environmental/service strategy.
Explain why another generic “ANC is important” campaign could fail.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:
LIPPS LEARN · HEALTH COMMUNICATION · WEEK 11





Campaign planning Theory of change Indicators Evaluation

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text: Campaign planning Theory of change Indicators Evaluation

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:
This week in one sentence
Design a coherent health communication campaign from problem diagnosis through objectives, strategy, implementation, monitoring and evaluation.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
section: ORIENT · A successful campaign because 100,000 flyers were printed?
text:
ORIENT · A successful campaign because 100,000 flyers were printed?
A programme reports that its maternal-health campaign was successful because it produced 100,000 flyers, aired 300 radio spots and reached 1.2 million social-media impressions. The original objective was to increase early antenatal booking. No measure of awareness, comprehension, intention, service enquiries or booking was collected.
Activities and reach are useful implementation data. They are not automatically evidence that the campaign changed the intended outcome.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
section: LEARN 1 · Start with the problem hierarchy
text:
LEARN 1 · Start with the problem hierarchy
Separate the health problem from the behavioural or service problem and from the communication problem. For example: maternal complications are the health problem; late antenatal initiation may be a behaviour/service problem; misunderstanding when ANC should begin may be one communication determinant.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:
LEARN 2 · Write measurable objectives
An objective should specify who, what change, how much, and by when where feasible. “Raise awareness” is weak unless awareness is defined. “Increase from 45% to 65% the proportion of first-time pregnant women who know ANC should begin in the first trimester within six months” is clearer.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
section: LEARN 3 · Build a communication theory of change
text:
LEARN 3 · Build a communication theory of change
Connect determinant → communication mechanism → exposure/experience → intermediate change → behaviour → health contribution. Include assumptions about service availability and social context. A theory of change makes it possible to identify where failure occurred.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:
LEARN 4 · Align strategy components
The audience, objective, message, messenger and channel should fit one another. A complex decision requiring privacy and dialogue is poorly matched to a billboard. A reminder problem may be well suited to SMS if phones are private and numbers are stable.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:
LEARN 5 · Use an outcome ladder
Inputs are resources. Activities are what the programme does. Outputs are products delivered. Reach/exposure captures contact with communication. Intermediate outcomes include knowledge, beliefs, skills, norms or intentions. Behaviour/service outcomes reflect action. Health outcomes are usually influenced by many additional factors.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:
LEARN 6 · Process evaluation explains implementation
Measure whether communication was delivered as planned, with adequate quality, frequency and coverage. Fidelity asks whether the intervention matched its intended design. Dose concerns amount delivered or received. Process data help distinguish strategy failure from implementation failure.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
section: LEARN 7 · Outcome evaluation needs a counterfactual idea
text:
LEARN 7 · Outcome evaluation needs a counterfactual idea
A simple before-after change may reflect secular trends, other programmes, seasonality or changing populations. Stronger designs may use comparison groups, interrupted time series, repeated cross-sectional surveys or experimental allocation where ethical and feasible. Communication evaluation should borrow rigor from epidemiology.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
section: LEARN 8 · Attribution becomes harder further down the chain
text:
LEARN 8 · Attribution becomes harder further down the chain
It is usually easier to attribute a change in message comprehension to a campaign than a decline in mortality. Health outcomes depend on service quality, access, policy, biology and other exposures. Be explicit about contribution versus attribution.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
section: LEARN 9 · Qualitative evidence explains mechanisms and unintended effects
text:
LEARN 9 · Qualitative evidence explains mechanisms and unintended effects
Interviews, observation, feedback logs and focus groups can reveal why a message was trusted, why a channel excluded some groups, how norms shifted or why a seemingly successful campaign produced stigma.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:
LEARN 10 · Evaluate equity and cost
Ask who was reached, who benefited, who was missed and what it cost. A campaign with strong average effects can still widen disparities if already advantaged groups receive most of the benefit.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
section: DEEPEN · A campaign is a managed intervention, not a collection of products
text:
DEEPEN · A campaign is a managed intervention, not a collection of products
Campaign planning should connect the health problem to a communication problem, a defined audience, measurable objectives, a strategy, implementation activities and an evaluation plan. The NCI Making Health Communication Programs Work model emphasises planning, developing and testing concepts and materials, implementation, and assessment.

Start with a communication diagnosis
Specify the behaviour or decision, then separate communication determinants from service and structural determinants. If contraceptive uptake is limited because stock-outs are frequent, a campaign that increases demand without addressing supply may worsen trust.


Objectives form a ladder
Distinguish outputs from outcomes. “Broadcast 100 radio spots” is an activity. “Increase correct knowledge of where free screening is available from 45% to 70%” is a communication objective. “Reduce cervical cancer mortality” is an important health goal but too distal to use as the sole communication indicator.


Strategy before products
A strategy states who must do what, what currently prevents that action, what value proposition or mechanism will be used, who should communicate, through which channels and when. Posters, videos and radio spots are products that implement the strategy.


Implementation planning
Specify responsibilities, production timelines, approvals, partner coordination, media placement, training, community mobilisation, supply dependencies and contingency plans. A strategy that assumes commodities or services that are unavailable is internally inconsistent.


Monitoring and evaluation
Use a results chain:
inputs → activities → outputs → reach/exposure → comprehension/trust → intention/decision → behaviour/service use → health outcome.
Different study designs support different claims. A before-and-after increase may be encouraging but does not automatically prove campaign causation if services, prices, policies or secular trends changed at the same time.


Adaptive management
Monitoring should trigger decisions. If reach is high but comprehension is low, revise the message. If comprehension is high but uptake is low, investigate trust, feasibility and service constraints rather than simply buying more airtime.


What could fool us?
Programme dashboards often reward easily counted outputs. Teams may therefore produce more materials even when the bottleneck is elsewhere. Campaign evaluation should pre-specify the most important indicators and the decisions each indicator will inform.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
section: FIELD LAB · Build a campaign logic model
text:
FIELD LAB · Build a campaign logic model
Consider a campaign to increase postpartum family-planning counselling.
Problem: many women leave maternity services without understanding available methods.
Communication objective: increase the proportion of postpartum women who can name at least two suitable options and know where to obtain counselling.
Strategy: train maternity staff in brief counselling, provide a simple decision aid, and reinforce referral information through discharge materials and SMS where safe.
Results chain:
trained staff + decision aid → counselling delivered → women exposed → understanding and confidence → counselling attendance or method choice → improved contraceptive access.
Each arrow contains an assumption. Staff may be trained but too busy to counsel. Women may understand but face partner opposition or stock-outs. Evaluation should therefore measure multiple stages rather than jumping from training delivered to contraceptive uptake.

Minimum campaign dashboard
Include one indicator for implementation quality, one for reach, one for comprehension/trust, one for intended behaviour and one for service capacity. Pre-specify what action the team will take if each indicator crosses a threshold.


Evaluation choice
If districts launch at different times, a staggered quasi-experimental analysis may be possible. If randomisation is feasible and ethical, cluster randomisation could support stronger causal inference. If only descriptive monitoring is available, state that limitation rather than converting correlation into impact.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
Design a six-month campaign to increase timely childhood vaccination after missed-dose rates rise in three districts. Routine data suggest missed appointments, but formative interviews identify transport barriers, uncertainty about catch-up eligibility, occasional stock-outs and rumours about side effects.

Separate health, service/behaviour and communication problems.
Write two measurable communication objectives.
Build a short theory of change.
Define audiences and channel mix.
List inputs, activities, outputs, reach indicators, intermediate outcomes and behaviour/service outcomes.
Choose an evaluation design and identify key threats to inference.
Add qualitative evaluation questions.
Add equity and cost indicators.
State what result would lead you to change the campaign rather than continue it.

title: Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation
text:

Why are outputs not outcomes?
What does implementation fidelity mean?
Why is a before-after comparison vulnerable to alternative explanations?
What is the difference between contribution and attribution?
Give one intermediate communication outcome between exposure and behaviour.
How can a campaign improve the average outcome while worsening equity?

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
text: Social media Digital metrics Privacy Low bandwidth

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
text:
This week in one sentence
Design and evaluate digital health communication while accounting for platform dynamics, privacy, accessibility, digital exclusion and the difference between engagement metrics and health outcomes.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: ORIENT · The campaign had two million impressions. Did it work?
text:
ORIENT · The campaign had two million impressions. Did it work?
A social-media campaign reports two million impressions, 60,000 likes and 12,000 shares. The objective was to increase uptake of adolescent HIV self-testing. The campaign does not track whether the intended age group saw the content, whether viewers understood where to obtain tests, or whether testing increased.
Digital platforms make some things easy to count. Easy-to-count metrics are not automatically the outcomes that matter.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: LEARN 1 · Digital channels change speed, scale and interaction
text:
LEARN 1 · Digital channels change speed, scale and interaction
Websites, SMS, messaging apps, social platforms, chatbots and mobile apps can support rapid dissemination, reminders, dialogue and tailored content. Their value depends on the communication task and user context.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: LEARN 2 · Platform selection begins with audience behaviour
text:
LEARN 2 · Platform selection begins with audience behaviour
Do not choose a platform because it is fashionable. Ask who uses it, how often, for what purpose, at what cost, with what privacy, and whether the desired action can follow naturally from the platform experience.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
text:
LEARN 3 · Understand the metric ladder
Impressions count displays. Reach estimates unique users exposed. Engagement includes reactions, comments or shares. Click-through indicates movement to another resource. Conversion captures a defined action. Each metric is further from health impact than teams sometimes imply.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
text:
LEARN 4 · Algorithms shape visibility
Social platforms rank and recommend content using proprietary systems. Emotional, novel or controversial material can receive disproportionate attention. Organic reach can change without any change in message quality. Platform metrics should therefore be interpreted as products of both audience response and platform design.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: LEARN 5 · Social listening is systematic observation, not surveillance of individuals
text:
LEARN 5 · Social listening is systematic observation, not surveillance of individuals
Social listening identifies recurring questions, concerns, narratives and information gaps in public or appropriately consented spaces. It should be conducted with a defined purpose, privacy safeguards and caution about representativeness. Online conversation does not equal population opinion.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: LEARN 6 · Moderation is part of communication design
text:
LEARN 6 · Moderation is part of communication design
Comment spaces can contain genuine questions, abuse, misinformation, disclosure of personal health information or requests for clinical advice. Establish rules for response, escalation, deletion and crisis handling before the campaign launches.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: LEARN 7 · Privacy can be harmed by seemingly harmless features
text:
LEARN 7 · Privacy can be harmed by seemingly harmless features
A reproductive-health SMS appearing on a shared phone, a geotagged HIV-service check-in, or a public reply from a clinic account can disclose sensitive information. Collect the minimum data required and consider who else may see notifications or account activity.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: LEARN 8 · Mobile-first means more than shrinking a desktop page
text:
LEARN 8 · Mobile-first means more than shrinking a desktop page
Use readable text, large touch targets, compressed assets, captions, alt text, transcripts and forms that work on low-cost devices. A low-bandwidth path should preserve the essential message and action even when video or interactive content fails.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: LEARN 9 · Digital exclusion is an epidemiological issue
text:
LEARN 9 · Digital exclusion is an epidemiological issue
If the people most likely to need an intervention are least likely to have data, devices, literacy or private access, digital-only communication can widen inequity. Monitor reach by meaningful subgroups and provide non-digital alternatives.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: LEARN 10 · AI can assist, but human accountability remains
text:
LEARN 10 · AI can assist, but human accountability remains
Automated drafting, translation, summarisation and chatbots can increase speed. They can also hallucinate, reproduce bias, mishandle sensitive data or provide unsafe clinical advice. Use human review, defined scope, source verification, privacy controls and escalation to qualified professionals.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: DEEPEN · Digital communication changes the information environment
text:
DEEPEN · Digital communication changes the information environment
Digital platforms do more than transmit messages. They rank, recommend, personalise and amplify content. The same health message can therefore reach different people in different contexts, surrounded by comments, competing claims and platform-generated cues about popularity.

Platform affordances
Short-form video encourages different communication from a clinic portal or WhatsApp group. Design should consider discoverability, sharing, comment culture, privacy, persistence, moderation and whether users can ask questions.


Metrics hierarchy
Separate exposure metrics such as impressions and views from engagement metrics such as clicks and comments, communication outcomes such as comprehension or trust, and health or service outcomes such as vaccination or appointment completion. A viral post can be a communication failure if people share it because it is confusing or controversial.


Privacy and sensitive health information
A platform may expose a person’s interests, group membership or messages to employers, family members or advertisers. Do not assume that a direct message is private merely because it is not public. Collect the minimum data needed, explain its use and avoid unnecessary linkage of identity to sensitive health topics.


Digital exclusion
Device ownership, disability, data cost, network coverage, language and gendered control of phones influence who can benefit. Digital-first programmes should maintain meaningful alternatives rather than relegating offline audiences to an inferior service.


Moderation and community management
Comments can reveal confusion, misinformation and adverse experiences. Establish escalation rules for threats, clinical emergencies, abuse, personal data and misinformation. Moderation should distinguish disagreement from harmful conduct.


AI and automated communication
Chatbots can provide scalable answers but may generate incorrect or overconfident health information. High-risk outputs need constrained knowledge sources, transparent limitations, escalation to humans and monitoring. Automation should not masquerade as a clinician.


What could fool us?
Algorithms make platform data endogenous: the people who see a post are partly selected by prior behaviour and platform ranking. Comparing engagement across posts does not necessarily identify which message would work better in the whole population. Digital analytics are valuable operational data, not automatically causal evidence.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
section: FIELD LAB · Build a digital metrics ladder
text:
FIELD LAB · Build a digital metrics ladder
A useful dashboard separates what the platform did from what people understood and what happened next.








Level
Example metric
What it can tell you




exposure
unique reach, impressions
whether content was delivered


engagement
clicks, shares, comments
whether users interacted


communication
comprehension, trust, confidence
whether the message changed a proximal communication outcome


behaviour
appointment completion, hotline use
whether the intended action occurred


health/service
diagnosis, treatment initiation
downstream programme outcome



Do not skip levels when interpreting results. A high click rate with low comprehension indicates a different problem from low reach.

Digital safety review
Before launch, answer: What personal data are collected? Is the channel private enough for the topic? Can users opt out? What happens if someone reports self-harm, abuse or an emergency? Who moderates harmful comments? How are AI-generated answers constrained and audited? What non-digital alternative exists?


A/B testing caution
Randomised message testing can improve subject lines or calls to action, but optimise for the right outcome. A headline that maximises clicks by provoking fear may reduce trust. The optimisation metric is part of the ethical design.

title: Digital Health and Social Media Communication
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A youth-friendly service plans a WhatsApp and Instagram campaign offering information about STI testing. Young people report concerns about privacy, some share phones with family, rural data costs are high, and staff cannot answer messages 24 hours a day.

Define the communication objective and conversion event.
Decide what should be public content versus private interaction.
Specify privacy safeguards for notifications and direct messages.
Design a low-bandwidth alternative.
Create a moderation and escalation policy for clinical questions and abuse.
Select five digital metrics and state what each can and cannot prove.
Explain how social listening would be conducted ethically.
Identify where AI assistance could be useful and where human review is mandatory.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
text: Message design Plain language Pre-test Revision

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
text:
This week in one sentence
Develop clear, actionable health messages from defined objectives and improve them through systematic pre-testing with intended audiences.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
Message Development and Pre-testing
text:
ORIENT · “Scientifically perfect” and communicatively useless
A vaccination poster reads: “Eligible individuals are advised to receive the bivalent booster to optimise immunogenicity and mitigate severe morbidity.” The technical team approves it because every word is accurate. Community pre-testing shows that many people do not know whether they are “eligible,” what “bivalent” means, or where to go.
Accuracy is necessary. It is not sufficient.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
section: LEARN 1 · Start from an objective and one priority action
text:
LEARN 1 · Start from an objective and one priority action
A message should serve a defined communication objective. Decide what the audience needs to understand or do first. Trying to place every fact on one poster usually produces information overload.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
text:
LEARN 2 · Use a message hierarchy
A practical hierarchy is core message → supporting reason/evidence → specific action → where/when/how → source. The core message should survive even if a person reads or hears only the first few seconds.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
text:
LEARN 3 · Actionability needs operational detail
“Seek care early” is weak if people do not know what “early” means, which symptoms matter, where to go, when services are open or whether the service costs money. Communication should remove avoidable uncertainty around the desired action.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
text:
LEARN 4 · Framing changes perception
Gain frames emphasise benefits of action; loss frames emphasise costs of inaction. Both can be legitimate, but fear or loss framing should not exaggerate risk or shame audiences. Strong emotion without efficacy can produce avoidance rather than action.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
text:
LEARN 5 · Plain language preserves meaning
Use familiar terms, active voice, concrete verbs, short sentences and logical order. Put the important action first. Replace institutional language with audience language, but do not oversimplify to the point of inaccuracy.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
section: LEARN 6 · Numbers and visuals can mislead unintentionally
text:
LEARN 6 · Numbers and visuals can mislead unintentionally
Truncated axes, distorted icons, inconsistent denominators, tiny footnotes and decorative graphics can create false impressions. Visual design should make the intended comparison easier, not more dramatic.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
section: LEARN 7 · Pre-testing asks whether the message works as intended
text:
LEARN 7 · Pre-testing asks whether the message works as intended
Key domains include comprehension, attention, relevance, acceptability, credibility, cultural fit, actionability and unintended interpretations. Recall can be useful but should not be confused with behaviour change.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
section: LEARN 8 · Use methods matched to the question
text:
LEARN 8 · Use methods matched to the question
Cognitive interviews can explore how people interpret wording. Focus groups can reveal shared reactions and social meaning. Intercept tests can quickly compare alternatives. Digital A/B tests can compare observable engagement, but clicks alone do not prove understanding or health impact.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
section: LEARN 9 · Pre-test with intended users, not only colleagues
text:
LEARN 9 · Pre-test with intended users, not only colleagues
Experts know too much about the topic to reliably predict what a first-time reader will understand. A message that seems obvious in the programme office may be ambiguous in the real setting.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
section: LEARN 10 · Revision is part of the design
text:
LEARN 10 · Revision is part of the design
Document what changed and why. If pre-testing reveals a service barrier rather than a message problem, change the service or expectation rather than trying to “wordsmith” around it.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
section: DEEPEN · Build the message from the decision backwards
text:
DEEPEN · Build the message from the decision backwards
A message should begin with the action or decision it must support. Before writing copy, specify the audience, the desired action, the main barrier, the benefit that matters to the audience and the evidence that must be conveyed.

One main message does not mean one sentence
People can process supporting details, but the material should make the main point unmistakable. The CDC Clear Communication Index asks whether the main message and call to action are obvious and whether numbers are explained in ways people can use. A technically complete brochure that hides the key action on page four is poorly designed.


Plain language is precision
Plain language removes unnecessary complexity without removing scientific meaning. Replace jargon, shorten sentences, use familiar words, define unavoidable technical terms and make instructions concrete. “Present for clinical evaluation if symptoms persist” is less actionable than “Return to the clinic if the fever is still present after two days.”


Communicating numbers
Use consistent denominators, meaningful frequencies and absolute risks when possible. “Risk doubled” can sound dramatic even when risk changed from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000. Visuals should clarify rather than decorate.


Pre-testing is diagnosis, not voting
Ask intended users what they think the message means, what action they believe is expected, what is confusing, what feels credible and whether anything is offensive or unrealistic. Avoid asking only, “Do you like it?” A liked message can still be misunderstood.


Translation and adaptation
Literal translation can preserve words while losing meaning, tone or social acceptability. Back-translation is useful but insufficient. Test the adapted message with people who actually use the language in the intended setting.


Iteration
Pre-testing should change the product. Document the issue identified, the revision made and whether the revised version solved the problem. This creates an audit trail and prevents teams from treating pre-testing as ceremonial approval.


What could fool us?
People may explain a message correctly in an interview because the interviewer prompts them. Testing in a quiet office can overestimate comprehension under real-world conditions. A visually attractive message may score well with programme staff but fail among the intended audience. Test where possible under conditions that resemble actual use.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
section: FIELD LAB · From dense message to usable instruction
text:
FIELD LAB · From dense message to usable instruction
Draft: “Eligible beneficiaries are advised to present at designated health facilities for hypertension screening and subsequent clinical evaluation where indicated.”
The sentence is technically understandable to professionals but forces the public to decode several ideas.
Reworked: “High blood pressure often has no symptoms. If you are 30 years or older, get your blood pressure checked at the nearest participating health centre this month. The check takes a few minutes.”
The revision makes the risk, audience, action, place and timing easier to identify. Whether it is actually effective still requires pre-testing.

Five pre-test probes
Ask intended users:

What is the main point in your own words?
Who is this for?
What should the person do next?
What is confusing, worrying or hard to believe?
Is the action realistically possible for someone like you?

Record the answer before explaining the intended meaning. Once the interviewer teaches the message, the pre-test is contaminated.


Revision log
Maintain a simple table with version, problem identified, evidence source, revision made and result of re-test. This becomes part of the quality record and is especially useful when multiple partners approve the same material.

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A family-planning programme drafts: “Modern contraceptive methods are safe, effective and available. Visit your nearest facility today.” Formative research shows that many women worry about side effects, some need discreet access, adolescents fear judgement from providers, and several methods are intermittently out of stock.

Identify the communication objective.
Write a core message and supporting information for one priority audience.
Make the call to action specific.
Identify one claim that needs evidence qualification.
Design five pre-test questions covering different domains.
Choose two pre-testing methods and justify them.
Identify one problem that should trigger service change rather than message revision.
Produce a revised message after hypothetical feedback that “safe” was interpreted as “no side effects.”

title: Message Development and Pre-testing
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

What is the difference between a core message and supporting information?
Why is “seek care early” often not actionable enough?
Name four domains a message pre-test should examine.
Why can expert review not replace audience pre-testing?
What is a risk of fear appeals when efficacy is low?
What does a high click-through rate fail to tell you?
