title: Learn the discipline. Practise the reasoning.
text:
LIPPS LEARN



LIPPS Learn delivers structured public-health courses that move from explanation to application to assessment. The goal is not to memorise terminology, but to recognise a problem, choose a defensible approach and interpret evidence correctly.

Explore Epidemiology Explore Health Communication

title: Learn the discipline. Practise the reasoning.
text:
Flagship courses


12 weeks Weekly quiz Applied cases

Epidemiology
Learn how epidemiologists define health problems, measure disease, compare groups, choose study designs, recognise bias, evaluate screening tests, investigate outbreaks and judge causal claims.
Best suited to: public-health, medicine, nursing, allied-health and postgraduate learners.
View the 12-week course →



12 weeks Weekly quiz Applied cases

Health Communication
Learn how people receive, interpret and act on health information—from interpersonal communication and audience analysis to campaign design, digital media, misinformation and risk communication.
Best suited to: public-health, health-promotion, clinical and communication learners.
View the 12-week course →

title: Learn the discipline. Practise the reasoning.
text:
The LIPPS weekly learning cycle
Every week uses the same structure so students know exactly how to study.


01 — ORIENT
Learning outcomes, key question and why the topic matters.


02 — LEARN
Narrative teaching with diagrams, examples and core concepts.


03 — APPLY
A realistic public-health case, worked example or decision problem.


04 — PRACTISE
Objective questions with immediate explanatory feedback.


05 — DEMONSTRATE
A timed weekly quiz that tests recognition, application and interpretation.

title: Learn the discipline. Practise the reasoning.
text:
Assessment that rewards preparation
LIPPS uses objective questions for weekly checks, but the mastery target is application rather than recall. The current v1 pilot banks contain a mixture of strong applied items, repeated calculation variants and foundation-level concept checks. Before high-stakes institutional use, the mastery pools must be separated from practice items and reviewed against a formal blueprint.


Scenario first
Instead of asking for a definition, questions present a short public-health situation and ask the learner to identify the best interpretation, design, measure or action.


Time-disciplined
Weekly mastery quizzes use a short, transparent time limit that gives a prepared learner enough time to read, reason and answer without rewarding extensive external searching.


Randomised
Questions are sampled from larger topic banks, options can be shuffled, and calculation questions can use parameterised values so learners do not all receive identical tests.



Accessible by design
Copy and paste remain available. LIPPS does not depend on disabling normal browser functions to protect an assessment. Institutions can provide approved extra-time accommodations while retaining the same question blueprint.

Read the LIPPS assessment model →
See the university pilot assessment blueprints →

title: Learn the discipline. Practise the reasoning.
text:
Public syllabus. Private learning record.
The public LIPPS website explains each course and keeps the syllabus discoverable. LIPPS Learn, powered by Moodle, handles enrolment, lessons, quizzes, grades and progress.

LIPPS website → Choose a course → LIPPS Learn (Moodle) → Study → Practise → Timed quiz → Progress

This separation keeps LIPPS open and discoverable while giving enrolled learners and universities a proper learning-management environment.

title: Learn the discipline. Practise the reasoning.
Health-Facility Readiness Under Incomplete Information
text:
Health systems Facility assessment R


Emergency and fragile settings often require rapid decisions from facility-assessment data collected under imperfect access, incomplete records and uneven operational conditions.



How should facility readiness be estimated and communicated when the observed assessment data are incomplete and the decision-maker still needs an operational answer?



Demonstration status: synthetic/public teaching data only in the LIPPS starter. Replace with a documented, ethically appropriate dataset before publication.




Audit completeness and structural missingness.
Define indicator denominators explicitly.
Construct domain-level readiness measures.
Quantify uncertainty rather than present scores as exact truths.
Conduct sensitivity analyses around important assumptions.
Interpret operationally rather than rank facilities mechanically.




Document missing fields, duplicate facilities, impossible combinations, unavailable services and any distinction between not assessed, not available and not functioning.



See Survey Analysis Strategies and Data Quality.



# Demonstration placeholder for the project analysis.
# Replace with a reproducible script/notebook when the teaching dataset is added.



This starter deliberately contains no invented empirical results. The published project should generate all tables and figures from the accompanying dataset and code.



Readiness estimates should be interpreted against the assessment frame, indicator definitions, missingness and operational context.

What could fool us?
A readiness score may appear objective while embedding arbitrary indicator weights, missing-data assumptions, incomparable denominators or unequal access to facilities during data collection.




Published projects should state dataset provenance, licence, software versions, code repository, last update and citation information.

The attached CDC Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition is used as the primary source foundation where it directly supports the topic.
Primarily source-grounded: definition and applications of epidemiology; person-place-time description; study-design distinctions; cohort and case-control logic; measures of frequency and association; surveillance; outbreak investigation; sensitivity, specificity and predictive value positive; basic p-value and confidence-interval interpretation.
Explicit LIPPS extensions: complex-survey analysis implications; prevalence ratio/difference; matching; censoring and time-varying exposure; allocation concealment, blinding, cluster randomisation and intention-to-treat; quasi-experimental taxonomy; differential/non-differential misclassification; mediators, colliders and effect modification; NPV, likelihood ratios, ROC/AUC, serial/parallel algorithms, agreement/kappa and diagnostic-study biases; estimands, internal/external validity language and the LIPPS EVIDENCE appraisal framework.
The course pages label these additions so the source is not made to support concepts it does not develop.



The course now has a coherent progression:
Think epidemiologically → measure frequency → compare groups → describe patterns → understand observational designs → understand intervention designs → recognise threats to validity → evaluate tests → conduct surveillance/outbreak reasoning → critically interpret evidence.
Each new week contains:

explicit learning outcomes;
an orienting public-health problem;
explanatory teaching sections;
applied examples or calculations;
a larger integrated problem;
practice questions;
a timed mastery specification;
source/adaptation notes; and
forward/back course navigation.





Copy/paste remains available.
AI resilience relies on item design, random banks, scenario application, parameterised calculations, option shuffling and calibrated timing.
The current time limits are pilot settings, not fixed validity claims.
Moodle user/group overrides should provide approved extra time.
Timing must be calibrated against actual student response distributions so that reading speed, disability, network/device latency or language proficiency does not become the construct being tested.




The current 680 items are pilot teaching items, not a psychometrically validated examination bank. Before formal high-stakes use:

have a second epidemiology subject-matter expert review all items;
pilot items with students;
examine item difficulty, discrimination and distractor performance;
examine response times and non-response near timeout;
rewrite ambiguous or overly cueable distractors;
check calculation tolerances and Moodle import behaviour;
review accessibility with keyboard and screen-reader workflows;
check local curriculum alignment and assessment regulations; and
run native quarto render once Quarto is installed in the deployment environment.




Quarto is not installed in the current build environment, so native Quarto rendering was not executed here. Static HTML previews were generated with Pandoc for content and navigation inspection. A final quarto render remains required before production deployment.



A deeper audit found substantial repeated parameterisation in several banks. This is useful for calculation practice but can inflate the apparent breadth of assessment coverage. Mastery pools should reduce repeated numerical variants and increase interpretation, design choice, bias diagnosis and integrated decision items. See QA-UNIVERSITY-READINESS.md.

title: LIPPS
section: Find the right way to answer the question.
text:
Find the right way to answer the question.
Explore practical guidance on research design, sampling, survey methodology, statistical analysis, measurement, diagnostic studies, causal reasoning, data quality, qualitative methods and interpretation.


Design
Choose a study design that matches the research question, estimand, setting and feasible level of inference.


Sampling
Select people, households, facilities and clusters in ways that support valid estimation.


Surveys
Move correctly from survey design to weighting, variance estimation, modelling and interpretation.


Analysis
Choose analytical strategies based on the outcome, design, estimand and assumptions—not software menus.


Causal reasoning
Recognise bias, confounding, mediation, interaction and the limits of causal claims.


Interpretation
Turn estimates, uncertainty and model outputs into defensible scientific conclusions.


EXPLORE METHODS

title: LIPPS
section: A good analysis does not begin with software.
text:
A good analysis does not begin with software.

Question → Design → Measurement → Data → Analysis → Interpretation → Decision


What could the evidence be hiding? At every stage, LIPPS asks what could make the observed evidence misleading: selection, measurement error, missingness, bias, modelling assumptions, uncertainty or context.

title: LIPPS
section: Bring rigorous methods to your own work.
text:
Bring rigorous methods to your own work.
LIPPS Studio supports universities, research teams and organisations with research design, epidemiological analysis, survey analysis, statistical modelling, data-quality assessment, dashboards, research-methods training and institutional capacity building.
WORK WITH LIPPS

title: LIPPS
text:
Reason beyond the output.
Evidence is always observed through something: a sample, a measurement, a record, a model or an interpretation. What we observe may therefore not perfectly represent what actually happened.
The name LIPPS is inspired by the Signor–Lipps effect in palaeontology—a reminder that an incomplete record can produce a misleading picture of reality.
Research faces the same challenge. Samples are incomplete. Measurements contain error. Records are missing. Associations can mislead. Context matters.
LIPPS exists to help people reason beyond the output.
ABOUT LIPPS

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
text:
LIPPS LEARN · HEALTH COMMUNICATION · WEEK 09





RCCE Uncertainty Trust Emergency

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
text: RCCE Uncertainty Trust Emergency

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
text:
This week in one sentence
Communicate rapidly and transparently during health threats while acknowledging uncertainty, supporting protective action, listening to affected communities and adapting as evidence changes.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
Risk and Crisis Communication
text:
ORIENT · Waiting for perfect information
Several patients develop severe unexplained haemorrhagic illness. Laboratory confirmation is pending. Officials delay public communication because they fear being wrong. Meanwhile, rumours spread that the hospital is hiding deaths and people begin avoiding care.
In emergencies, silence also communicates. The question is not whether uncertainty exists; it is how to communicate responsibly while uncertainty exists.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: LEARN 1 · Risk communication is real-time exchange for protective decisions
text:
LEARN 1 · Risk communication is real-time exchange for protective decisions
WHO defines risk communication as the real-time exchange of information, advice and opinions between experts or officials and people facing a hazard. The purpose is to enable informed decisions that reduce harm. It includes media work, digital communication and community engagement.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: LEARN 2 · Speed and accuracy are not opposites
text:
LEARN 2 · Speed and accuracy are not opposites
Communicate early with what is verified, clearly distinguish preliminary information, and update as evidence changes. Delaying until every detail is certain creates information voids and can allow rumours to define the situation.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: LEARN 3 · Say what is known, unknown and being done
text:
LEARN 3 · Say what is known, unknown and being done
A useful uncertainty structure is: What we know now → what we do not yet know → what people should do now → what authorities are doing to learn more → when the next update will come. This preserves usefulness without false certainty.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: LEARN 4 · Risk perception is not determined by probability alone
text:
LEARN 4 · Risk perception is not determined by probability alone
People may perceive greater risk when hazards are unfamiliar, involuntary, catastrophic, invisible, unfair or associated with low institutional trust. Communicators should understand these perceptions rather than dismiss them as irrational.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: LEARN 5 · Action messages should be feasible and prioritised
text:
LEARN 5 · Action messages should be feasible and prioritised
During a crisis, cognitive load is high. Prioritise a small number of protective actions, explain who should act, where and when, and update instructions as the situation changes. Avoid flooding audiences with every technical detail at once.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: LEARN 6 · Empathy and respect support credibility
text:
LEARN 6 · Empathy and respect support credibility
Acknowledge fear, loss, inconvenience and uncertainty. Empathy does not mean exaggerating emotion; it signals that public concerns are understood. Dismissive language can undermine technically accurate guidance.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
text:
LEARN 7 · Coordination prevents contradiction
Response agencies should align core facts, terminology, action recommendations and update schedules. Differences in institutional roles can be explained, but preventable contradictions rapidly damage confidence.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: LEARN 8 · Community engagement is part of emergency communication
text:
LEARN 8 · Community engagement is part of emergency communication
WHO’s current RCCE approach emphasises community-centred emergency programmes. Listening mechanisms should identify questions, rumours, barriers and unintended effects of response measures, and those insights should reach operational teams.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: LEARN 9 · Changing guidance should be explained, not hidden
text:
LEARN 9 · Changing guidance should be explained, not hidden
When evidence changes, explain what changed and why. A transparent revision can strengthen credibility; pretending that earlier guidance never existed invites distrust.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
text:
LEARN 10 · Prepare before the emergency
Build spokesperson capacity, audience maps, channel agreements, translation workflows, social-listening systems, approval pathways and simulation exercises before a crisis. Preparedness reduces the delay between signal and useful communication.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: DEEPEN · Communicating when evidence is incomplete
text:
DEEPEN · Communicating when evidence is incomplete
Risk communication becomes most important when information is changing, consequences matter and people are anxious. Waiting for perfect certainty can create an information vacuum that others fill.
CDC’s Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication approach emphasises communication that is early, accurate, credible, empathetic, action-oriented and respectful. WHO’s RCCE framework similarly places communities at the centre of preparedness and response.

The first announcement
A strong first announcement should state what happened, what is known, what is not yet known, what authorities are doing, what people should do now, and when more information will be provided. Do not create false reassurance by turning uncertainty into certainty.


Risk is interpreted socially
People judge risk through more than probability. Dread, unfamiliarity, fairness, control, trust and whether children are affected can change perceived risk. A communication team should understand these concerns rather than dismissing them as irrational.


Empathy before explanation
Acknowledging fear, loss or disruption creates space for technical information. Empathy does not mean exaggerating danger or agreeing with false claims. It signals that the response understands what people are experiencing.


Spokesperson discipline
Spokespeople should know what they can confirm, what they cannot confirm and who has authority to speak. Speculation becomes especially damaging when different agencies contradict one another. Coordination should reduce unnecessary inconsistency without suppressing legitimate uncertainty.


Update rhythm
Commit to the next update even when no major new finding is expected. “We will update at 4 p.m.” is more credible than silence. Correct previous information openly when evidence changes and explain why the recommendation changed.


Community feedback during crisis
Hotlines, local leaders, health workers and digital monitoring can reveal emerging questions and rumours. Feedback must be analysed quickly enough to change communication or operations.


What could fool us?
A drop in public questions may reflect reassurance, but it may also mean people stopped trusting official channels. High media coverage can coexist with low comprehension. Crisis evaluation should therefore triangulate reach, understanding, trust, action and operational data.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
section: FIELD LAB · Draft the first public statement
text:
FIELD LAB · Draft the first public statement
A first statement can follow this order:

Acknowledge: recognise what people are experiencing.
State what is known: use only verified information and a clear cut-off time.
State what is not known: identify the most important uncertainties.
Give action: tell people what they can do now.
Describe the response: explain what authorities are doing.
Commit to an update: give a time or trigger for the next communication.

Example opening: “We are investigating a cluster of acute watery diarrhoea reported since yesterday in three villages. Samples are being tested. People in the affected area should use treated or boiled water, wash hands with soap, and seek care immediately for severe diarrhoea or signs of dehydration. We will provide the next update at 4 p.m. today.”
The statement avoids declaring a cause before evidence is available while still enabling protective action.

Update log
Maintain a table of time, new evidence, message change, reason for change, channels used and unresolved questions. This prevents contradictory statements and makes later evaluation possible.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A district reports suspected cholera after severe flooding. Laboratory confirmation will take 24 hours. Several water points are damaged, social media claims that chlorine is poisonous, and residents say previous emergency messages arrived only in English.

Draft the first public statement using known/unknown/action/update structure.
Select three immediate protective actions and explain why they are prioritised.
Identify audiences requiring different operational information.
Choose messengers and channels for the first 12 hours.
Design a community-listening mechanism.
Plan how to respond to the chlorine concern without amplifying it unnecessarily.
State what you would communicate when laboratory confirmation arrives.
Identify one operational response problem that communication must escalate.

title: Risk and Crisis Communication
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

title: Foundations of Health Communication
text: Foundation Communication process Trust Actionability

title: Foundations of Health Communication
text:
This week in one sentence
Explain health communication as a strategic public-health process that connects evidence, audiences, messages, channels, feedback and action.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Foundations of Health Communication
Foundations of Health Communication
section: ORIENT · The poster that nobody understood
text:
ORIENT · The poster that nobody understood
A district launches a technically accurate poster telling caregivers to seek care promptly for childhood danger signs. The poster contains dense clinical language, appears only at health facilities, and was developed without talking to caregivers. Staff later conclude that “the community is resistant” because care-seeking does not change.
A health communicator asks different questions: Who needed the information? What decision were they expected to make? Could they understand the message? Did they trust the source? Did the message reach them before the decision point? Was the recommended action actually feasible?

title: Foundations of Health Communication
section: LEARN 1 · Health communication is a public-health function, not decoration
text:
LEARN 1 · Health communication is a public-health function, not decoration
Health communication is the strategic use of communication processes to inform and influence decisions that improve health. It includes much more than producing posters, giving health talks or posting on social media. It begins with a defined health or behavioural problem, identifies who must make or support a decision, studies the context in which that decision occurs, and then selects messages, messengers and channels that can realistically help.
A communication product is therefore not the intervention by itself. A radio spot, counselling script or WhatsApp post is one component of a larger communication strategy.

title: Foundations of Health Communication
section: LEARN 2 · Information sent is not the same as communication achieved
text:
LEARN 2 · Information sent is not the same as communication achieved
A simple linear model imagines a sender transmitting a message through a channel to a receiver. That model is useful, but real health communication is more transactional: people interpret, question, resist, reinterpret and respond. Feedback changes subsequent communication. Social norms, language, power, trust, competing messages and practical barriers all shape meaning.
A message can be delivered exactly as intended and still fail because the audience did not notice it, did not understand it, did not believe it, or could not act on it.

title: Foundations of Health Communication
text:
LEARN 3 · The communication chain
A practical diagnostic sequence is source → message → channel → audience → interpretation → response → feedback. Around that chain sits context: culture, politics, health-system experience, urgency, media environment, literacy, cost and access. “Noise” can be literal, such as a poor radio signal, or conceptual, such as conflicting advice from trusted people.

title: Foundations of Health Communication
section: LEARN 4 · Start with the decision you want to support
text:
LEARN 4 · Start with the decision you want to support
Communication objectives should describe what a defined audience should know, feel, decide or do as a result of communication. They are different from distal health outcomes. “Reduce maternal mortality” is a programme goal; “increase the proportion of pregnant women who can correctly identify three emergency danger signs and know where to seek urgent care” is closer to a communication objective.
The more specific the intended decision, the easier it is to design and evaluate communication.

title: Foundations of Health Communication
section: LEARN 5 · Levels of health communication interact
text:
LEARN 5 · Levels of health communication interact
Interpersonal communication includes counselling, clinical encounters and peer dialogue. Organisational communication includes communication within facilities and institutions. Community communication involves dialogue with groups, leaders and local structures. Mass communication includes radio, television, print and large-reach campaigns. Digital communication includes social media, messaging platforms, websites, apps and SMS.
These levels reinforce one another. A radio campaign may create awareness, while a village health worker answers questions and a clinic makes the recommended service available.

title: Foundations of Health Communication
section: LEARN 6 · Effective communication has quality dimensions
text:
LEARN 6 · Effective communication has quality dimensions
WHO’s strategic communication approach emphasises communication that is actionable, accessible, relevant, timely, understandable and credible. These are useful design tests. A message can be scientifically correct but arrive too late. It can be clear but impossible to act on. It can be accessible online but not to people without data bundles or smartphones.
LIPPS adds one question: What evidence would show that the communication actually helped the intended decision?

title: Foundations of Health Communication
section: LEARN 7 · Trust is part of the message
text:
LEARN 7 · Trust is part of the message
People evaluate not only what is said but who says it and whether that source has behaved credibly before. Trust is affected by consistency, transparency, competence, respect, fairness and previous experience with health services. Borrowing a famous spokesperson cannot compensate for an institution that repeatedly gives contradictory or dismissive information.

title: Foundations of Health Communication
section: LEARN 8 · Communication failure is often misdiagnosed as audience failure
text:
LEARN 8 · Communication failure is often misdiagnosed as audience failure
When behaviour does not change, communicators should resist blaming “ignorance”, “culture” or “resistance” too quickly. The failure may lie in unclear objectives, poor audience insight, inaccessible services, contradictory recommendations, weak messenger credibility, inappropriate timing or a channel that never reached the intended group.
The first skill in health communication is therefore diagnosis, not message writing.

title: Foundations of Health Communication
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A district wants adults with persistent cough to seek tuberculosis testing earlier. Current posters say: “All presumptive TB clients should report to the nearest DOTS facility for sputum evaluation.” Testing is free, but community interviews show that many people do not know what “presumptive”, “DOTS” or “sputum evaluation” mean. Some worry that being seen at the TB clinic will expose their HIV status. Others cannot leave work during clinic hours.

State the health problem separately from the communication problem.
Identify the primary audience and at least two secondary audiences.
Write one measurable communication objective.
Identify source, message, channel, audience, context, feedback and likely noise.
List at least three non-communication barriers that messaging alone cannot solve.
Explain why “more posters” may not be the best first response.
Propose one interpersonal, one community and one mass/digital communication component that could work together.
State what you would measure before claiming success.

LIPPS LEARN · HEALTH COMMUNICATION · WEEK 04





Listening Teach-back Shared decisions Trust

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
text: Listening Teach-back Shared decisions Trust

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
text:
This week in one sentence
Use patient-centred interpersonal communication to elicit concerns, explain information clearly, check understanding and support informed decisions.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: ORIENT · The patient nodded—but did not understand
text:
ORIENT · The patient nodded—but did not understand
A clinician tells a patient with newly diagnosed hypertension to “reduce sodium, adhere to medication and review in four weeks.” The patient nods throughout. At the next visit, the clinician discovers that the patient stopped the tablets after three days because symptoms improved and did not understand what foods contain salt. Nodding was interpreted as comprehension.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 1 · The encounter is a communication system
text:
LEARN 1 · The encounter is a communication system
Clinical communication includes agenda setting, eliciting concerns, explanation, emotional response, decision-making, checking understanding and follow-up. The clinician brings technical expertise; the patient brings goals, lived experience, beliefs, constraints and preferences.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
text:
LEARN 2 · Listening is an intervention
Open questions invite the patient’s account; closed questions can clarify details. Reflective listening tests whether you understood. Summaries organise the conversation and expose disagreement. Interrupting early can make the consultation faster in the short term but less efficient when crucial concerns emerge later.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 3 · Empathy is not the same as agreement
text:
LEARN 3 · Empathy is not the same as agreement
Empathy communicates that the person’s experience has been heard and taken seriously. It does not require agreeing with every belief. A response such as “I can see why that result frightened you; let us go through what it means” can maintain trust while correcting misunderstanding.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 4 · Teach-back checks the communication, not the intelligence
text:
LEARN 4 · Teach-back checks the communication, not the intelligence
Teach-back asks the patient to explain the plan in their own words: “I want to make sure I explained this clearly. How will you take these tablets when you get home?” If the explanation is wrong, the communicator re-explains and checks again. The responsibility is placed on the clarity of the explanation.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 5 · Shared decision-making requires genuine options
text:
LEARN 5 · Shared decision-making requires genuine options
When more than one reasonable option exists, shared decision-making combines clinical evidence with patient values and preferences. It is not simply giving the patient a leaflet or asking them to choose without support.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 6 · Motivational interviewing: evoke rather than lecture
text:
LEARN 6 · Motivational interviewing: evoke rather than lecture
Selected motivational interviewing skills—open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries—can help people explore ambivalence. The approach respects autonomy and tries to elicit the person’s own reasons for change rather than using argument or threat. Full motivational interviewing requires practice beyond one course module.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 7 · Risk communication works better with balanced, concrete formats
text:
LEARN 7 · Risk communication works better with balanced, concrete formats
Use consistent denominators, absolute risks and visual aids when helpful. Explain both potential benefit and harm. Check what the number means to the patient. Avoid presenting a relative reduction without baseline risk when that could exaggerate perceived benefit.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 8 · Language barriers require more than speaking slowly
text:
LEARN 8 · Language barriers require more than speaking slowly
Where professional interpretation is needed and available, use it rather than relying automatically on children or untrained relatives, particularly for sensitive or high-stakes discussions. Speak to the patient, use short segments, avoid jargon and confirm understanding.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 9 · Power, stigma and confidentiality change what people are willing to say
text:
LEARN 9 · Power, stigma and confidentiality change what people are willing to say
Patients may withhold information if they expect judgement, disclosure or discrimination. Privacy, respectful language and explicit confidentiality expectations are therefore part of data quality as well as ethics.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: LEARN 10 · Close with an executable plan
text:
LEARN 10 · Close with an executable plan
Before ending, clarify what happens next, where, when, what warning signs matter, and what to do if the plan becomes difficult. A plan that cannot be executed is not improved by repeating it more loudly.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: DEEPEN · The clinical encounter is a decision environment
text:
DEEPEN · The clinical encounter is a decision environment
Interpersonal communication is not simply a polite way to transmit instructions. It shapes whether concerns are disclosed, whether risks are understood and whether a patient can participate in a decision. A technically correct explanation can fail if the patient is interrupted, embarrassed, frightened, rushed or uncertain whether the conversation is confidential.

A practical consultation sequence
LIPPS uses five moves: invite → listen → explain → check → agree.

Invite the patient’s agenda before assuming the problem.
Listen for concerns, expectations, prior experiences and constraints.
Explain the most important information in plain language and manageable chunks.
Check understanding using teach-back rather than “Do you understand?”
Agree on the next step, including what to do if circumstances change.

Teach-back is not a test of the patient. The clinician asks the patient to explain the plan in their own words so the clinician can test whether the explanation worked.


Shared decision-making and informed choice
When more than one reasonable option exists, communication should help the patient understand choices, likely benefits, harms and uncertainty, then incorporate what matters to that patient. Persuasion becomes ethically problematic when information is selectively framed to push a preferred choice while pretending the decision is shared.


Difficult conversations
Bad news, sexual and reproductive health, HIV testing, mental health and end-of-life discussions require privacy, empathy and clear language. Empathy is not agreement with every belief. It is recognition of the person’s experience before moving to information or action.


Motivational interviewing as a communication stance
For ambivalent behaviour, arguing can strengthen resistance. A motivational approach uses open questions, reflective listening and eliciting the person’s own reasons for change. This week introduces the stance; it does not certify students as motivational-interviewing practitioners.


Confidentiality and power
A young person may give very different answers if a parent, partner or security officer is in the room. Communication quality therefore depends on the physical and social environment, not merely the clinician’s wording.


What could fool us?
Patient satisfaction is not identical to understanding, and understanding is not identical to adherence. A patient may correctly understand a plan but be unable to afford it. Conversely, apparent “non-compliance” may reveal that the original plan was not feasible. Interpretation should separate communication quality from structural barriers.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
section: FIELD LAB · Rewrite a difficult consultation
text:
FIELD LAB · Rewrite a difficult consultation
Version A
Clinician: “Your blood pressure is high. You need to take these tablets every day. Any questions?”
Patient: “No.”
The exchange is efficient but reveals almost nothing about understanding, concerns or feasibility.
Version B
Clinician: “Before I explain the tablets, what worries you most about what we found today?”
Patient: “I feel well. I am worried the medicine will make me dependent on it.”
Clinician: “That concern makes sense. High blood pressure often causes no symptoms, but over time it can damage the heart, kidneys and brain. The medicine controls the pressure; it does not create dependence. What have you heard about these medicines?”
After discussion, the clinician explains the plan in short chunks and asks: “Just so I know I explained it clearly, how will you take the tablets when you get home?”
The second consultation is not simply longer. It is better targeted: it discovers the patient’s concern, explains the relevant mechanism, checks comprehension and creates a basis for agreement.

Observation checklist
During a simulated encounter, record whether the provider: elicits the agenda; avoids interruption; uses plain language; acknowledges emotion; explains options; checks understanding; asks about feasibility; protects confidentiality; and ends with a clear agreed next step.
Use the checklist for feedback, not as a mechanical scorecard. A consultation can tick every box and still feel dismissive if tone, timing or power are ignored.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A 22-year-old patient newly diagnosed with HIV says, “I feel fine, so I do not understand why I need tablets every day.” The clinic is busy. The patient is worried that family members will discover the diagnosis and has heard online that treatment damages the kidneys.

Write two open questions that explore concerns without judgement.
Give one empathic reflection.
Explain the purpose of treatment in plain language without overwhelming the patient.
Address the kidney concern while acknowledging uncertainty appropriately.
Use teach-back to check understanding.
Identify the confidentiality issue.
Use one motivational-interviewing technique to explore readiness.
End with a clear follow-up and safety plan.

title: Interpersonal and Clinical Communication
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

What does teach-back assess?
How does empathy differ from reassurance?
Why are open questions useful early in a consultation?
When is shared decision-making appropriate?
Why might a family member be a problematic interpreter?
Give one example of a closing question that checks whether the plan is feasible.

text:
This page is an instructor-facing assessment specification for Foundations of Health Communication. It establishes the quality standard that should be used when the remaining Health Communication banks are rewritten.


Week 1 should not reward memorising isolated definitions. A prepared learner should be able to diagnose a communication problem, distinguish communication from programme constraints, select defensible objectives, interpret audience response and judge whether a communication claim is supported by evidence.
The redesigned bank contains 30 genuinely distinct items rather than multiple paraphrases of the same definition.

LO1: distinguish health communication from dissemination, publicity and information transfer alone;
LO2: analyse communication as a transactional process involving source, message, channel, audience, context, feedback and noise;

LO4: select and combine interpersonal, organisational, community, mass and digital levels appropriately;

Task: Give students a short public-health scenario containing a mixture of message, channel, trust, audience and service-delivery problems. In 800–1,000 words, students prepare a diagnostic brief that answers:

What is the health problem?
What is the communication problem — and what is not primarily a communication problem?
Who is the primary audience? Who enables or constrains the decision?
What specific decision or action should communication support?
Where are the likely weaknesses in source, message, channel, context, feedback or trust?
Which WHO communication quality dimensions are most threatened?
What one communication objective would be appropriate?
What evidence would you collect before claiming the communication worked?

Students should be rewarded for diagnosis before solution. A polished poster proposal with weak problem analysis should not score highly.














Criterion
4 — Excellent
3 — Good
2 — Developing
1 — Weak
0 — Missing / unsafe




Problem diagnosis
Clearly separates the health problem, communication problem and non-communication constraints; prioritises them logically.
Mostly separates the problems with minor ambiguity.
Identifies several issues but mixes communication and programme barriers.
Treats the problem mainly as “lack of awareness” without evidence.
No meaningful diagnosis or makes a clearly unsafe interpretation.


Audience + decision analysis
Identifies primary and supporting audiences, decision roles and contextual constraints with a clear rationale.
Correct audiences and decision identified but analysis is incomplete.
Audience is broadly identified but decision roles are vague.
Audience is defined only demographically or without relation to a decision.
No defensible audience or decision identified.


Communication-process reasoning
Correctly analyses source, message, channel, context, feedback, trust and noise, focusing on the elements that matter most.
Analyses most relevant elements accurately.
Lists elements but provides limited interpretation.
Uses communication terms superficially or incorrectly.
No usable process analysis.


Objective + proposed response
Provides a specific measurable communication objective and a response logically matched to the diagnosis; acknowledges what communication cannot solve.
Objective and response are generally appropriate with minor gaps.
Objective or response is partly appropriate but generic.
Response jumps to a channel/product without a defensible objective.
Proposed response is irrelevant, misleading or potentially harmful.


Evidence + judgement
Specifies appropriate indicators for reach/understanding/trust/action and states limits on causal claims; reasoning is concise and evidence-aware.
Identifies useful indicators and mostly cautious interpretation.
Mentions measurement but does not clearly link evidence to claims.
Relies mainly on outputs such as posters printed or views.
No evaluation logic or makes unsupported causal claims.



Suggested pass standard: 10/20, with no score of 0 in Problem diagnosis or Evidence + judgement. Institutions can adjust this threshold to their regulations.



Every future mastery or institutional question should, where possible:

begin with a plausible public-health decision or communication situation;
require application, analysis or evaluation rather than term recognition alone;
use distractors that reflect realistic reasoning errors;
have one defensibly best answer;
give explanatory feedback that teaches the reasoning, not merely labels the answer;
avoid testing trivia that could be answered without understanding the communication problem;
distinguish communication failure from service, policy or access failure; and
avoid overclaiming causation from reach, recall or simple before/after observations.

title: Health Communication Week 1 — Assessment Blueprint
text:
Task: Give students a short public-health scenario containing a mixture of message, channel, trust, audience and service-delivery problems. In 800–1,000 words, students prepare a diagnostic brief that answers:

What is the health problem?
What is the communication problem — and what is not primarily a communication problem?
Who is the primary audience? Who enables or constrains the decision?
What specific decision or action should communication support?
Where are the likely weaknesses in source, message, channel, context, feedback or trust?
Which WHO communication quality dimensions are most threatened?
What one communication objective would be appropriate?
What evidence would you collect before claiming the communication worked?

Students should be rewarded for diagnosis before solution. A polished poster proposal with weak problem analysis should not score highly.

title: Health Communication Week 1 — Assessment Blueprint
text:
Criterion
4 — Excellent
3 — Good
2 — Developing
1 — Weak
0 — Missing / unsafe




Problem diagnosis
Clearly separates the health problem, communication problem and non-communication constraints; prioritises them logically.
Mostly separates the problems with minor ambiguity.
Identifies several issues but mixes communication and programme barriers.
Treats the problem mainly as “lack of awareness” without evidence.
No meaningful diagnosis or makes a clearly unsafe interpretation.


Audience + decision analysis
Identifies primary and supporting audiences, decision roles and contextual constraints with a clear rationale.
Correct audiences and decision identified but analysis is incomplete.
Audience is broadly identified but decision roles are vague.
Audience is defined only demographically or without relation to a decision.
No defensible audience or decision identified.


Communication-process reasoning
Correctly analyses source, message, channel, context, feedback, trust and noise, focusing on the elements that matter most.
Analyses most relevant elements accurately.
Lists elements but provides limited interpretation.
Uses communication terms superficially or incorrectly.
No usable process analysis.


Objective + proposed response
Provides a specific measurable communication objective and a response logically matched to the diagnosis; acknowledges what communication cannot solve.
Objective and response are generally appropriate with minor gaps.
Objective or response is partly appropriate but generic.
Response jumps to a channel/product without a defensible objective.
Proposed response is irrelevant, misleading or potentially harmful.


Evidence + judgement
Specifies appropriate indicators for reach/understanding/trust/action and states limits on causal claims; reasoning is concise and evidence-aware.
Identifies useful indicators and mostly cautious interpretation.
Mentions measurement but does not clearly link evidence to claims.
Relies mainly on outputs such as posters printed or views.
No evaluation logic or makes unsupported causal claims.



Suggested pass standard: 10/20, with no score of 0 in Problem diagnosis or Evidence + judgement. Institutions can adjust this threshold to their regulations.

LIPPS LEARN · HEALTH COMMUNICATION · WEEK 10





Infodemic Misinformation Social listening Resilience

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
text: Infodemic Misinformation Social listening Resilience

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
text:
This week in one sentence
Identify harmful information problems, prioritise them by likely health impact and respond through listening, accurate communication, trusted messengers, community engagement and resilience-building.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: ORIENT · The rumour is false—but should you repeat it?
text:
ORIENT · The rumour is false—but should you repeat it?
A voice note claims that a new vaccine causes infertility. It has circulated in several closed messaging groups and a local radio presenter mentions it on air. A health agency drafts a poster with the rumour in huge red letters: “THE VACCINE DOES NOT CAUSE INFERTILITY.” Before publishing, the team should ask whether the correction will reduce harm or inadvertently spread the claim to people who had never heard it.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 1 · Define the information problem carefully
text:
LEARN 1 · Define the information problem carefully
Misinformation is false or misleading information shared without necessarily intending harm. Disinformation involves deliberate creation or spread of false or misleading information for strategic purposes. A rumour is unverified information circulating within a community. An infodemic is an overabundance of information—including false or misleading information—that creates confusion and can undermine health action.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 2 · Infodemics are not only about false facts
text:
LEARN 2 · Infodemics are not only about false facts
People can be overwhelmed by contradictory guidance, outdated information, technical complexity, scams and true information stripped of context. Management therefore requires improving the overall information environment, not merely fact-checking false posts.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 3 · Information voids are a warning signal
text:
LEARN 3 · Information voids are a warning signal
When people have urgent unanswered questions, others fill the gap. Monitor what people are asking: eligibility, safety, side effects, access, cost, cause, responsibility and uncertainty. Fast, clear answers to genuine questions can prevent harmful narratives from gaining traction.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 4 · Social listening should produce actionable insight
text:
LEARN 4 · Social listening should produce actionable insight
Collect recurring questions and narratives, assess where they circulate, identify affected audiences, estimate likely harm and determine what response is possible. WHO frames infodemic management around listening, promoting understanding of risk and expert advice, building resilience to misinformation, and engaging communities for positive action.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 5 · Not every false claim deserves a mass response
text:
LEARN 5 · Not every false claim deserves a mass response
Prioritise according to potential health harm, reach, velocity, credibility of the source, vulnerability of the audience and whether the claim changes behaviour. Publicly rebutting an obscure claim can amplify it.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 6 · Corrections should make the useful truth easy to remember
text:
LEARN 6 · Corrections should make the useful truth easy to remember
Lead with the accurate information and the action people need. Briefly identify the false claim only when necessary for recognition, explain why it is wrong using clear evidence, and repeat the accurate conclusion. Avoid ridicule; it can harden identity-based resistance and damage relationships.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 7 · Prebunking builds resilience before exposure
text:
LEARN 7 · Prebunking builds resilience before exposure
Prebunking or inoculation approaches warn people about common manipulation techniques or likely misleading narratives before they encounter them. The aim is not to predict every rumour, but to strengthen recognition of unreliable tactics and encourage verification habits.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 8 · Trusted messengers and community dialogue matter
text:
LEARN 8 · Trusted messengers and community dialogue matter
A technically correct correction from a distrusted institution may fail. Work with health workers, community leaders, journalists and other credible intermediaries while ensuring they understand the evidence and are not used merely as endorsement props.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 9 · Measure beyond number of corrections issued
text:
LEARN 9 · Measure beyond number of corrections issued
Possible indicators include time from detection to response, unanswered information needs, reach of accurate content among affected audiences, changes in belief certainty, intended protective action, trust, and whether harmful narratives decline or persist. Attribution is difficult because information environments are dynamic.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: LEARN 10 · Ethics and privacy still apply
text:
LEARN 10 · Ethics and privacy still apply
Social listening should minimise collection of identifiable information, avoid targeting individuals for punishment, and distinguish public-interest analysis from intrusive surveillance. Vulnerable groups should not be exposed or stigmatised through screenshots or examples.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: DEEPEN · Manage information risk, not every incorrect sentence
text:
DEEPEN · Manage information risk, not every incorrect sentence
WHO describes an infodemic as an overabundance of information, including false or misleading information, that can create confusion, mistrust and harmful behaviour. Infodemic management is therefore broader than fact-checking individual posts.

Distinguish the information problem
Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without necessarily intending harm. Disinformation is deliberately false or manipulated information intended to deceive. Harmful communication may also involve technically true information used out of context. The response depends on reach, credibility, audience vulnerability and likely health impact—not only truth status.


Listen before correcting
Social listening, community feedback, hotline questions and frontline-worker reports help identify recurring concerns and information voids. Code concerns by topic, audience, location, channel and potential consequence. Protect privacy and avoid storing unnecessary personal identifiers.


Prioritise
Not every rumour deserves amplification. A practical matrix considers reach, growth, credibility, behavioural consequence and affected population. A false claim seen by ten people may need quiet correction; a rapidly growing claim that discourages emergency care may require immediate coordinated response.


Prebunking and debunking
Prebunking anticipates predictable misleading tactics or claims before they spread widely. Debunking corrects a claim after exposure. Corrections should lead with accurate information, explain the problem clearly, avoid repeating sensational falsehoods unnecessarily and give people a useful action.


Fill information voids
Silence can be an intervention failure. When authorities do not explain an adverse event, service interruption or policy change, alternative explanations flourish. Rapid, transparent communication reduces the space for speculation.


Trusted messengers and resilience
People judge information partly through relationships. Work with trusted local messengers, but do not use trust as a shortcut for poor evidence. Long-term resilience also requires media and health literacy, community dialogue and institutions that respond to legitimate concerns.


What could fool us?
Online volume is not the same as population belief. Bots and highly active users can distort apparent prevalence. Removing a post can move the claim into less visible channels. Evaluate whether the response changes understanding, confidence or harmful behaviour—not only whether the content disappears.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
section: FIELD LAB · Triage an information signal
text:
FIELD LAB · Triage an information signal
Use a simple priority score rather than reacting equally to every rumour.








Dimension
Low priority
High priority




reach
isolated
rapidly expanding


credibility
implausible source
trusted or authority-like source


health consequence
little behavioural effect
delays care or promotes dangerous action


vulnerability
low-risk audience
people facing immediate health risk


persistence
fading
recurring across channels



A high-priority signal should trigger rapid verification, message preparation, messenger selection and monitoring. A low-priority signal may be best handled quietly through targeted clarification to avoid amplification.

Correction structure
Fact first → brief explanation → clear action → trusted source.
Example: “The measles vaccine cannot cause measles infection. It uses a weakened virus that trains the immune system. Children who are due for vaccination should attend the listed clinics this week. Updated clinic information is available from…”
The exact wording must fit the local evidence and audience. The structure keeps accurate information more prominent than the false claim.


Listening dashboard
Track topic, question/claim, source/channel, audience, location, trend, potential harm, response owner and status. Avoid retaining personal identifiers unless genuinely necessary.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
During an immunisation campaign, rumours circulate that the vaccine is part of a fertility-control programme. Some versions are low reach; another is repeated by a widely followed local personality. Health workers report that caregivers are asking whether the vaccine contains hormones.

Classify the information problems: rumour, misinformation, disinformation or unknown intent.
Identify the information void.
Create a prioritisation matrix using reach, harm, vulnerability and actionability.
Decide which claim requires public correction and which should be monitored.
Draft a short correction that begins with accurate information and a practical action.
Select trusted messengers and explain why.
Propose one prebunking/resilience activity.
Specify indicators for the next two weeks.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why is misinformation different from disinformation?
What makes an infodemic broader than a list of false claims?
Why can publicly rebutting a low-reach rumour be harmful?
Name WHO’s four broad infodemic-management activities.
What is an information void?
What ethical concern arises when social listening captures identifiable posts from vulnerable individuals?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management
text:
DEMONSTRATE · Week 10 mastery quiz
Pilot Mastery Quiz: 10 objective questions randomly sampled from a curated Week 10 bank of 30 items.
Initial time limit: 12 minutes. Mode: one question at a time; randomised item selection; answer options shuffled; limited attempts; feedback released according to course or institutional settings.

Assessment principle
Knowing the material should be the fastest strategy. Timing is calibrated to reward prepared reading and reasoning, not to replace sound question design or approved accessibility accommodations.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
text:
LIPPS LEARN · HEALTH COMMUNICATION · WEEK 07





Channels Media mix Reach Messengers

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
text: Channels Media mix Reach Messengers

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
text:
This week in one sentence
Select and combine communication channels and messengers according to audience access, trust, objective, reach, frequency, interactivity, cost and decision timing.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: ORIENT · “Put it on social media” is not a strategy
text:
ORIENT · “Put it on social media” is not a strategy
A programme wants to increase childhood immunisation in remote communities. The communications team proposes TikTok because it is “where everyone is.” Data show that many caregivers use basic phones, local radio has high reach, village health teams are trusted, and missed vaccination is strongly associated with clinic distance and uncertainty about outreach dates.
Channel choice should follow audience and objective evidence—not team preference.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: LEARN 1 · Channels perform different communication jobs
text:
LEARN 1 · Channels perform different communication jobs
Interpersonal channels are strong for dialogue and personalised questions. Community channels can support norms, local problem solving and trust. Mass media provide broad reach. Digital channels can offer speed, targeting and interaction. Print can provide durable reference information. No channel dominates every objective.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: LEARN 2 · Choose channels against explicit criteria
text:
LEARN 2 · Choose channels against explicit criteria
Consider reach, frequency, credibility, accessibility, cost, speed, interactivity, privacy, message complexity, language and proximity to the decision point. A long counselling conversation can explain complex trade-offs; a roadside billboard cannot.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: LEARN 3 · Reach is not frequency and neither is impact
text:
LEARN 3 · Reach is not frequency and neither is impact
Reach is the number or proportion exposed. Frequency is how often they are exposed. Engagement indicates some interaction. None of these alone proves comprehension, behaviour change or health impact.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: LEARN 4 · Owned, earned, paid and shared media
text:
LEARN 4 · Owned, earned, paid and shared media
Owned channels are controlled by the organisation, such as a website or SMS list. Earned media is attention obtained through journalism or public interest. Paid media purchases placement. Shared media circulates through social networks and communities. Each has different control, credibility and cost.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
text:
LEARN 5 · Integrated communication creates reinforcement
A radio announcement can create awareness, an SMS can provide date and location, a community health worker can answer questions, and a facility sign can confirm the service point. Integration should reduce contradiction and make the pathway to action easier.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
text:
LEARN 6 · Messengers are strategic choices
A messenger should have credibility with the intended audience, understand the content and be able to communicate respectfully. The most senior official is not automatically the most trusted messenger. Health workers, peers, religious leaders, teachers, survivors or local experts may be more appropriate for particular objectives.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
text:
LEARN 7 · Media relations require preparation
Spokespersons should know key messages, likely questions, uncertainty boundaries and what cannot yet be answered. Bridges back to core points should not become evasive. Correct errors quickly and maintain consistency across spokespeople.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: LEARN 8 · Channel choice can create inequity
text:
LEARN 8 · Channel choice can create inequity
Digital-only strategies can exclude people without smartphones, data, literacy or privacy. Public loudspeakers can expose sensitive information. Printed materials may fail for visually impaired audiences. Every channel plan should include an exclusion analysis.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: LEARN 9 · Timing is part of channel strategy
text:
LEARN 9 · Timing is part of channel strategy
A reminder after the clinic has closed is useless. Communication should reach people before and during the decision window. Frequency should be sufficient for recall without creating fatigue.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: LEARN 10 · Monitor delivery and decision outcomes
text:
LEARN 10 · Monitor delivery and decision outcomes
Track whether content was delivered, who was reached, who understood, whether intended actions became easier and whether some groups were missed. Channel metrics are implementation evidence, not substitutes for programme outcomes.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: DEEPEN · Channels are delivery systems, not strategy by themselves
text:
DEEPEN · Channels are delivery systems, not strategy by themselves
“Use radio and social media” is not a communication strategy. Channel choice should follow the audience, objective, trust environment, required interaction, urgency, frequency and cost.

Channel characteristics
Mass media can provide broad reach quickly but may offer limited personal clarification. Community and interpersonal channels can support dialogue and trust but require trained people and time. Digital channels allow rapid targeting and feedback yet can exclude people without devices, data, literacy or safe private access.


Owned, earned, paid and community channels

Owned: programme websites, SMS lists, clinic screens and official social accounts.
Earned: news coverage, interviews and organic discussion not directly purchased.
Paid: advertisements, sponsored posts and purchased airtime.
Community: local leaders, health workers, peer networks, faith organisations and community gatherings.

A resilient strategy usually combines channels so that one channel creates awareness while another supports questions, trust or action.


Reach, frequency and timing
Reach asks who encountered the communication. Frequency asks how often. Repetition can support recall, but excessive exposure can produce fatigue. Timing should match the moment when the audience can act: a reminder sent after the clinic has closed is technically delivered but operationally useless.


Messenger-channel fit
The most trusted messenger may not control the highest-reach channel. A national expert can explain technical evidence, while a local health worker can address practical concerns and a peer can demonstrate social feasibility. Coordination matters so these voices do not contradict one another.


Media relations
Journalists need timely, clear and verifiable information. Prepare spokespeople to state the main message, acknowledge uncertainty, avoid speculation and correct errors without becoming defensive. Media monitoring should identify both reach and emerging misunderstanding.


Low-bandwidth design
For many public-health contexts, communication plans should assume intermittent data, shared phones and basic handsets. SMS, radio, printable materials and community networks remain important. Digital sophistication is not a substitute for accessibility.


What could fool us?
High impressions do not prove that the intended audience saw or trusted a message. A popular channel may be inappropriate for a sensitive topic. Channel analytics often describe users of the platform rather than the target population. Always interpret channel metrics against the communication objective.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
section: FIELD LAB · Give every channel a job
text:
FIELD LAB · Give every channel a job
For a cervical-screening campaign, a channel mix might look like this:









Channel
Primary job
Why it fits

The same message should not simply be copied into every channel. Radio can tell a short story; SMS needs concise logistics; a health worker can respond interactively.

Reach-frequency decision
A channel plan should state the intended audience, estimated reach, repetition schedule and decision timing. Repetition is valuable when it supports memory or confidence, but excessive frequency can create fatigue. Monitor both exposure and negative feedback.


Media briefing drill
Prepare a spokesperson to answer three questions in 30 seconds each: What is the problem? What should the public do? What remains uncertain? If the spokesperson cannot answer without jargon or speculation, the campaign is not ready for earned media.

title: Communication Channels and Media Strategy
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A district wants to increase uptake of scheduled hypertension screening days among adults over 40. Urban residents commonly use WhatsApp and radio; rural residents rely more on radio, churches, markets and village health teams. Screening is offered monthly at fixed sites. Men are less likely to attend during working hours.

State the communication objective.
Compare at least five potential channels using reach, trust, timing, interactivity and cost.
Design an integrated urban and rural media mix.
Choose appropriate messengers.
Explain how the strategy changes if confidentiality becomes a concern.
Identify one channel that looks attractive but is poorly matched to the objective.
Specify reach, frequency and action indicators.
Identify one service change that should accompany communication.
