title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
text:
LIPPS LEARN · HEALTH COMMUNICATION · WEEK 12





Ethics Equity AI Capstone

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
text: Ethics Equity AI Capstone

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
text:
This week in one sentence
Evaluate health communication for ethical integrity, equity, accessibility and responsible use of emerging technologies, then integrate the full course using the LIPPS SIGNAL framework.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
text:
ORIENT · High reach, low dignity
A campaign to encourage HIV testing uses images of visibly ill people and the slogan “Do not be the one who infects your family.” Reach is high and testing increases briefly, but people living with HIV report increased stigma and some avoid clinics because they fear being recognised.
A communication programme should not be judged only by whether it changes behaviour. Ethical harms and unequal burdens are outcomes too.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 1 · Ethics applies to both content and process
text:
LEARN 1 · Ethics applies to both content and process
Health communication should respect autonomy, promote benefit, minimise avoidable harm and distribute benefits and burdens fairly. Truthfulness, transparency and respect for persons are especially important because health messages can influence intimate decisions.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
text:
LEARN 2 · Persuasion has limits
Public health legitimately tries to encourage protective behaviour. Persuasion becomes ethically problematic when it relies on deception, hidden sponsorship, humiliation, coercive threats or manipulation that undermines informed choice. Urgency does not remove the need for honesty.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
text:
LEARN 3 · Fear can produce harm
Fear appeals may attract attention, but exaggerated threats, shame or blame can increase stigma, fatalism or avoidance. When serious risk is communicated, pair it with clear, feasible protective action and avoid assigning moral worth to disease status.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 4 · Images and stories carry power
text:
LEARN 4 · Images and stories carry power
Consent for a photograph does not automatically make every future use appropriate. Consider dignity, context, re-identification, unequal power and whether stories portray communities only as victims. Representation should avoid tokenism and stereotypes.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 5 · Privacy is part of communication ethics
text:
LEARN 5 · Privacy is part of communication ethics
Digital targeting, message history, location data, chat transcripts and audience segmentation can reveal sensitive health information. Use data minimisation, purpose limitation, secure handling and clear consent where applicable. Do not collect personal data merely because analytics make it possible.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 6 · Equity means more than translating a poster
text:
LEARN 6 · Equity means more than translating a poster
Ask which groups have less access to information, trusted messengers, digital devices, literacy support or health services. Universal design, accessible formats, local languages, low-bandwidth options and alternative channels can reduce exclusion.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 7 · AI creates speed and new failure modes
text:
LEARN 7 · AI creates speed and new failure modes
Generative AI can draft, translate, summarise and personalise communication. It can also invent facts, reproduce stereotypes, expose confidential information, produce unsafe medical advice and create convincing synthetic media. High-stakes health communication requires verified sources and accountable human review.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 8 · Personalisation can become manipulation or surveillance
text:
LEARN 8 · Personalisation can become manipulation or surveillance
Targeting messages based on behaviour or inferred vulnerability can improve relevance but may become intrusive, discriminatory or exploitative. Ask whether people reasonably expect the data use, whether sensitive attributes are inferred, and whether the targeting could harm them.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 9 · Conflicts of interest should be visible
text:
LEARN 9 · Conflicts of interest should be visible
Audiences should know when sponsors, commercial interests or political incentives may affect communication. Hidden sponsorship can undermine trust even when the factual content is correct.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 10 · LIPPS SIGNAL: a capstone planning framework
text:
LEARN 10 · LIPPS SIGNAL: a capstone planning framework
Use S — Situation: define the health and communication problem. I — Intended audience and insight: identify who must decide and what evidence says about context. G — Goal: specify the communication objective and intended mechanism. N — Narrative and needed action: decide what people need to understand, feel or do. A — Access: select messenger, channel, timing, accessibility and service pathway. L — Listen and learn: build feedback, monitoring, evaluation and adaptation.
SIGNAL is a LIPPS synthesis for structuring—not replacing—more detailed programme planning.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: LEARN 11 · Final test: does the communication earn its effect ethically?
text:
LEARN 11 · Final test: does the communication earn its effect ethically?
A strong plan should be understandable, evidence-based, feasible, inclusive, respectful and measurable. Ask not only “Will this work?” but also “For whom?”, “At what cost?”, “Who could be harmed?”, and “What would make us change course?”

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: DEEPEN · Ethical communication is part of effectiveness
text:
DEEPEN · Ethical communication is part of effectiveness
Communication that achieves a short-term behaviour change by humiliating, deceiving or excluding people is not high-quality public-health communication. Ethics should be built into problem definition, audience research, message design, data collection, targeting, evaluation and technology choices.

Autonomy and truthful persuasion
Health communication often aims to influence behaviour. Ethical persuasion provides relevant evidence, explains uncertainty and respects the person’s ability to decide. Manipulation hides material information, exploits vulnerability or creates a false impression of certainty.


Stigma and fear
Fear can attract attention, but fear without efficacy can produce avoidance, denial or stigma. Messages about HIV, TB, sexually transmitted infections, obesity, mental health or outbreak risk should avoid implying that affected people are irresponsible or dangerous simply because of their condition.


Equity
Ask not only whether average outcomes improved but who was excluded, who carried new burdens and who benefited least. A digital campaign that improves access for urban smartphone users while reducing investment in other channels may widen inequity.


Privacy, targeting and data governance
Audience segmentation can become surveillance when sensitive data are collected without necessity or clear consent. Minimise data, restrict access, establish retention rules and avoid targeting that could reveal a person’s health status to others.


Generative AI and synthetic media
AI can support drafting, translation, summarisation and chat interfaces, but it can also fabricate evidence, introduce bias or create highly persuasive synthetic content. Human review is essential for health claims. Disclose material use of synthetic media where deception is plausible, and never invent patient testimony or community endorsement.


The LIPPS SIGNAL capstone
Use S — Situation, I — Intended audience and insight, G — Goal, N — Narrative and needed action, A — Access, L — Listen and learn as a final integration tool. SIGNAL is not a substitute for formal theory or evaluation; it is a disciplined checklist that keeps communication connected to a real decision and a feedback loop.


Final critical question
Before publishing, ask: If this communication works exactly as intended, could it still harm someone? Then consider stigma, privacy, exclusion, service capacity, misunderstanding and unintended incentives.


What could fool us?
Ethical review cannot rely only on the communicator’s intention. Harms may appear in subgroups that were absent from pre-testing. AI systems can behave differently after deployment than in demonstrations. Ethical communication therefore requires monitoring, incident reporting and willingness to revise or withdraw content.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
section: FIELD LAB · Run an ethics and equity pre-mortem
text:
FIELD LAB · Run an ethics and equity pre-mortem
Before launch, imagine the communication caused harm. Ask what the most plausible failure would have been.







Domain
Pre-mortem question




autonomy
could people be manipulated or materially misled?


stigma
could a group be blamed, shamed or exposed?


equity
who cannot access or act on the message?


privacy
could targeting or notifications reveal health status?


service capacity
could successful communication create demand the system cannot meet?


AI
could automated content fabricate, discriminate or overstate certainty?


evidence
are we claiming more than the evaluation design supports?



Document the mitigation before publication. For higher-risk interventions, assign an owner and review date to each mitigation.

SIGNAL worked example
For an adolescent mental-health helpline:

Situation: low use despite high reported distress.
Intended audience and insight: adolescents know the helpline exists but fear confidentiality breaches.
Goal: increase confidence that help-seeking is private and safe.
Narrative and needed action: explain confidentiality clearly and give a discreet way to initiate contact.
Access: provide channels that work on shared phones and for low-data users.
Listen and learn: monitor confidentiality questions, complaints, comprehension and actual use.

The framework reveals that the central issue is not awareness. It also forces the team to examine privacy and access before celebrating higher call volume.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A health authority wants to use an AI chatbot and targeted social-media advertising to increase uptake of mental-health services among university students. The advertising platform can target users inferred to be interested in depression-related content. The chatbot can answer common questions but occasionally gives overconfident clinical advice. Students fear that counselling use could become known to peers or administrators.
Apply LIPPS SIGNAL: 1. Define the situation and communication problem. 2. Identify intended audiences and required formative insight. 3. Write a measurable goal. 4. Define the narrative and action without stigmatising users. 5. Design access: channels, privacy, low-bandwidth options and escalation to human care. 6. Decide whether inferred mental-health targeting is ethically acceptable and justify your position. 7. Specify AI guardrails, source verification and human oversight. 8. Build listening and evaluation mechanisms. 9. Identify at least four possible unintended harms. 10. State the conditions under which the programme should be paused or redesigned.

title: Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

What is the difference between persuasion and coercion?
Why can a campaign that changes behaviour still be ethically poor?
Give one privacy risk of personalised digital health communication.
What additional safeguard is needed when AI produces high-stakes health information?
How does equity differ from giving everyone exactly the same communication?
Apply the six letters of LIPPS SIGNAL to a simple health communication problem.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text:
LIPPS LEARN · HEALTH COMMUNICATION · WEEK 05





Participation Community listening Power RCCE

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text: Participation Community listening Power RCCE

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text:
This week in one sentence
Design community engagement as a two-way, accountable process that shares information, listens, adapts interventions and builds workable solutions with affected communities.

The LIPPS lens
Good health communication asks not only whether a message was delivered, but who interpreted it, under what conditions, what action became possible, and what evidence supports the claimed effect.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: ORIENT · The meeting had 200 people—but no engagement
text:
ORIENT · The meeting had 200 people—but no engagement
A response team holds a large community meeting during a cholera outbreak. Officials speak for 90 minutes, distribute flyers and leave. Attendance is recorded as evidence of “community engagement.” No questions are documented, women speak very little, local water vendors are absent, and the team has no mechanism to report back on concerns.
Large attendance can be mobilisation. It is not automatically participation or engagement.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: LEARN 1 · Engagement is relational, not event-based
text:
LEARN 1 · Engagement is relational, not event-based
Community engagement is an ongoing process of developing relationships and structures through which affected people help shape decisions and solutions. In emergencies, WHO frames communities as partners in creating responses that are acceptable and workable.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text:
LEARN 2 · A useful participation continuum
Communication can move from inform → consult → involve → collaborate → share leadership/empower. Not every decision can be fully delegated, but programmes should be clear about what is genuinely open to influence. Pretending to consult when decisions are already fixed damages trust.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: LEARN 3 · Stakeholder mapping should include power and trust
text:
LEARN 3 · Stakeholder mapping should include power and trust
List groups who are affected, who influence decisions, who control resources, who are trusted, who may be excluded and who can block or enable implementation. A high-ranking official may have formal power but low community trust; a local midwife or market leader may have high practical influence.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text:
LEARN 4 · Representation is never automatic
Community leaders do not necessarily represent women, adolescents, people with disabilities, displaced people, minority language groups or stigmatised populations. Ask who is missing from the room and who may not be safe speaking publicly.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text:
LEARN 5 · Listening creates programme data
Questions, complaints, rumours and resistance can reveal operational problems. If people repeatedly say vaccination teams arrive after working hours, the response is not merely to “correct misinformation.” It may require changing service delivery.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text:
LEARN 6 · Feedback loops must close
A functional loop is listen → document → analyse → decide → act → report back. If communities provide information but never hear what happened, engagement becomes extractive.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: LEARN 7 · Trust is built through behaviour
text:
LEARN 7 · Trust is built through behaviour
Transparency, consistency, respectful treatment, visible response to concerns and honest acknowledgement of constraints can strengthen trust. Communication teams cannot manufacture trust with slogans when programme behaviour contradicts the message.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: LEARN 8 · RCCE links communication and operational response
text:
LEARN 8 · RCCE links communication and operational response
Risk communication and community engagement work best when connected to surveillance, case management, vaccination, WASH, logistics and other response pillars. Community insight should change operations where evidence shows a barrier.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: LEARN 9 · Participation has ethical and safeguarding requirements
text:
LEARN 9 · Participation has ethical and safeguarding requirements
Engagement should avoid exposing people to retaliation, stigma or political risk. Consent, privacy, safe participation, fair compensation where appropriate and mechanisms for complaints matter, particularly in humanitarian settings.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: LEARN 10 · Measure quality, not just attendance
text:
LEARN 10 · Measure quality, not just attendance
Useful indicators may include diversity of participation, proportion of priority concerns receiving a documented response, time to close feedback loops, changes made because of community input, trust measures and whether affected groups can explain how to raise concerns.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: DEEPEN · Engagement changes decisions, not only messages
text:
DEEPEN · Engagement changes decisions, not only messages
Community engagement is often weakened into “sensitisation”: officials decide, then communities are informed. Genuine participation can change what problem is prioritised, how an intervention is designed, who delivers it and how implementation is corrected.

Participation has degrees
Information sharing, consultation, involvement, collaboration and community-led decision-making are not interchangeable. The appropriate level depends on the decision, urgency, legal responsibilities and available time, but teams should be honest about which level they are offering. Calling a one-way briefing “co-design” damages trust.


Representation and power
Inviting recognised leaders is useful but insufficient. Leadership structures can exclude women, adolescents, displaced people, people with disabilities, minority language groups or politically marginalised households. Engagement plans should ask: Who is affected? Who speaks? Who is missing? Who can safely disagree?


Build a feedback loop
A functioning loop has four parts: collect concerns, analyse and prioritise them, adapt the response when justified, and communicate back what changed or why it did not. Collecting complaints without closure can become extractive.


Community listening as data
Rumours, questions, hotline logs, community health-worker reports and meeting notes can reveal confusion or distrust early. They are not automatically representative survey data. Use them as signals, triangulate them and document how decisions were made.


Worked example · Cholera prevention
If residents report that chlorinated water tastes unpleasant, the response should not begin by labelling them resistant. Investigate whether dosing is correct, whether taste is expected at safe concentrations, whether alternative unsafe water sources are easier to access, and what trusted local explanations exist. The final response may involve technical correction, transparent explanation and community monitoring—not messaging alone.


Accountability and do-no-harm
Engagement creates expectations. Never promise resources you cannot deliver. Protect confidentiality when feedback could expose individuals to stigma or retaliation. In conflict settings, even selecting meeting locations or community representatives can have political consequences.


What could fool us?
High meeting attendance can coexist with low influence. Repeated consultation can create “participation fatigue” while decisions remain unchanged. Community agreement recorded in public meetings may hide private dissent. Evaluate not only how many people participated but whose input altered what.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
section: FIELD LAB · Design a feedback loop that actually closes
text:
FIELD LAB · Design a feedback loop that actually closes
Imagine a cholera response in a large settlement. Community health workers report three recurring concerns: chlorine taste, long water-point queues and confusion about where suspected cases should go.
A weak system simply records these concerns. A stronger system assigns each concern to a decision pathway:









Signal
Owner
Decision
Feedback to community




chlorine taste
WASH technical team
check dosing and explain safe range
report test result and any correction


long queues
operations team
adjust distribution schedule or add points
announce changed hours/locations


referral confusion
health/RCCE team
simplify referral instructions
publish clear route and test comprehension



The essential step is closure. Community members should be able to see whether their input changed the response. Where a request cannot be met, explain why rather than allowing silence to imply neglect.

Participation audit
At the end of an engagement cycle, ask: Which groups contributed? Which groups were missing? What decisions were genuinely open to influence? What changed because of community input? What was outside community control? Were any people exposed to stigma or retaliation by participating?
These questions turn engagement from a meeting count into an accountability process.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
An Ebola preparedness programme plans vaccination and infection-prevention activities in a border district. Community leaders support the programme, but market traders fear loss of business if cases are announced, young people rely heavily on social media, and some religious leaders are sceptical of vaccination. Previous emergency teams promised feedback but rarely returned.

Map at least six stakeholders by influence, trust and likely role.
Identify groups likely to be underrepresented if the programme consults only formal leaders.
Design three listening mechanisms.
Create a feedback loop showing who documents, analyses, acts and reports back.
Identify one operational issue that communication alone cannot solve.
Propose indicators of engagement quality.
Explain how you would engage sceptical leaders without turning them into token endorsers.
Identify one safeguarding risk and mitigation.

title: Community Engagement and Participatory Communication
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why is mobilisation not the same as engagement?
What is the risk of relying only on formal leaders?
What makes a feedback loop “closed”?
Give one example of a community concern that should change operations rather than messages.
Why can consultation damage trust when decisions are already fixed?
Name one indicator of engagement quality other than attendance.

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 01

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
text:
Epidemiology is not primarily a collection of statistical tests. It is a disciplined way of asking what is happening to health in a population, how often it is happening, to whom, where, when, why it may be happening, and what should be done with that knowledge.
Foundation Population thinking Applied reasoning Objective quiz

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
text:
This week in one sentence
Define the health event, locate it in a population, put the number in context, compare what you observe with what you would expect, and use the result to inform action.

The LIPPS lens
A number is not yet evidence. A trend is not yet an explanation. A statistical association is not yet a cause. Epidemiological thinking begins by asking what else must be known before the observation can support a conclusion.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: ORIENT · A district says malaria has doubled
text:
ORIENT · A district says malaria has doubled
Consider this fictional teaching scenario.

A district health team reports 240 laboratory-confirmed malaria cases this month, compared with 120 last month. A message quickly circulates that malaria transmission has doubled.

It sounds straightforward. It is not.
Before accepting that conclusion, an epidemiologist would ask:

Did the number of people tested also change?
Did the case definition change?
Did more facilities report this month?
Did a new diagnostic test become available?
Are both months comparable in season and population size?
Are cases concentrated in particular places or groups?
Is the increase above what is normally expected at this time of year?


Your first decision
Which statement is the most defensible from the information given?
A. Malaria incidence doubled.
B. Malaria transmission doubled.
C. The reported number of confirmed cases doubled.
D. A malaria outbreak has been confirmed.
Best answer: C. The other statements require information that has not yet been supplied.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
text:
LEARN 1 · What is epidemiology?
A widely used public-health definition describes epidemiology as the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, together with the application of that study to the control of health problems.
The definition is short, but almost every word matters.

Study
Epidemiology is systematic inquiry. It depends on deliberate collection, analysis and interpretation of observations. Quantitative reasoning is important, but epidemiology also draws on biological, behavioural, social and other knowledge when explaining patterns.


Distribution
Distribution asks how health events are distributed in the population.
It has two ideas:
Frequency — How much disease or another health event is occurring?
Pattern — How is it distributed by person, place and time?
A count tells you how many events were observed. It does not, by itself, tell you how common the event is relative to the population from which the events arose.


Determinants
Determinants are factors that influence the occurrence of health-related events. Epidemiologists examine differences in exposures, behaviours, environments, demographic characteristics and other factors that may help explain why some groups experience more disease than others.


Health-related states or events
Modern epidemiology is not limited to infectious disease. Its methods can be applied to chronic disease, injury, disability, maternal and child health, occupational and environmental health, behaviours, service use and many other conditions affecting population health.


Specified populations
Epidemiology is explicitly population-based. We need to know which population the observations came from and which population our conclusion is intended to describe.


Application
Epidemiology is not complete when the analysis ends. In public-health practice, the knowledge generated should help guide prevention, control, planning, policy, evaluation or another appropriate action.

Do not memorise the definition as a sentence.
Be able to interrogate it. What was measured? In whom? How was occurrence distributed? What might explain it? What decision could the evidence inform?

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: LEARN 2 · The five questions behind epidemiological thinking
text:
LEARN 2 · The five questions behind epidemiological thinking
A useful way to organise a health event is the familiar five-W structure.








Question
Epidemiological equivalent
Example question




What?
Health event / case definition
What exactly counts as a malaria case?


Who?
Person
Which age, sex, occupation or risk groups are affected?


Where?
Place
Which villages, facilities or geographic areas are affected?


When?
Time
When did the increase begin, and is there a seasonal pattern?


Why / how?
Determinants, causes, risk factors, transmission
What exposures or conditions could explain the pattern?



The first four questions mainly help us characterise what we observe. The fifth moves us toward explaining it.

A useful discipline
When you encounter a health claim, delay the question “Which statistical test should I use?”
First ask:

What is the health event?
What is the population?
What is the relevant time period?
What is the denominator?
What is the comparison?
What alternative explanations could produce the observation?

Only then should the analytical method enter the discussion.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: LEARN 3 · The epidemiologist’s patient is the population
text:
LEARN 3 · The epidemiologist’s patient is the population
Clinical medicine and epidemiology often examine the same disease from different levels.







Clinical question
Epidemiological question




Does this patient have cholera?
Is cholera occurrence higher than expected in this population?


What treatment does this patient need?
What source or exposure could be driving cases?


What is this patient’s prognosis?
Which groups have the highest risk, and how is risk changing?


What investigation should I order?
What data and comparisons are needed to explain the population pattern?



The clinician’s immediate unit of concern is usually the individual. Epidemiology views individuals collectively to understand the health of the population.
The disciplines are complementary. Clinical observations can generate epidemiological signals, while epidemiological evidence can change clinical and public-health practice.

LIPPS checkpoint
A hospital reports 18 children with severe diarrhoea in one week. The hospital ordinarily sees 6–10 such cases per week.
The clinician asks: How should each child be treated?
The epidemiologist asks: Is this increase real, who is affected, what exposures are shared, and is anyone else at risk?

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: LEARN 4 · Frequency is not just a count
text:
LEARN 4 · Frequency is not just a count
Suppose:

District A reports 200 cases.
District B reports 100 cases.

It is tempting to say District A has more disease.
But suppose District A has 1,000,000 residents and District B has 100,000.
The counts still matter for planning resources, but comparing population occurrence requires a denominator. This is the logic behind rates, risks and proportions that we will study formally in Week 2.

The foundational habit
Whenever you see a number, ask:

Out of how many?

Whenever you see a percentage, ask:

What exactly is in the numerator and denominator?


Evidence can mislead through denominator blindness.
A district can report more cases because it has more people, more testing, more complete reporting, or a different population structure. Week 1 teaches you to notice that problem; Week 2 teaches you how to quantify it.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
text:
LEARN 5 · Descriptive and analytic epidemiology

Descriptive epidemiology: what is happening?
Descriptive epidemiology characterises health events by time, place and person. It helps identify patterns and generate hypotheses.
Typical questions include:

When did cases increase?
Where are cases concentrated?
Which groups are most affected?
Is the pattern seasonal?



Analytic epidemiology: why might it be happening?
Analytic epidemiology goes further by comparing groups in order to examine whether an exposure or characteristic is associated with an outcome.
A critical idea is the comparison group.
If nearly every person with an illness ate a particular food, that observation may look persuasive. But if nearly everyone who remained well also ate that food, it becomes much less informative. The comparison gives the exposure history meaning.


Descriptive does not mean unimportant
Description can itself guide immediate action when a pattern is striking and delay could cause harm. More commonly, descriptive patterns generate hypotheses that are subsequently examined more rigorously.
We return to descriptive epidemiology in Week 4 and individual analytic study designs in Weeks 5–8. For now, understand the logic connecting pattern → hypothesis → comparison → interpretation.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: LEARN 6 · Four people who changed epidemiological thinking
text:
LEARN 6 · Four people who changed epidemiological thinking

Hippocrates — look for natural explanations
Around 400 BCE, Hippocratic thinking challenged purely supernatural explanations of disease and considered environmental and host-related influences on illness.
LIPPS lesson: health patterns may have systematic explanations that can be investigated.


John Graunt — count population events
In 1662, John Graunt analysed mortality records and quantified patterns in births, deaths, infant mortality, sex differences, seasonal variation and urban-rural differences.
LIPPS lesson: routinely collected records can reveal population patterns when organised and compared.


William Farr — make population measurement systematic
Farr advanced the systematic collection, classification, analysis and reporting of mortality statistics and helped establish practices associated with vital statistics and surveillance.
LIPPS lesson: useful evidence requires systems that produce comparable information over time.


John Snow — description, comparison and action
During the 1854 London cholera investigations, Snow mapped where deaths occurred, investigated water sources, compared cholera mortality across populations receiving water from different companies, and used the findings to support public-health action.
The famous map matters, but the deeper lesson is the sequence of reasoning:
observe → describe → hypothesise → compare → interpret → act.
In one comparison reproduced in the CDC lesson, districts supplied only by Southwark and Vauxhall had a cholera death rate of 5.0 per 1,000, while districts supplied only by Lambeth had 0.9 per 1,000. This supported the contaminated-water hypothesis, while still leaving room to ask whether the populations differed in other relevant ways.


Quick calculation
Without yet worrying about the formal name of the measure, approximately how many times larger is 5.0 than 0.9?
5.0 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 5.6.
Week 3 will formalise this kind of comparison.

What made Snow’s work epidemiological was not simply drawing a map.
It was the combination of defined observations, population pattern, a plausible hypothesis, comparison, critical interpretation and action.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: LEARN 7 · What is epidemiology used for?
text:
LEARN 7 · What is epidemiology used for?
The CDC lesson presents several broad uses that remain useful for organising public-health thinking.

Assess the health of a community
Epidemiological information helps determine what health problems exist, where they occur, which groups are at greater risk, which problems are increasing or declining, and whether services correspond to population need.


Inform individual decisions
Population evidence eventually influences personal choices and clinical recommendations through knowledge about risks and preventive interventions.


Complete the clinical picture
When a new or poorly understood condition emerges, aggregation of cases can help define its clinical spectrum, natural history and groups at risk.


Search for causes and prevent recurrence
Epidemiological studies can identify exposures and other factors that support prevention and control. Epidemiology may not, by itself, establish every element of biological causation, but it can generate evidence strong enough to support appropriate public-health action.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: LEARN 8 · Core epidemiological functions in public-health practice
text:
LEARN 8 · Core epidemiological functions in public-health practice
Epidemiology is not a single activity. The CDC framework identifies several interconnected functions.








Function
What it means in practice
Example




Surveillance
Ongoing collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination of health information for action
Reviewing weekly disease reports and looking for unusual patterns


Field investigation
Investigating cases, clusters or signals in their real-world setting
Visiting affected communities and tracing likely exposures


Analytic studies
Using structured comparisons to test explanations
Comparing exposure histories of affected and unaffected groups


Evaluation
Assessing whether programmes or systems are relevant, effective, efficient or achieving intended results
Evaluating whether a screening programme reaches its target population


Linkages
Working across disciplines, institutions and jurisdictions
Epidemiologists working with clinicians, laboratories, environmental health teams and community leaders


Policy development
Translating evidence and local understanding into recommendations or policy input
Using evidence to recommend a prevention or control measure



A single problem may move through several functions: surveillance detects a signal, field investigation clarifies it, analytic work tests hypotheses, evaluation examines the response, linkages make implementation possible, and policy turns evidence into action.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
text:
LEARN 9 · Define → count → divide → compare
The CDC lesson reduces the basic epidemiological approach to three memorable operations: count, divide and compare. LIPPS places the decisions that must happen before and after those operations around them.

1. Define
Before counting cases, decide what qualifies as the health event. A case definition provides standard criteria for classification.
In outbreak work, a case definition may include clinical criteria and restrictions on time, place and person. If the case definition changes during surveillance, reported case numbers can change even when underlying disease occurrence does not.


2. Count
How many events occurred?
Counts are essential for workload, commodity and service planning. But they often cannot support fair population comparisons by themselves.


3. Divide
Relate events to an appropriate population denominator. Week 2 develops this formally.


4. Compare
Compare across populations, exposure groups, places or time periods. Ask what would normally be expected.


5. Interpret
Consider design, measurement, chance, bias, confounding, context and alternative explanations.


6. Act
Communicate what the evidence supports and use it appropriately for public-health decision making.

A LIPPS habit worth keeping for the entire course
When an analysis produces an impressive number, trace backwards: How was the event defined? Who entered the numerator? Who belonged in the denominator? What was the comparison? What else could produce the pattern?

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: APPLY · Turn a vague concern into an epidemiological question
text:
APPLY · Turn a vague concern into an epidemiological question

Fictional scenario
A district health officer says:

“Teenage pregnancy is becoming a serious problem in our district.”

That is a concern, not yet an epidemiological question.


Step 1 — What?
What exactly will count as the outcome? Pregnancy among girls aged 15–19? Births among girls aged 15–19? First pregnancy? Current pregnancy? A routine-service indicator?


Step 2 — Who?
Which population are we describing? All girls aged 15–19 resident in the district? Girls attending health facilities? School-going adolescents?
These are not interchangeable populations.


Step 3 — Where?
The entire district, selected sub-counties, schools, facilities or communities?


Step 4 — When?
Current prevalence? Annual occurrence? Change from 2024 to 2026? A five-year trend?


Step 5 — Compared with what?
Previous years? Another district? Different sub-counties? Different school-attendance groups?


A more useful question

How did a clearly defined adolescent-pregnancy measure change across sub-counties in District X from 2024 to 2026?

The denominator and data source still need scrutiny, but the question is now measurable.


Your task
Rewrite this statement as an epidemiological question:

“Hypertension is very common among our patients.”

Specify what, who, where, when and the comparison or denominator you need.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: WORKED EXAMPLE · Reported increase or real increase?
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · Reported increase or real increase?
Return to the fictional malaria scenario.



Month
Confirmed cases
People tested
Reporting facilities




Month 1
120
600
18


Month 2
240
1,600
30



The number of confirmed cases doubled.
But positivity among those tested changed from:

Month 1: 120 / 600 = 20%
Month 2: 240 / 1,600 = 15%

This still does not tell us the true incidence of malaria in the district. Testing may be selective; the tested population may differ; seasonality and facility reporting changed. But it demonstrates why a raw count can produce a misleading first impression.

What did we learn?
The defensible statement is:

Reported confirmed case counts increased, while positivity among those tested decreased; additional information is required to infer what happened to population disease occurrence.

The sentence separates what was observed from what is being inferred.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

1. Which part of the epidemiological definition is mainly concerned with person, place and time?
A. Application
B. Distribution
C. Determinants
D. Intervention
Answer: B. Distribution includes frequency and pattern, including person, place and time.


2. Why is a denominator important when comparing two populations?
A. It guarantees there is no bias.
B. It provides population context for the number of events.
C. It proves causation.
D. It eliminates confounding.
Answer: B. A denominator tells us the population in which the events occurred.


3. Which activity is most clearly analytic epidemiology?
A. Plotting cases by village.
B. Tabulating cases by age.
C. Comparing prior exposures in people with and without disease.
D. Counting weekly case reports.
Answer: C. The defining feature is an appropriate comparison used to assess an exposure-outcome relationship.


4. A surveillance programme broadens its case definition. What is the most immediate concern when interpreting the subsequent rise in cases?
A. The disease must have become more severe.
B. The apparent increase may partly reflect changed classification.
C. The denominator is no longer relevant.
D. Analytic epidemiology cannot be used.
Answer: B. A broader definition can identify more cases even without a true change in underlying occurrence.


5. Which statement best distinguishes epidemiology from clinical care?
A. Epidemiology never considers individuals.
B. Clinical care never uses population evidence.
C. Epidemiology primarily examines health collectively in defined populations.
D. Epidemiology is concerned only with infectious diseases.
Answer: C. The distinction is primarily the level of concern, not complete separation of the disciplines.


6. Which sequence best captures John Snow’s epidemiological contribution as presented in this lesson?
A. Model → p-value → publication
B. Description → hypothesis → comparison → action
C. Diagnosis → treatment → discharge
D. Randomisation → blinding → trial
Answer: B. His work illustrates movement from observed population pattern to hypothesis, comparison and public-health action.


7. Which is NOT one of the core public-health epidemiology functions introduced this week?
A. Surveillance
B. Field investigation
C. Analytic studies
D. Individual prescribing
Answer: D. Individual prescribing is primarily a clinical function.


8. A district reports 300 cases this year and 200 last year. What should be your first epidemiological reaction?
A. The disease increased by 50%.
B. An outbreak has occurred.
C. Determine whether definitions, population, detection and reporting are comparable.
D. Fit a regression model.
Answer: C. Comparability of measurement and population must be established before interpreting the change.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
text:
SUMMARY · The Week 1 mental model
DEFINE — What exactly counts as the event?
LOCATE — Who, where and when?
COUNT — How many?
CONTEXTUALISE — Out of how many, and under what measurement system?
COMPARE — Different from what?
EXPLAIN — What hypotheses could account for the pattern?
INTERPRET — What does the evidence support, and what does it not support?
ACT — What is the appropriate public-health response?
If you learn that habit, the statistics that follow will make substantially more sense.

title: Epidemiology and Epidemiological Thinking
section: Primary source used to build this lesson
text:
Primary source used to build this lesson
This LIPPS lesson is an original teaching adaptation of Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Lesson One: Introduction to Epidemiology (updated May 2012).
The definition, historical sequence, uses, core functions, case-definition logic, descriptive/analytic distinction and the count–divide–compare framework are adapted from that source. Scenarios labelled fictional or LIPPS examples were created for this course and are not claims about actual Ugandan districts or programmes.

title: Case-Control Studies
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 06





Intermediate Case-control Controls Odds ratio

title: Case-Control Studies
text: Intermediate Case-control Controls Odds ratio

title: Case-Control Studies
text:
This week in one sentence
Design and interpret case-control studies by defining cases, selecting controls from the source population, measuring prior exposure and using odds ratios without pretending sampled case-control data provide risks.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Case-Control Studies
Case-Control Studies
section: ORIENT · Why not simply ask sick people what they ate?
text:
ORIENT · Why not simply ask sick people what they ate?
During a hepatitis outbreak, nearly every case-patient reports eating at a popular restaurant. That observation sounds impressive until you learn that almost everyone in the community eats there.
Cases alone tell you what exposures were common among cases. They do not tell you whether those exposures were more common than expected.
A case-control study therefore adds a carefully selected group of people without the outcome and compares prior exposure between cases and controls.

title: Case-Control Studies
text:
LEARN 1 · Direction of sampling
A case-control study begins with outcome status.

Cases have the disease or outcome of interest.
Controls do not have that outcome.
Investigators then ascertain and compare prior exposures.

This differs from a cohort study, which starts from exposure groups and observes subsequent outcomes.
The design can be drawn as:
Outcome present → look back / reconstruct exposure
Outcome absent → look back / reconstruct exposure
The word “look back” does not mean every case-control study depends on memory. Exposure may be obtained from records, stored specimens, registries or other historical sources.

title: Case-Control Studies
Case-Control Studies
section: LEARN 3 · The source population is the hidden denominator
text:
LEARN 3 · The source population is the hidden denominator
The most useful way to think about controls is not “healthy people who look like the cases.” Controls should represent the population that produced the cases with respect to the opportunity for exposure.
A practical counterfactual question is:

If this control person had developed the outcome during the study period, would they have had a reasonable chance of being identified as a case in this study?

If the answer is no, the control may not represent the same source population.
This source-population logic is more important than superficial similarity.

title: Case-Control Studies
text:
LEARN 4 · Choosing controls
The attached CDC material stresses that control selection is one of the most important decisions in a case-control study. Possible sources include population controls, neighbours, friends or patients from the same clinical system.
Each choice can solve one problem while creating another.
Neighbour controls may improve geographic comparability but can overmatch environmental exposures.
Hospital controls may be easy to recruit but their illnesses may themselves be associated with the exposure.
Friend controls may share behaviours too closely with cases.
Population controls may best represent the source population but can be difficult or costly to recruit.
A control group that is systematically different from the case source population can generate a spurious association or hide a real one.

title: Case-Control Studies
section: LEARN 5 · Why the odds ratio is the natural measure
text:
LEARN 5 · Why the odds ratio is the natural measure
In a standard case-control study, investigators choose how many cases and controls to enrol. The sampled proportion of people who are cases is therefore created by the study design and does not equal population disease risk.
That is why you ordinarily cannot calculate:

disease incidence;
absolute risk;
risk difference; or
risk ratio

directly from the sampled case-control totals.
The odds ratio, however, can be estimated:
\[
OR = \frac{ad}{bc}
\]
for the conventional two-by-two table.
The attached CDC text therefore identifies the odds ratio as the measure of choice for typical case-control data.

title: Case-Control Studies
text:
LEARN 6 · Interpret odds as odds
Suppose:




Cases
Controls




Exposed
60
30


Unexposed
40
70



Then:
\[
OR = \frac{60\times70}{40\times30}=3.5
\]
A correct interpretation is:

The odds of prior exposure among cases were 3.5 times the odds of prior exposure among controls.

Under standard case-control assumptions this estimates an exposure-outcome odds ratio. For a rare outcome, the OR may approximate the risk ratio that would have been obtained in the source population.
Do not automatically write “cases were 3.5 times more likely to become ill.” The sampled case-control data did not estimate the probability of illness directly.

title: Case-Control Studies
section: LEARN 7 · Rare-disease approximation is useful but often abused
text:
LEARN 7 · Rare-disease approximation is useful but often abused
The attached source notes that when disease is uncommon, the odds ratio can approximate the risk ratio reasonably well.
As the outcome becomes common, odds and risk diverge. An OR of 3 can correspond to a much smaller risk ratio when baseline risk is high.
The rule is therefore not:

OR means RR.

It is:

Under particular designs and conditions, the OR can estimate or approximate a relative measure of risk; interpretation should still use the correct quantity and context.

title: Case-Control Studies
Case-Control Studies
section: LEARN 9 · Selection bias can be built in before analysis begins
text:
LEARN 9 · Selection bias can be built in before analysis begins
Imagine studying whether alcohol use is associated with acute pancreatitis and choosing hospital controls with conditions strongly related to alcohol. Exposure among controls will be artificially high, potentially pulling the odds ratio toward the null.
No regression model can fully repair a fundamentally inappropriate control group.
The attached CDC material defines bias as a systematic difference that results in a mistaken estimate of association. Control selection is one of the clearest examples of design-stage bias.

title: Case-Control Studies
section: LEARN 10 · Matching is a design tool, not a badge of quality
text:
LEARN 10 · Matching is a design tool, not a badge of quality

LIPPS extension Matching is not developed in detail in the attached CDC lesson, but it is common in case-control research and needs to be recognised.

Matching selects controls to resemble cases on variables such as age, sex or facility.
Potential advantages include efficiency and control of strong confounding by matching factors. Potential disadvantages include overmatching, difficulty finding controls and the inability to estimate effects of a factor on which cases and controls are perfectly matched.
Most importantly, matched sampling requires an analysis that respects the matching structure. Matching does not automatically control confounding if the analysis ignores the design.

title: Case-Control Studies
section: LEARN 11 · When case-control designs are especially useful

title: Case-Control Studies
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional hospital network identifies 120 adults with a newly diagnosed liver injury syndrome over 18 months. Investigators suspect use of an unregulated herbal preparation. They can access pharmacy histories, interview patients and identify adults from the same catchment population.
Design the case-control study:

Write a case definition that does not include herbal exposure.
Define the source population.
Propose one defensible control-selection strategy and one tempting but problematic strategy.
Explain how many controls per case you might consider and why simply adding many controls eventually yields diminishing benefit.
Specify how herbal exposure should be measured in both groups.
If 72 cases and 36 controls report the preparation, while 48 cases and 84 controls do not, calculate the OR.
Interpret the OR correctly.
Identify one plausible recall bias and one selection bias.
State whether the sampled table allows you to calculate the population risk of liver injury.
List additional evidence needed before claiming the herbal preparation caused the syndrome.

title: Case-Control Studies
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why must controls come from the population that gave rise to the cases?

Intermediate Trials Randomisation Quasi-experiments

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text: Intermediate Trials Randomisation Quasi-experiments

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text:
This week in one sentence
Distinguish randomised experiments from observational and quasi-experimental evaluations and judge how allocation and comparison design affect causal interpretation.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
section: ORIENT · An intervention happened and outcomes improved
text:
ORIENT · An intervention happened and outcomes improved
A district introduces a new maternal referral programme. Facility deliveries rise from 58% before implementation to 72% afterwards.
Did the programme cause the increase?
Not necessarily. Other things may have changed at the same time: transport, staffing, reporting, population composition, another campaign or a secular trend.
An intervention is not automatically an experiment, and a before-after difference is not automatically an effect.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
section: LEARN 1 · What makes a study experimental?
text:
LEARN 1 · What makes a study experimental?
The attached CDC text distinguishes experimental from observational studies by whether the investigator determines the exposure or intervention through a controlled process.
In a clinical trial, participants may be assigned to a new intervention or a comparison condition and followed for outcomes. In community trials, the unit of intervention can be a group or community.
The analytical logic remains comparison, but assignment creates an opportunity for stronger causal inference.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text:
LEARN 2 · Why randomisation matters
Random allocation gives eligible units a chance of receiving each study condition according to a random mechanism.
Its main causal advantage is not that the groups become identical. It is that, with adequate implementation and sample size, both measured and unmeasured baseline causes of the outcome are expected to be balanced on average, apart from chance.
Randomisation therefore protects against systematic treatment selection.
A single randomised study can still have baseline imbalance by chance; randomisation is a process, not a guarantee of perfect symmetry.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
section: LEARN 3 · The comparison group remains essential

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text:
LEARN 4 · Allocation concealment and blinding

LIPPS extension These trial-quality concepts are not developed in detail in the attached introductory CDC chapter.

Allocation concealment prevents those enrolling participants from predicting the next assignment, reducing selection manipulation.
Blinding prevents selected participants, clinicians, outcome assessors or analysts from knowing assignment when that knowledge could alter behaviour or measurement.
Blinding is not always possible. A health worker usually knows whether a new workflow has been introduced. The design should then focus on objective outcomes, standardised measurement and blinded outcome assessment where feasible.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text:
LEARN 5 · Individual versus cluster randomisation
Sometimes an intervention is delivered to groups rather than individuals—for example, a facility-level triage protocol or village-level health campaign.
Randomising whole facilities or communities can reduce contamination but creates correlation among people within the same cluster.

LIPPS extension Cluster-randomised trials require sample-size and analysis methods that account for clustering. Treating all individuals as independent can overstate precision.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text:
LEARN 6 · Efficacy versus effectiveness
The attached CDC source distinguishes:
Efficacy — performance under ideal or controlled conditions.
Effectiveness — performance under typical field conditions.
The difference is not merely vocabulary. It changes what population, adherence, delivery conditions and implementation problems the estimate represents.
A highly efficacious intervention can have modest real-world effectiveness when uptake, adherence, supply or implementation is poor.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text:
LEARN 7 · Non-adherence and intention-to-treat

LIPPS extension Intention-to-treat is introduced here because it is fundamental to interpreting randomised trials.

Participants do not always follow their assigned intervention. Analysing only those who complied can recreate confounding because compliers may differ systematically from non-compliers.
Intention-to-treat analysis compares groups according to original random assignment, preserving the causal protection of randomisation for the effect of assignment.
Per-protocol questions can also be scientifically useful, but they require additional assumptions and should not casually replace the randomised comparison.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
section: LEARN 8 · When randomisation is not feasible
text:
LEARN 8 · When randomisation is not feasible
Randomisation may be unethical when an intervention is already known to be beneficial, politically unacceptable, operationally impossible, or inappropriate for a system-wide policy already being implemented.
Researchers then use observational or quasi-experimental designs.
The key question becomes:

How can we construct the most credible comparison possible without random assignment?

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text:
LEARN 9 · Quasi-experimental designs

LIPPS extension The attached CDC introduction does not provide a detailed quasi-experimental taxonomy. This section is an applied extension.

Simple before-after: compare outcome before and after intervention. Easy but highly vulnerable to time-related confounding.
Controlled before-after: add a comparable non-intervention group and examine whether change differs between groups.
Interrupted time series: use many repeated observations before and after an intervention to estimate changes in level or trend.
Controlled interrupted time series: add a comparison series to strengthen attribution.
Other advanced quasi-experimental strategies exist, but the principle remains: exploit design structure to approximate the counterfactual more credibly.

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
section: LEARN 10 · Design does not compensate for poor execution

title: Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A health ministry plans to introduce a new infection-prevention coaching package in 24 hospitals. Political leaders want all hospitals eventually to receive it, but implementation capacity allows only 12 to start immediately.
Consider three possible evaluations:
A. Compare the 12 early hospitals before versus after implementation.
B. Randomly select which 12 receive the package first and compare outcomes with the waiting hospitals during the same period.
C. Use 24 monthly observations before and 12 after national rollout, with no concurrent control.
For each option:

Name the design.
Describe its comparison or counterfactual logic.
Identify its strongest threat to causal interpretation.
State what outcome-measurement features would reduce bias.
Explain what clustering means if patient-level outcomes are analysed.
Distinguish efficacy from effectiveness in this programme.
Explain why analysing only hospitals that implemented the package perfectly might bias the effect estimate.
Rank the three designs for causal strength under otherwise good execution and justify your ranking.

text:

LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 10





Intermediate Screening Sensitivity · Specificity Predictive values

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text: Intermediate Screening Sensitivity · Specificity Predictive values

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
This week in one sentence
Evaluate screening and diagnostic classification using sensitivity, specificity and predictive values, then extend interpretation to likelihood ratios, thresholds and multi-test strategies.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: ORIENT · A positive test is not the same as disease
text:
ORIENT · A positive test is not the same as disease
A screening programme uses a test with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity in a population where disease prevalence is 1%.
Many students hear “95% specificity” and expect nearly every positive test to be a true case.
That intuition is wrong because the number of false positives also depends on how many people without disease are tested.
Diagnostic interpretation is a problem of conditional probability.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: LEARN 1 · Build the diagnostic two-by-two table
text:
LEARN 1 · Build the diagnostic two-by-two table
Start with true disease status determined by the best available reference classification.




Disease +
Disease −




Test +
True positive (TP)
False positive (FP)


Test −
False negative (FN)
True negative (TN)



The attached CDC material uses the same logic for surveillance-system sensitivity, specificity and predictive value positive.
The denominator determines the question being answered.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 2 · Sensitivity
Sensitivity asks:

Among people who truly have the condition, what proportion does the test identify as positive?

\[
Sensitivity = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}
\]
High sensitivity means relatively few false negatives.
Sensitivity is useful when missing true cases carries important consequences, but maximising sensitivity alone can create many false positives if specificity falls.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 3 · Specificity
Specificity asks:

Among people who truly do not have the condition, what proportion does the test correctly classify as negative?

\[
Specificity = \frac{TN}{FP+TN}
\]
High specificity means relatively few false positives.
Sensitivity and specificity condition on true disease status, not on the observed test result.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: LEARN 4 · Predictive values reverse the conditioning direction
text:
LEARN 4 · Predictive values reverse the conditioning direction
Positive predictive value (PPV) asks:

Among those who test positive, what proportion truly have the condition?

\[
PPV = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}
\]
Negative predictive value (NPV) asks:

Among those who test negative, what proportion truly do not have the condition?

\[
NPV = \frac{TN}{FN+TN}
\]

Source boundary The attached CDC source explicitly develops predictive value positive in the surveillance context. NPV is included here as a LIPPS diagnostic-testing extension.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 5 · Why prevalence changes PPV
Consider 10,000 people with 1% prevalence.
There are 100 true cases and 9,900 non-cases.
With 90% sensitivity:

TP = 90
FN = 10

With 95% specificity:

TN = 9,405
FP = 495

So:
\[
PPV = \frac{90}{90+495} \approx 15.4\%
\]
Despite good sensitivity and specificity, only about 15% of positive results are true positives in this low-prevalence setting.
As prevalence rises, PPV usually rises and NPV usually falls, holding test properties constant.

This is why “the test is 95% accurate” is usually an unhelpful sentence.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: LEARN 6 · Sensitivity and PPV answer different questions
text:
LEARN 6 · Sensitivity and PPV answer different questions
This distinction should become automatic.
Sensitivity: start with people who truly have disease → ask how many test positive.
PPV: start with people whose test is positive → ask how many truly have disease.
The same true-positive cell appears in both formulas, but the denominators differ.
Confusing these quantities leads directly to poor patient counselling and poor screening-policy interpretation.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 7 · Likelihood ratios

LIPPS extension Likelihood ratios are not developed in the attached CDC source.

Likelihood ratios describe how much a test result changes the odds of disease.
\[
LR+ = \frac{Sensitivity}{1-Specificity}
\]
\[
LR- = \frac{1-Sensitivity}{Specificity}
\]
A large LR+ provides stronger evidence toward disease; a small LR− provides stronger evidence against disease.
Likelihood ratios combine sensitivity and specificity and can be used with pre-test odds to obtain post-test odds.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 8 · Thresholds create trade-offs
Many tests begin with a continuous value: blood pressure, biomarker concentration, risk score or optical density. A threshold converts that value into positive/negative classification.
Lowering a threshold usually:

identifies more true cases → sensitivity rises;
also labels more non-cases positive → specificity falls.

Raising the threshold usually does the reverse.
There is no universally “best” threshold. The appropriate choice depends on the consequences of false negatives and false positives, disease prevalence, downstream testing capacity and purpose of screening.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 10 · Serial and parallel testing

LIPPS extension Multi-test algorithms are not developed in the attached source.

Serial testing: a second test is performed or required after the first positive. This tends to increase overall specificity but can reduce sensitivity.
Parallel testing: a person may be classified positive if either of two tests is positive. This tends to increase sensitivity but can reduce specificity.
The exact combined performance depends on test dependence and algorithm rules. Do not mechanically multiply test characteristics without checking assumptions.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 11 · Agreement is not accuracy
Two tests can agree with each other and both be wrong if neither is compared with an adequate reference standard.
Accuracy questions ask how a test corresponds to true disease status.
Agreement questions ask how two raters or tests correspond to each other.
Measures such as percent agreement and kappa address agreement, not necessarily diagnostic truth.

LIPPS extension Agreement and kappa are not developed in the attached CDC lesson.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: LEARN 12 · What could fool us in a diagnostic study?
text:
LEARN 12 · What could fool us in a diagnostic study?
Important threats include:
Spectrum effects — performance differs across disease severity or patient mix.
Verification bias — only some participants, often those with positive index tests, receive the reference standard.
Imperfect reference standard — the “gold standard” itself misclassifies disease.
Incorporation bias — the index test contributes to the reference diagnosis.
Reader or review bias — interpreters know other test results.
These problems change what apparent sensitivity and specificity mean.
A diagnostic-accuracy estimate belongs to the population, threshold, specimen process and reference standard under which it was obtained.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional typhoid screening study tests 2,000 febrile patients. A reference classification identifies 200 true disease cases. The index test is positive in 170 of those 200 cases and positive in 270 of the 1,800 non-cases.

Construct the 2×2 table.
Calculate sensitivity.
Calculate specificity.
Calculate PPV.
Calculate NPV.
Calculate LR+ and LR−.
Explain why PPV would differ if the same sensitivity and specificity were applied in a much lower-prevalence general population.
If the screening threshold is lowered, predict the usual direction of change in sensitivity and specificity.
Explain why a high percent agreement with another rapid test would not establish accuracy.
Identify how the study could be biased if only index-test-positive patients received the reference test.
Write a counselling statement that avoids telling every positive patient that they “have typhoid” with certainty.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

A test detects 90 of 100 true cases. What is its sensitivity?
Why does specificity use non-diseased people in its denominator?
How is PPV conceptually different from sensitivity?

Does high AUC guarantee a high PPV in a low-prevalence population?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.
