title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 12





Capstone Causal reasoning Critical appraisal Interpretation

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text: Capstone Causal reasoning Critical appraisal Interpretation

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
This week in one sentence
Integrate design, measurement, comparison, bias, confounding, precision and context to decide what an epidemiological result means, what it does not mean and how confidently it can guide action.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: ORIENT · The p-value is 0.001. So what?
text:
ORIENT · The p-value is 0.001. So what?
A study reports:

“Participants exposed to Programme X had 35% lower mortality, p=0.001.”

Before celebrating, an epidemiologist should ask:

Was Programme X assigned or self-selected?
When was exposure measured relative to mortality?
Who entered the study and who was lost?
Were mortality outcomes measured equally?
Which variables influenced both programme participation and prognosis?
What was the absolute mortality difference?
What does the confidence interval allow?
Does the study population resemble the population where a decision will be made?

A small p-value cannot answer those questions.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 1 · First identify the kind of claim
text:
LEARN 1 · First identify the kind of claim
Four claims are often confused.
Description: What is happening?
Example: hypertension prevalence is 28%.
Association: How does an outcome differ between groups?
Example: hypertension prevalence is higher among Group A.
Prediction: How well can measured information forecast an outcome?
Example: a risk model identifies people likely to be hospitalised.
Causal effect: What would differ if the exposure or intervention were changed?
Example: what would mortality have been if the same population had received versus not received the intervention?
The analysis should be judged against the type of claim, not merely against whether a model was fitted.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 2 · Name the estimand before interpreting the estimate

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 3 · Start critical appraisal with design, not the Results table
text:
LEARN 3 · Start critical appraisal with design, not the Results table
The attached CDC material repeatedly emphasises comparison groups and distinguishes observational from experimental study designs.
Ask:

How were participants selected?
What determined exposure or intervention status?
When was exposure measured relative to outcome?
What comparison group represents the expected or counterfactual experience?
Did follow-up and measurement differ across groups?
What quantity can the design estimate directly?

A study design does not determine truth, but it constrains which interpretations are defensible.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 4 · Temporality is necessary but not sufficient
text:
LEARN 4 · Temporality is necessary but not sufficient
A cause must precede its effect, so temporal ordering matters.
Cross-sectional simultaneous measurement often creates ambiguity. Cohort follow-up improves temporal ordering. Randomised assignment can strengthen causal interpretation further.
But even perfect temporality does not remove confounding or selection bias. Smoking can precede an outcome without being the cause if smoking is simply correlated with the true cause.
Temporality answers when; causal identification also requires a credible comparison.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 5 · Measurement determines what the variables actually mean
text:
LEARN 5 · Measurement determines what the variables actually mean
A variable label can hide measurement problems.
“Vaccinated” might mean card-confirmed dose, caregiver recall or registry entry.
“Hypertension” might mean one reading, repeated readings, medication history or diagnosis code.
“Exposure” might mean current status even though the biologically relevant window was years earlier.
Critical appraisal asks:

Is the operational definition appropriate?
Is measurement equally valid across groups?
Is timing appropriate?
Are cut-offs defensible?
How much missingness exists?
Could misclassification change the association?

You cannot interpret an estimate more precisely than the variables from which it was constructed.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 6 · Bias and confounding are alternative explanations

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 7 · P-values address compatibility with a null model, not importance

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 8 · Confidence intervals carry magnitude and precision together
text:
LEARN 8 · Confidence intervals carry magnitude and precision together
The attached CDC material notes that wide confidence intervals are compatible with a broad range of effect sizes, while narrow intervals indicate greater precision.
For ratio measures such as RR or OR, the usual null value is 1.
For absolute differences, the usual null value is 0.
But interpretation should go beyond whether the interval crosses the null.
Example:
RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.50–1.04
The data are compatible with effects ranging from a substantial reduction to little or modest increase. “Not statistically significant” throws away most of that information.
Ask whether the interval includes effects that would change a public-health decision.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 9 · Statistical significance is not public-health importance
text:
LEARN 9 · Statistical significance is not public-health importance
Suppose an enormous study estimates a risk reduction from 10.00% to 9.80% with p < 0.001.
The relative reduction is small and the absolute reduction is 0.2 percentage points. Depending on intervention cost, harm and scale, that may be trivial—or it may still matter if millions are exposed and the intervention is cheap.
Now consider a small emergency study suggesting mortality reduction from 30% to 20% but with a wide confidence interval. The estimate may be operationally important despite statistical uncertainty.
Decision relevance requires magnitude, precision, burden, feasibility, harms and context.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
LEARN 10 · Internal validity versus applicability

LIPPS extension The attached CDC course discusses representativeness and practical public-health application, but the explicit internal/external validity framework is developed here.

Internal validity: Is the study’s estimate credible for the population actually studied?
External validity / applicability: Would the estimate be expected to hold in another population, place, time or implementation condition?
A perfectly representative sample does not rescue internal bias. Conversely, a highly internally valid study in a narrow population can still be useful elsewhere when mechanisms and context support transport.
Generalisation is an argument, not a checkbox.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
LEARN 11 · Causal language has levels
Consider increasing levels of causal commitment:
Descriptive: “Mortality was lower among participants receiving the programme.”
Associational: “Programme receipt was associated with lower mortality.”
Adjusted associational: “After adjustment for measured confounders, programme receipt remained associated with lower mortality.”
Causal: “The programme reduced mortality.”
The final sentence requires a design and assumptions capable of supporting a causal effect estimate.
Words such as impact, effect, attributable, prevented, caused, reduced carry causal meaning and should be used intentionally.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
section: LEARN 12 · Evidence can support action without proving everything

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
LEARN 13 · The LIPPS EVIDENCE framework

LIPPS synthesis EVIDENCE is a LIPPS-created appraisal mnemonic, not an acronym from the attached CDC source.

Use it when reading a manuscript, programme report, dashboard or headline.
E — Exact question
What population, exposure/intervention, outcome and time are actually being studied?
V — Valid design
Does the design create a credible comparison for that question?
I — Information quality
How well were exposure, outcome and covariates measured?
D — Denominators and data structure
Are the correct populations, sampling design, clustering, follow-up and missing data handled?
E — Explanations competing
What bias, confounding, reverse causation or alternative mechanism could explain the result?
N — Numerical meaning
What are the absolute and relative effects, uncertainty intervals and practical magnitude?
C — Context
Does the evidence apply to this population, health system and decision?
E — Expression
Does the wording of the conclusion match what the evidence supports?
The framework operationalises the LIPPS motto: Evidence is never the whole story.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
LEARN 14 · A final interpretation workflow
When presented with any epidemiological result:

Restate the question.
Identify the design.
Identify the measure and its denominator.
Inspect absolute and relative results.
Read the confidence interval.
Check temporal ordering.
Examine selection and measurement.
Identify plausible confounding.
Ask what was adjusted for and why.
Consider competing explanations.
Judge applicability.
Rewrite the conclusion in language the design earns.
State what decision, if any, the evidence reasonably supports.

If you can do this reliably, you are no longer merely calculating epidemiological statistics—you are thinking epidemiologically.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional paper reports a cohort study of 8,000 adults comparing users and non-users of a new community health programme. Mortality over two years is 3.0% among programme users and 4.5% among non-users. The adjusted hazard ratio is 0.70 (95% CI 0.52–0.95; p=0.02). Programme participation was voluntary. Users were younger, wealthier and lived closer to facilities; adjustment included age and sex but not distance or wealth. Loss to follow-up was 4% among users and 14% among non-users.
Apply LIPPS EVIDENCE:

State the exact causal and associational questions separately.
Identify what the cohort design contributes.
Calculate the crude risk ratio and risk difference from the reported risks.
Interpret the adjusted hazard ratio without equating it automatically to risk ratio.
Explain what the confidence interval says about precision and compatibility.
Identify major selection and confounding concerns.
Explain why voluntary programme uptake matters.
Explain why differential loss to follow-up matters.
State what information is missing about measurement.
Evaluate the claim: “Programme X reduced mortality by 30%.”
Rewrite the conclusion more defensibly.
State whether the findings could still support a pilot expansion and what additional evaluation you would request.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

What is the difference between an association question and a causal-effect question?
Why should critical appraisal begin with study design rather than the p-value?
Does temporality by itself establish causation?

Apply the first and last letters of LIPPS EVIDENCE to a claim: what exact question is being asked, and does the expression match the evidence?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

title: Causal Interpretation and Critical Appraisal
text:
Source foundation and LIPPS extensions
Primary source foundation: the attached CDC course’s repeated emphasis on population comparison, systematic and unbiased methods, the distinction between observational and experimental studies, cautious causal inference, p-values, confidence intervals and applying epidemiological evidence to public-health action.
LIPPS extensions: estimands, internal/external validity terminology, the structured causal-language ladder and the LIPPS EVIDENCE appraisal framework are clearly identified as original instructional extensions rather than content from the source.
Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. October 2006; updated May 2012.

title: Measures of Association and Effect

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
This week in one sentence
Measure the outcome in each comparison group first; only then choose a measure that expresses the comparison in a form that answers the public-health question.

The LIPPS lens
A large relative association can correspond to a small absolute difference, and a small relative association can matter greatly when the outcome is common. Never interpret the ratio without looking at the underlying risks or rates.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
Measures of Association and Effect
section: ORIENT · “Three times higher” — but three times what?
text:
ORIENT · “Three times higher” — but three times what?
Consider two fictional communities followed for one year.



Community
Population initially at risk
New cases
One-year risk




A
1,000
60
6%


B
1,000
20
2%



A report could state:

“Community A had three times the risk of disease compared with Community B.”

That is true because:
\[
RR = 0.06 / 0.02 = 3.0
\]
But the same data can also be expressed as an absolute difference:
\[
RD = 0.06 - 0.02 = 0.04 = 4\text{ percentage points}
\]
So both of these statements describe the same comparison:

relative: risk was three times as high;
absolute: there were 4 additional cases per 100 people at risk.

Neither description is automatically “better.” The useful measure depends on the question.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 1 · Comparison is the hallmark of analytic epidemiology
text:
LEARN 1 · Comparison is the hallmark of analytic epidemiology
The attached CDC text emphasises that the key to epidemiological analysis is comparison. A high disease frequency in one group becomes more interpretable when compared with an appropriate group representing what might otherwise be expected.
The broad structure is:
Observed group
versus
Comparison group
Examples include:

exposed versus unexposed;
vaccinated versus unvaccinated;
intervention versus control;
one district versus another;
one time period versus another; or
people with one characteristic versus people without it.

The source lists risk ratio, rate ratio, odds ratio and proportionate mortality ratio as examples of comparative measures.

Before calculating anything
Ask:

What exactly are the two groups?
What outcome is being compared?
Is the outcome measured as a risk, rate, prevalence, odds or mortality proportion?
Is the comparison group a defensible representation of the expected level?
Does the design allow this quantity to be estimated directly?


A measure of association cannot rescue a bad comparison group.
If the groups are not meaningfully comparable, a beautifully calculated ratio can still be misleading.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
LEARN 2 · The two-by-two table
For a binary exposure and a binary outcome, epidemiologists often begin with a two-by-two table.




Outcome +
Outcome −
Total




Exposed
a
b
a + b


Unexposed
c
d
c + d


Total
a + c
b + d
N



From this table:
\[
Risk_E = \frac{a}{a+b}
\]
\[
Risk_U = \frac{c}{c+d}
\]
\[
RR = \frac{Risk_E}{Risk_U}
\]
\[
RD = Risk_E - Risk_U
\]
\[
OR = \frac{ad}{bc}
\]

The table is not the analysis by itself
A two-by-two table is an organising device. What you calculate from it depends on the study design and the question.
For example, in a typical case-control study the investigator selects the number of cases and controls. The row or column totals therefore do not reconstruct population risks. In that setting, the odds ratio remains estimable, while risk and risk ratio generally are not.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 3 · Risk ratio: a relative comparison of risks
text:
LEARN 3 · Risk ratio: a relative comparison of risks
The attached CDC source defines the risk ratio (RR), also called relative risk, as the risk in the group of primary interest divided by the risk in the comparison group.
\[
RR = \frac{Risk_E}{Risk_U}
\]

Interpreting the null value
RR = 1.0
The risks are equal in the two groups.
RR > 1.0
Risk is higher in the numerator group.
RR < 1.0
Risk is lower in the numerator group.


Fictional example
During an outbreak, 45 of 150 people who attended Event A became ill. Among 200 people who attended Event B, 20 became ill.
\[
Risk_A = 45/150 = 0.30
\]
\[
Risk_B = 20/200 = 0.10
\]
\[
RR = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0
\]
Interpretation:

People in Event A had three times the risk of illness during the observation period compared with people in Event B.

Do not automatically write:

Event A caused three times more illness.

That causal wording requires more than the ratio alone.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 4 · The same ratio can hide very different public-health consequences
text:
LEARN 4 · The same ratio can hide very different public-health consequences
Consider two comparisons.

Comparison 1
Risk in exposed = 20%
Risk in unexposed = 10%
\[
RR = 2.0
\]
\[
RD = 20\%-10\%=10\text{ percentage points}
\]


Comparison 2
Risk in exposed = 2%
Risk in unexposed = 1%
\[
RR = 2.0
\]
\[
RD = 2\%-1\%=1\text{ percentage point}
\]
The relative association is identical in both examples: RR = 2.0.
But the absolute difference is very different.
This is why a report should not rely on the relative measure alone when an absolute measure can also be communicated meaningfully.

Relative measures answer: “How many times as high?”
Absolute measures answer: “How much higher?”

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
LEARN 5 · Risk difference / excess risk
The attached CDC chapter explicitly uses the term risk difference or excess risk in its vaccine-effectiveness section for the difference between risks in two groups. LIPPS expands that idea here because it is fundamental to interpreting absolute effects.
\[
RD = Risk_E - Risk_U
\]

Fictional example
Risk among exposed = 18%
Risk among unexposed = 6%
\[
RD = 0.18 - 0.06 = 0.12
\]
The risk difference is 0.12, or 12 percentage points.
Interpretation:

There were 12 additional cases per 100 people at risk in the exposed group compared with the unexposed group during the specified period.



Null value
For a difference measure, the null value is 0, not 1.

ratio measure → null = 1;
difference measure → null = 0.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 6 · Rate ratio: compare speeds, not just proportions
text:
LEARN 6 · Rate ratio: compare speeds, not just proportions
When the outcome is measured using person-time, the corresponding relative comparison is a rate ratio.
\[
Rate\ Ratio = \frac{Incidence\ rate_E}{Incidence\ rate_U}
\]
The CDC source uses the same interpretive framework as for a risk ratio:

1.0 → equal rates;
above 1.0 → higher rate in the numerator group;
below 1.0 → lower rate in the numerator group.


Fictional example
A cohort records:

exposed group: 48 cases during 2,400 person-years;
unexposed group: 30 cases during 3,000 person-years.

\[
Rate_E = 48/2400 = 0.020 = 20/1,000\ person\text{-}years
\]
\[
Rate_U = 30/3000 = 0.010 = 10/1,000\ person\text{-}years
\]
\[
Rate\ Ratio = 20/10 = 2.0
\]
Interpretation:

The incidence rate in the exposed group was twice the incidence rate in the unexposed group.

Do not call this a “twofold risk” if what you actually estimated was a rate ratio.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
LEARN 7 · Odds are not risks
Students often treat odds and risk as interchangeable. They are not.
If 20 people develop disease and 80 do not:

Risk
\[
Risk = 20/(20+80) = 0.20
\]
The risk is 20%.


Odds
\[
Odds = 20/80 = 0.25
\]
The odds are 0.25, or 1 to 4.
Risk compares cases with all people at risk.
Odds compare cases with non-cases.
When disease is rare, risk and odds are numerically close. As disease becomes more common, they diverge.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 8 · Odds ratio: the cross-product comparison
text:
LEARN 8 · Odds ratio: the cross-product comparison
From the two-by-two table:




Outcome +
Outcome −




Exposed
a
b


Unexposed
c
d



The odds ratio is:
\[
OR = \frac{a/b}{c/d} = \frac{ad}{bc}
\]
The attached CDC text notes that this is sometimes called the cross-product ratio because the diagonal products are compared.

Fictional example




Disease
No disease




Exposed
40
60


Unexposed
20
80



\[
OR = \frac{40\times80}{60\times20} = \frac{3200}{1200} = 2.67
\]
Interpretation:

The odds of disease among exposed participants were approximately 2.7 times the odds among unexposed participants.

That is the cleanest wording.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 9 · Why the odds ratio is central to case-control studies
text:
LEARN 9 · Why the odds ratio is central to case-control studies
In a typical case-control study, investigators deliberately enrol people with the outcome and people without it. The number of controls is usually chosen by the investigators rather than arising naturally from the population at risk.
Therefore, the sampled proportion of cases is not the population risk.
The attached CDC text makes the practical consequence explicit:

risk generally cannot be calculated directly from a typical case-control sample;
risk ratio generally cannot therefore be calculated directly;
rate ratio generally cannot be calculated directly; but
the odds ratio can be calculated.

That is why the odds ratio is the standard measure of association for the usual case-control design.

Design determines what can be estimated.
Do not choose a measure because it is familiar. Choose it because the sampling and follow-up structure permit it.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 10 · When OR approximates RR — and when it does not
text:
LEARN 10 · When OR approximates RR — and when it does not
The CDC chapter shows that when an outcome is uncommon, an odds ratio can be close to the corresponding risk ratio. It also warns that the more common the outcome, the further the odds ratio may be from the risk ratio.

Uncommon outcome
Risk exposed = 5%
Risk unexposed = 1%
\[
RR = 5.0
\]
The corresponding odds ratio is approximately 5.2 — very close.


Common outcome
Risk exposed = 60%
Risk unexposed = 20%
\[
RR = 3.0
\]
But:
\[
Odds_E = 0.60/0.40 = 1.5
\]
\[
Odds_U = 0.20/0.80 = 0.25
\]
\[
OR = 1.5/0.25 = 6.0
\]
The OR is 6.0, while the RR is 3.0.


The interpretation error
It would be incorrect to say:

“The exposed group was six times as likely to develop the outcome.”

The OR of 6 refers to odds, not risk.
When outcomes are common, this distinction becomes especially important.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LIPPS EXTENSION · Prevalence ratio in cross-sectional studies
text:
LIPPS EXTENSION · Prevalence ratio in cross-sectional studies
Source note: the attached CDC lesson used for Week 3 does not explicitly teach the prevalence ratio. LIPPS includes it as an extension because it is directly relevant to modern cross-sectional public-health analysis.
In a cross-sectional study, the investigator often measures the prevalence of an outcome in two groups.
\[
PR = \frac{Prevalence_E}{Prevalence_U}
\]

Fictional example
A survey finds hypertension in:

120 of 300 adults with high salt intake → 40%;
60 of 300 adults with lower salt intake → 20%.

\[
PR = 0.40/0.20 = 2.0
\]
Interpretation:

The prevalence of hypertension was twice as high among adults in the high-salt group as among adults in the lower-salt group at the time represented by the survey.

Notice the wording:
prevalence was twice as high — not “risk was twice as high” and not “high salt doubled the risk.”
A cross-sectional study usually cannot establish whether the exposure preceded the outcome.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 11 · Relative and absolute measures should be read together
text:
LEARN 11 · Relative and absolute measures should be read together
Suppose a preventive intervention reduces one-year disease risk from 4% to 2%.

Relative comparison
\[
RR = 0.02/0.04 = 0.50
\]
The intervention group had half the risk.


Absolute comparison
\[
RD = 0.02 - 0.04 = -0.02
\]
The absolute risk was 2 percentage points lower.
A communicator could truthfully say:

“Risk was reduced by 50%.”

But without the underlying risks, a reader may imagine a much larger absolute change than 4% to 2%.


LIPPS reporting rule
Where possible, report:
risk or rate in each group + relative measure + absolute measure + uncertainty.
That combination gives the reader much more information than a single dramatic ratio.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 12 · Attributable proportion among the exposed
text:
LEARN 12 · Attributable proportion among the exposed
The attached CDC source presents attributable proportion, also called attributable risk percent, as a measure of public-health impact.
A common formula is:
\[
AP_E = \frac{Risk_E - Risk_U}{Risk_E}\times100\%
\]
It can be expressed similarly using rates.

Fictional example
Risk among exposed = 30%
Risk among unexposed = 10%
\[
AP_E = \frac{0.30-0.10}{0.30}\times100 = 66.7\%
\]
Under a causal interpretation and assuming the groups are otherwise sufficiently comparable:

Approximately two-thirds of the disease occurrence among the exposed group could be attributed to the exposure.



Important restraint
The word attributable is stronger than “associated.” If the association is confounded, biased or non-causal, the attributable interpretation is not justified.
The attached source itself cautions that the measure relies on causal assumptions.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 13 · Vaccine efficacy and vaccine effectiveness
text:
LEARN 13 · Vaccine efficacy and vaccine effectiveness
The attached CDC text distinguishes:
Vaccine efficacy — performance under ideal conditions, such as a clinical trial.
Vaccine effectiveness — performance under usual field conditions.
Both are expressed as a proportionate reduction in disease among vaccinated people compared with unvaccinated people.
\[
VE = \frac{Risk_U - Risk_V}{Risk_U}\times100\%
\]
or equivalently:
\[
VE = (1-RR)\times100\%
\]
when the RR is defined as vaccinated risk divided by unvaccinated risk.

Fictional example
Risk vaccinated = 8%
Risk unvaccinated = 20%
\[
RR = 0.08/0.20 = 0.40
\]
\[
VE = (1-0.40)\times100 = 60\%
\]
Interpretation:

Disease occurrence was 60% lower among the vaccinated group relative to the unvaccinated group under the conditions represented by the study.

Again, the validity of a causal effectiveness claim depends on the design and control of alternative explanations.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 14 · Protective associations require careful wording
text:
LEARN 14 · Protective associations require careful wording
When a ratio is below 1, students sometimes become confused.
Suppose:
\[
RR = 0.70
\]
The exposed group has 70% of the risk observed in the comparison group.
The relative reduction is:
\[
1 - 0.70 = 0.30 = 30\%
\]
So one may say:

Risk was 30% lower in the exposed group.

Do not say the exposure “reduced risk by 0.70%.”
Likewise, if:
\[
OR = 0.70
\]
the clean interpretation is:

The odds were 30% lower in the exposed group.

Do not silently turn odds into risk.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 15 · Precision and the null value
text:
LEARN 15 · Precision and the null value
A point estimate is not the whole result.
A ratio of 2.0 can be estimated very precisely or very imprecisely. A risk difference of 5 percentage points can be tightly or loosely estimated.
For introductory interpretation, remember:

RR, rate ratio, OR, PR: null value = 1;
risk difference / prevalence difference: null value = 0.

Confidence intervals around these measures provide information about precision and the range of values compatible with the data and analysis assumptions.
Detailed interval estimation and critical appraisal are revisited later in the course. For now, avoid treating a point estimate as exact truth.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 16 · Association is not automatically causation
text:
LEARN 16 · Association is not automatically causation
The attached CDC chapter states that measures such as risk ratios, rate ratios and odds ratios provide evidence about relationships between exposure and disease. That is not the same as proving that the exposure caused the disease.
A measured association can be influenced by:

selection processes;
measurement error;
confounding;
reverse temporality;
chance;
model choices; or
genuine causal effects.

Those issues are developed later in the course.

Language discipline
For an observational comparison, prefer:

“Exposure was associated with higher risk…”

rather than:

“Exposure increased risk…”

unless the design, analysis and assumptions support a causal interpretation.

LIPPS rule
The mathematical sign of an association does not tell you whether the relationship is causal.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: APPLY · Choose the measure before doing the arithmetic
text:
APPLY · Choose the measure before doing the arithmetic

Scenario A · Closed cohort
Two groups are followed for one year from a disease-free baseline. You know the number developing disease and the number initially at risk in each group.
Most direct relative measure: Risk ratio.
Useful absolute measure: Risk difference.


Scenario B · Unequal follow-up time
Two treatment groups contribute different amounts of person-time and new outcomes are counted.
Most direct relative measure: Rate ratio.


Scenario C · Case-control study
Investigators select 200 cases and 400 controls and compare prior exposure.
Natural measure: Odds ratio.


Scenario D · Cross-sectional survey
A survey measures current exposure and current hypertension status in a representative sample.
Natural descriptive relative measure: Prevalence ratio.
Causal caution: Temporality may be unclear.


Scenario E · Vaccine comparison
Risks are measured among vaccinated and unvaccinated groups.
Useful measures: Risk ratio, risk difference and vaccine efficacy/effectiveness where causal interpretation is appropriate.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: WORKED EXAMPLE · One outbreak table, several answers
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · One outbreak table, several answers
Consider a fictional foodborne-outbreak investigation among 180 event attendees.




Became ill
Did not become ill
Total




Ate goat stew
54
36
90


Did not eat goat stew
18
72
90




1. Risk among exposed
\[
54/90 = 0.60 = 60\%
\]


2. Risk among unexposed
\[
18/90 = 0.20 = 20\%
\]


3. Risk ratio
\[
RR = 0.60/0.20 = 3.0
\]
People who ate the goat stew had three times the risk of illness compared with those who did not.


4. Risk difference
\[
RD = 0.60-0.20 = 0.40
\]
There were 40 additional cases per 100 attendees among goat-stew eaters compared with non-eaters.


5. Odds ratio
\[
OR = \frac{54\times72}{36\times18}=6.0
\]
The odds of illness among goat-stew eaters were six times the odds among non-eaters.
Notice that the OR of 6 is much larger than the RR of 3 because the outcome is common.


6. Attributable proportion among the exposed
\[
AP_E = \frac{0.60-0.20}{0.60}\times100 = 66.7\%
\]
If the relationship is truly causal and alternative explanations are adequately addressed, approximately two-thirds of illness among exposed attendees could be attributed to the exposure.


What could fool us?
Even a dramatic table does not settle every question. Ask:

Was exposure recalled accurately?
Were all attendees identified?
Were cases defined consistently?
Did goat-stew eaters also share another exposure?
Could selection into the analysis differ by illness status?
Is the timing compatible with the suspected food vehicle?

This is exactly why evidence is never the whole story.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

1. Which value is the null for a risk ratio?
A. 0
B. 1
C. 50
D. 100
Answer: B. A ratio of 1 means the two risks are equal.


2. Which value is the null for a risk difference?
A. 0
B. 1
C. −1
D. 100
Answer: A. A difference of zero means no absolute difference between the groups.


3. Risk is 30% in the exposed group and 10% in the unexposed group. What is the RR?
A. 0.20
B. 2.0
C. 3.0
D. 20
Answer: C. 0.30 / 0.10 = 3.0.


4. Using the same data, what is the risk difference?
A. 3 percentage points
B. 10 percentage points
C. 20 percentage points
D. 30 percentage points
Answer: C. 30% − 10% = 20 percentage points.


5. Which measure is most natural in a typical case-control study?
A. Incidence proportion
B. Risk ratio
C. Odds ratio
D. Point prevalence
Answer: C. The investigator determines the number of cases and controls, so population risks usually cannot be reconstructed directly.


6. Why should an OR of 4.0 not automatically be described as “four times the risk”?
A. Odds and risk are different quantities.
B. OR can never exceed 1.
C. Risk has no denominator.
D. OR is a difference measure.
Answer: A. The odds ratio compares odds, not risks.


7. In a cross-sectional survey, hypertension prevalence is 36% in Group A and 18% in Group B. What is the prevalence ratio?
A. 0.5
B. 1.0
C. 2.0
D. 18
Answer: C. 0.36 / 0.18 = 2.0.


8. A vaccine study gives RR = 0.25 for vaccinated versus unvaccinated participants. What is the corresponding relative vaccine efficacy/effectiveness?
A. 25%
B. 50%
C. 75%
D. 125%
Answer: C. (1 − 0.25) × 100 = 75%.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
Measures of Association and Effect
text:
WEEK 3 SUMMARY
The central sequence is:
Measure each group → compare the groups → choose relative and/or absolute expression → interpret in the language of the measure → check whether the design supports the claim.
Remember:
RR compares risks.
Rate ratio compares incidence rates.
OR compares odds.
PR compares prevalences.
Risk difference expresses absolute difference in risk.
Attributable proportion expresses the proportion of disease among exposed people attributable to the exposure under causal assumptions.
VE/effectiveness expresses relative reduction in disease among vaccinated people.
The measure is not the conclusion. It is one part of the evidence.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
Source and adaptation note
This week is primarily adapted from the attached CDC Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Lesson Three, especially its sections on measures of association and public-health impact (risk ratio, rate ratio, odds ratio, attributable proportion and vaccine efficacy/effectiveness).
The prevalence ratio section and the broader teaching emphasis on reporting relative and absolute measures together are LIPPS extensions included to support the 12-week course structure. They are not presented as content extracted from the attached CDC lesson.
All fictional examples and Moodle questions created for LIPPS are original teaching material unless explicitly described as source examples.

title: Assessment Model
text: LIPPS uses objective assessment because it can provide rapid, consistent marking at scale. The quality of the assessment therefore depends on what the questions require the learner to do.

title: Assessment Model
text:
Question design principles

Application before recall. Most questions use a short scenario, output, graph, table or decision problem.
One defensible best answer. Distractors should represent plausible misconceptions rather than tricks.
Large item banks. Quizzes sample from topic-specific banks rather than presenting the same fixed paper to every learner.
Randomisation where appropriate. Question order, options and parameterised calculations may vary.
Time discipline, not speed for its own sake. Timing should make extensive external searching inefficient while still allowing a prepared learner to read and reason.
Accessible assessment. Copy/paste and ordinary browser functions remain available; approved accommodations can extend time for an individual without changing the learning objectives.
Explanatory feedback. Practice items explain why an answer is correct and why common alternatives are not.
Item QA. Items should be reviewed for ambiguity, difficulty, distractor performance and discrimination as sufficient response data accumulate.

title: Assessment Model
text:
Timing principle
LIPPS does not use one universal seconds-per-question rule. Timing is piloted against the actual items.
A starting weekly mastery format may use 15–20 objective items in approximately 10–15 minutes, then be adjusted using observed completion times and item difficulty. Calculation-heavy assessments require more time than recognition and interpretation items.

Design objective
The prepared learner should have enough time. The unprepared learner should not gain an advantage from spending the assessment searching externally for every answer.

title: Assessment Model
section: Objective quizzes are not the whole course assessment
text:
Objective quizzes are not the whole course assessment
Objective quizzes are efficient for frequent checks of knowledge, interpretation and short decisions. They are not sufficient on their own for competencies that require producing or defending work.
For university pilots, LIPPS therefore pairs quizzes with authentic tasks such as study-design critiques, outbreak analyses, audience diagnoses, message pre-tests, risk-communication simulations and campaign plans.
See the proposed pilot assessment portfolios →

title: Assessment Model

title: Health Communication
text:
Course philosophy
LIPPS Health Communication is built around one principle:

Communication succeeds only when the intended audience can access it, interpret it, trust it and use it in a real decision.

The course therefore treats communication as a public-health intervention that must be diagnosed, designed, implemented and evaluated—not as the production of posters or social-media content.

title: Health Communication
section: By the end of the course, learners should be able to

title: Health Communication
text:
The 12-week course


01


Foundations of Health Communication


Explain health communication as a strategic public-health process that connects evidence, audiences, messages, channels, feedback and action.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



02


Communication and Behaviour-Change Theory


Use behavioural and communication theory to diagnose why a health behaviour occurs and to select plausible communication and non-communication responses.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



03


Audience Analysis, Culture and Health Literacy


Use formative audience insight, health-literacy principles and cultural context to design communication that people can access, understand and use.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



04


Interpersonal and Clinical Communication


Use patient-centred interpersonal communication to elicit concerns, explain information clearly, check understanding and support informed decisions.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



05


Community Engagement and Participatory Communication


Design community engagement as a two-way, accountable process that shares information, listens, adapts interventions and builds workable solutions with affected communities.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



06


Message Development and Pre-testing


Develop clear, actionable health messages from defined objectives and improve them through systematic pre-testing with intended audiences.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



07


Communication Channels and Media Strategy


Select and combine communication channels and messengers according to audience access, trust, objective, reach, frequency, interactivity, cost and decision timing.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



08


Digital Health and Social Media Communication


Design and evaluate digital health communication while accounting for platform dynamics, privacy, accessibility, digital exclusion and the difference between engagement metrics and health outcomes.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



09


Risk and Crisis Communication


Communicate rapidly and transparently during health threats while acknowledging uncertainty, supporting protective action, listening to affected communities and adapting as evidence changes.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



10


Misinformation, Disinformation and Infodemic Management


Identify harmful information problems, prioritise them by likely health impact and respond through listening, accurate communication, trusted messengers, community engagement and resilience-building.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



11


Communication Campaign Design and Evaluation


Design a coherent health communication campaign from problem diagnosis through objectives, strategy, implementation, monitoring and evaluation.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.



12


Ethics, Equity and the Future of Health Communication


Evaluate health communication for ethical integrity, equity, accessibility and responsible use of emerging technologies, then integrate the full course using the LIPPS SIGNAL framework.

Mastery: 10 timed scenario questions sampled from a curated 30-item bank.

title: Health Communication
text:
How every week works
ORIENT — begin with a realistic public-health communication problem.
LEARN — build concepts and decision frameworks.
APPLY — work through an integrated case.
PRACTISE — answer untimed reasoning questions with feedback in Moodle.
DEMONSTRATE — complete a short timed mastery quiz drawn from a larger question bank.
The weekly quizzes are designed to be AI-resilient rather than “AI-proof.” Scenario-based items, random banks, shuffled options and calibrated time limits make knowing the material the most efficient strategy while preserving normal accessibility and approved accommodations.
Read the LIPPS assessment model →

title: Health Communication
text:
Source backbone
The course draws on established health-communication and behavioural-science literature, with particular emphasis on the WHO Strategic Communications Framework, WHO Risk Communication and Community Engagement guidance and competency framework, WHO infodemic-management resources, behavioural theories commonly used in health promotion, and programme-planning principles from Making Health Communication Programs Work.
LIPPS adds original instructional syntheses, African public-health scenarios, structured decision problems and the LIPPS SIGNAL capstone framework.
Open the core reading list →

title: Health Communication
text:
Core readings and pilot status
The course is suitable for a university teaching pilot, but the current Moodle banks should not yet be used as a high-stakes examination bank. Many foundation items are useful for practice; mastery items must be separated, rewritten toward novel scenarios and then piloted.

text:
Course access
The public syllabus remains open. Lessons, quizzes, grades and learner progress are designed for LIPPS Learn on Moodle. title: Data Quality

Data Quality
Completeness, consistency, validity, uniqueness, timeliness, duplicates, impossible values, outliers, missingness, derived variables, data dictionaries, audit trails, reproducibility and version control.

Qualitative and Mixed Methods
Qualitative interviewing, focus groups, observation, sampling, information power, coding, thematic analysis, framework analysis, reflexivity, triangulation and mixed-method integration.

title: Statistical Analysis Strategies
text:
LIPPS organises statistical methods around the question and outcome, not around a disconnected list of tests.


Frequencies, proportions, means, medians, rates, percentiles and standardisation.



Effect estimates, differences, confidence intervals and appropriate parametric or non-parametric comparisons.



Logistic, log-binomial and modified Poisson approaches; odds ratios, risk ratios, prevalence ratios and predicted probabilities.



Poisson and negative-binomial models, offsets, rate ratios and overdispersion.



Linear models, transformations, residual diagnostics and robust alternatives.



Kaplan-Meier estimation, log-rank comparisons, Cox regression, proportional hazards and competing risks.



GEE, multilevel models, mixed models, random effects and intra-cluster correlation.



Repeated measures, time series, spatial analysis, Bayesian analysis, missing-data methods and small-sample approaches.

title: Sampling
text:
Sampling determines who or what can enter the evidence and how uncertainty should later be estimated.


Simple random sampling, systematic sampling, stratified sampling, cluster sampling, multistage sampling and probability proportional to size.



Purposive sampling, convenience sampling, snowball sampling, respondent-driven sampling and time-location sampling.



LIPPS will provide separate guidance for prevalence estimation, means, two-group comparisons, cohort and case-control studies, diagnostic studies, cluster surveys, survival studies, regression and finite populations.

title: LIPPS Epidemiology Week 3 — QA
LIPPS Epidemiology Week 3 — QA
text: Week 3 focuses on comparing disease occurrence between groups and interpreting measures of association/effect. It follows Week 2’s frequency measures and precedes Week 4’s descriptive epidemiology.

title: LIPPS Epidemiology Week 3 — QA
LIPPS Epidemiology Week 3 — QA
LIPPS Epidemiology Week 3 — QA
text:
Progression: comparison → 2×2 table → RR → absolute difference → rate ratio → odds → OR → OR vs RR → prevalence ratio extension → attributable proportion → vaccine efficacy/effectiveness → uncertainty and causal restraint.
Worked example uses one fictional outbreak table to calculate risk, RR, RD, OR and attributable proportion.
The lesson repeatedly distinguishes risk, rate, odds and prevalence language.
Relative and absolute effects are taught together to reduce exaggerated interpretation of ratios.
Causal claims are explicitly separated from numerical association.
No detailed regression modelling is introduced; that belongs in the Methods library and later applied material.

title: LIPPS GitHub setup — v2.2
text:
GitHub account / owner: carepointpro-Lipps
Repository: lipps
Default branch: main
Repository URL: https://github.com/carepointpro-Lipps/Lipps
Git remote: https://github.com/carepointpro-Lipps/Lipps.git

The production LIPPS domain is intentionally not hard-coded yet.



Keep the repository private while configuration and authentication are being tested. Public visibility can be enabled later if GitHub Pages or open-source access is desired.



After creating an empty lipps repository on GitHub, open a terminal in the extracted LIPPS folder and run:
git init
git branch -M main
git config user.email "YOUR_GIT_COMMIT_EMAIL"
git config user.name "carepointpro-Lipps"
git add .
git commit -m "Initial LIPPS v2.2"
git remote add origin https://github.com/carepointpro-Lipps/Lipps.git
git push -u origin main
If the folder is already a Git repository, do not run git init again. Check the existing remote with:
git remote -v
If origin exists but points somewhere else:
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/carepointpro-Lipps/Lipps.git



admin/config.yml is already pointed at:
backend:
  name: github
  repo: carepointpro-Lipps/Lipps
  branch: main
The remaining one-time requirement is authentication. The CMS can use either a repository-scoped GitHub token for a single-admin pilot or a GitHub OAuth flow for a cleaner production sign-in. Do not commit tokens, passwords, OAuth client secrets, or other credentials to this repository.



The workflow at .github/workflows/publish.yml renders the Quarto project and publishes it when changes reach main.
Before first production deployment:

confirm GitHub Actions is enabled;
confirm the workflow has the permissions needed for the chosen Pages deployment method;
test quarto render locally or in Actions;
select the public domain;
add the domain to Quarto and the Admin CMS;
connect the final Moodle URL to the LIPPS Learn navigation item.




The GitHub account email is intentionally not stored in this repository. Git commit email is configured locally on the computer doing the commit. If email privacy matters, use the GitHub-provided private commit email rather than exposing the account email in public commit metadata. Never put passwords, GitHub tokens, Moodle passwords, API keys, or OAuth secrets in .qmd, committed YAML, or public website files. Use GitHub Secrets or the authentication provider’s secret store.
